summary

Semiconductors are in an AI-driven supercycle: third-quarter 2026 global sales were $517.7 billion, up 24.1% on the prior quarter, and WSTS implies a 2026 market of about $1,655 billion, up roughly 108%. Guidance from Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and AMD points higher still, while the S&P 500 trades at 19.0 times forward earnings. Strength is narrow: memory and AI accelerators dominate, analog is recovering and U.S. solar is cutting guidance. Export controls and AI budget durability are the key risks; we could not source a sector forward multiple.
basics.intro

Semiconductor companies design or make the chips that compute, store, move and convert information in almost every electronic device, from AI data centres to cars and phones. Some only design chips and pay others to make them (fabless), some only manufacture for others (foundries), and some do both. GICS also puts solar cell and module makers here, because a solar cell is a semiconductor device. The companies that sell chipmaking machines and materials sit next door, in Semiconductor Materials & Equipment.
basics.products.0

Processors and AI accelerators: Logic chips that run calculations: CPUs for general computing, GPUs and custom accelerators that run many calculations in parallel to train and serve AI models. e.g. Nvidia data-centre GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs, Broadcom custom AI chips
basics.products.1

Memory: Chips that hold data. DRAM is fast working memory, HBM is DRAM stacked beside an AI accelerator for very high bandwidth, and NAND flash keeps data when the power is off. e.g. Micron DRAM, HBM and NAND
basics.products.2

Analog and power chips: Chips that handle real-world signals such as voltage, sound and temperature, and manage power in everything from factory equipment to cars. Products last for years, so sales are steadier than in logic or memory. e.g. Texas Instruments power management and signal-chain chips, Analog Devices
basics.products.3

Networking and connectivity: Chips that move data: switches and routers inside data centres, network cards, and Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and cellular chips in devices. e.g. Broadcom Tomahawk switch chips, Qualcomm modems
basics.products.4
Microcontrollers and embedded chips: Small, cheap computers-on-a-chip that control cars, appliances, meters and industrial machines. e.g. Microchip, NXP, Texas Instruments
basics.products.5

Foundry and manufacturing services: Making chips to other companies' designs. Leading-edge manufacturing is concentrated in very few firms. e.g. TSMC (not in the S&P 500), Intel Foundry, GlobalFoundries
basics.products.6
Solar cells and modules: Semiconductor panels that turn sunlight into electricity, sold to utilities and developers of solar farms. e.g. First Solar thin-film modules
basics.drivers.0

Data-centre and AI spending: The capital budgets of the big cloud and AI companies set demand for accelerators, networking chips and HBM. When they raise spending plans, orders for these products rise within quarters.
basics.drivers.1

End-market cycles: PCs, smartphones, cars and industrial equipment each have their own cycle. Analog and microcontroller makers depend more on cars and factories; memory makers more on phones, PCs and servers.
basics.drivers.2

The inventory cycle: In shortages customers order more than they need; afterwards they stop ordering while they work the stock down. Chip revenue therefore swings more sharply than demand for the end products.
basics.drivers.3

Memory supply and pricing: Memory is close to a commodity made by a handful of producers (Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron lead). Prices rise when they hold back new capacity and fall when they overbuild, and those prices drive memory makers' profits.
basics.drivers.4

Manufacturing technology and capacity: Leading-edge nodes and advanced packaging capacity decide who can ship the fastest chips and how many. A lead lets a company charge more; a shortfall caps revenue whatever the demand.
basics.drivers.5

Trade policy and subsidies: Export controls can cut off sales to China, tariffs change costs, and subsidies such as the U.S. CHIPS Act pay for new fabs. All of these move revenue and capital spending.
basics.drivers.6
Solar policy and panel prices: For solar makers, tax credits, tariffs on imported panels and global panel prices decide how profitable U.S. production is.
basics.terms.0
Fabless: A chip company that designs chips but outsources manufacturing to a foundry. It needs far less capital, but depends on the foundry's capacity.
basics.terms.1
Foundry: A manufacturer that makes chips designed by other companies.
basics.terms.2

IDM (integrated device manufacturer): A company that designs and makes its own chips in its own factories, such as Intel, Texas Instruments or Micron. Its costs are more fixed, so profits swing more with utilisation.
basics.terms.3
Wafer and fab: A wafer is the thin silicon disc on which hundreds of chips are made at once. A fab is the factory, which can cost many billions of dollars to build.
basics.terms.4

Process node: The name of a manufacturing generation, such as 3 nm. A newer node packs in more transistors for faster, more efficient chips. The number is now a label rather than a physical measurement.
basics.terms.5
Yield: The share of chips on a wafer that work. Higher yields mean lower cost per chip, which is why new nodes start expensive and get cheaper.
basics.terms.6
Utilisation: How much of a fab's capacity is running. Because most fab costs are fixed, gross margins rise and fall with it.
basics.terms.7
Advanced packaging: Joining several chips, such as a GPU and its HBM stacks, into one package. It is now a bottleneck for AI accelerator supply.
basics.terms.8
HBM (high-bandwidth memory): Stacks of DRAM placed right next to a processor so data moves very fast. Every leading AI accelerator uses it, and it sells at a premium to ordinary DRAM.
basics.terms.9
Design win: When a customer chooses a chip for a product it is building. Revenue follows a year or more later, so design wins are a leading indicator.
basics.terms.10
Book-to-bill: New orders divided by shipments in a period. Above 1 means orders are running ahead of sales.
basics.terms.11
Inventory days: How many days of sales a company, or the distributors selling its chips, hold in stock. A rising number often comes before price cuts and a downturn.
basics.terms.12
ASP (average selling price): Revenue divided by units sold. In memory, ASPs move with supply and demand and drive most of the profit swing.
basics.terms.13
Export controls: Government licensing rules that limit selling advanced chips, or the tools to make them, to certain countries, chiefly China.
watch.0
Whether hyperscaler and AI-lab spending keeps pace with Nvidia's roughly 70% fiscal 2028 growth outlook, which management called supply-constrained.
watch.1
Memory pricing and supply: Micron says 2027 supply is largely committed and tight through fiscal 2028, so any easing would hit margins.
watch.2
U.S. export-control changes for China-bound accelerators, since Nvidia's guidance assumes zero China data center compute revenue.
watch.3
U.S. solar policy, including Section 232 and tax credits, after First Solar cut 2026 sales guidance to $4.6 billion to $4.9 billion.
watch.4
Broadcom's next report, with fiscal Q4 AI semiconductor revenue guided to $21.7 billion.
bellwethers
Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, Micron, Texas Instruments, First Solar
fund.business.0

Revenue comes mainly from selling chips by the unit: AI accelerators and processors, memory, analog and power chips, networking chips and microcontrollers. Some firms add software, licensing and complete systems, as Nvidia does with AI server racks and networking. Solar makers sell modules by the watt. Earnings swing most with volume and, in memory, with price.
fund.business.1

Customers are other manufacturers, not consumers: cloud and AI companies buying accelerators and memory for data centres, PC and phone makers, carmakers and their suppliers, industrial equipment makers, and distributors that resell to thousands of smaller buyers. Concentration varies: AI chip vendors depend on a few hyperscalers, while analog makers such as Texas Instruments sell to a very broad base.
fund.business.2

Research and development is the largest controllable cost, at 15.36% of sales for U.S. chip firms in Damodaran's January 2026 data. Manufacturers carry heavy fixed costs in fabs (depreciation, power, chemicals, staff), while fabless designers pay foundries per wafer and buy packaging and test services. For AI accelerators, HBM memory is now a major input cost.
fund.business.3

Pricing power comes from performance rivals can't match, a software ecosystem customers have built on (Nvidia's CUDA is the classic case), long design cycles that lock a chip into a product for years, and tight supply. Memory has the least, because prices follow the supply-demand balance, which is why Micron could push through significant HBM price increases in a shortage.
fund.business.4

Manufacturers' main assets are fabs and equipment, plus inventory, which can be written down in a downturn. Fabless firms' main assets are intellectual property, engineering teams and often large goodwill from acquisitions, as at Broadcom. Liabilities are usually modest: market debt is only about 2.5% of capital for U.S. chip firms. Customer prepayments and supply agreements can be large in shortages.
fund.business.5

It depends on the model. Integrated manufacturers and memory makers are among the most capital-intensive businesses anywhere: Micron planned about $25 billion of capex in half a year. Fabless firms are asset-light: Broadcom spent about $0.5 billion of capex on $29.6 billion of revenue. Across U.S. chip firms net capex was 4.41% of sales, an average that hides the split.
fund.overview.0

WSTS figures imply a 2026 global chip market of about $1,655 billion, roughly double the year before. That follows a long period of far slower growth: U.S. chip firms grew revenue at 11.18% a year over the five years to January 2026. The 2026 jump is mostly memory prices and AI accelerators, so we would not extrapolate it.
fund.overview.1

WSTS splits the market into logic (processors, accelerators, custom chips), memory (DRAM and NAND), analog, microcontrollers and microprocessors, discretes, sensors and optoelectronics. Logic and memory are the largest, and memory is the most volatile: it grew about 305% year on year in the first half of 2026. Solar modules are a separate market that GICS happens to place here.
fund.overview.2

Chips sit in the middle of the electronics chain. Upstream are chip-design software and IP vendors, equipment makers such as ASML and Applied Materials, and suppliers of wafers, gases and chemicals. Then come chip designers, foundries, and packaging and test houses. Downstream, chips go into servers, phones, PCs, cars and machines built by companies in other sub-industries.
fund.overview.3

The industry began with integrated firms that designed and made their own chips. From the late 1980s the foundry model, led by TSMC, let fabless designers such as Nvidia, Qualcomm and Broadcom compete without fabs, and leading-edge manufacturing narrowed to a few firms as each new node grew costlier. Demand moved from PCs to phones, then to cloud data centres, and now to AI.
fund.overview.4

Design is concentrated in the U.S., home to most of the largest designers. Manufacturing is concentrated in Asia: leading-edge logic largely in Taiwan, memory in South Korea, plus Japan and China, with assembly and test across Southeast Asia. In 2026 sales growth has been strongest in the Americas, up 191.7% year on year in September, reflecting AI data-centre buying.
fund.competition.0

Few in each segment. Leading-edge foundry has one dominant player plus Samsung and Intel; DRAM has three main producers; AI accelerators are led by Nvidia, followed by AMD and custom chips designed with partners such as Broadcom. Analog, power and microcontrollers are wider, each with perhaps a dozen sizeable firms.
fund.competition.1

Nvidia leads AI accelerators, with data-centre revenue of $89.0 billion in one quarter. Broadcom leads custom AI chips and networking, with AI revenue of $16.7 billion in a quarter. AMD is strong in server CPUs and is the second GPU supplier. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron lead memory, Texas Instruments and Analog Devices lead analog, and TSMC leads foundry. We found no sourced market-share table.
fund.competition.2

Consolidated at the top and getting more so. Decades of mergers (Broadcom itself is the product of several large ones) and rising costs at each node have left a few winners in most segments. Analog and microcontrollers remain moderately fragmented, with many niche products.
fund.competition.3

Very high. A leading-edge fab costs many billions of dollars and takes years to build. A leading chip design needs large R&D budgets, scarce engineers, patents and, for processors, a software ecosystem. Micron's roughly $25 billion half-year capex shows the scale even for an incumbent. In cars and industry, qualification takes years before a newcomer earns revenue.
fund.competition.4

Large. R&D and fab costs are mostly fixed, so the firm that sells the most units of a design, or runs its fab fullest, has the lowest cost per chip and can fund the next generation. That is why profits concentrate in the leader of each segment, and why operating leverage is high: AMD's revenue rose 45% in Q3 2026 at a 56% non-GAAP gross margin.
fund.competition.5

Both. Memory, discretes and older-node chips are close to commodities, sold on price and specification. Leading AI accelerators, high-end processors and many analog parts are highly differentiated, which shows in gross margins: Nvidia guided about 74%, against an average of 58.97% for U.S. chip firms in January 2026.
fund.competition.6

It depends where you stand. Key suppliers hold power over chip designers, since there are few alternatives to TSMC at the leading edge or to ASML's lithography tools. In AI, a handful of hyperscale buyers have growing power and are designing their own chips to gain more. In today's shortage sellers have the upper hand, as Micron's committed 2027 supply and higher HBM prices show.
fund.drivers.0

Unit demand in the end markets (data centres, phones, PCs, cars, industry), chip content per device, which rises as products get smarter, and pricing, especially in memory. In 2026 AI data-centre spending is the dominant driver: Nvidia's preliminary outlook for fiscal 2028 is about 70% growth.
fund.drivers.1

Product mix and differentiation, fab utilisation for manufacturers (fixed costs spread over more or fewer wafers), memory prices, and yields on new processes. Pre-tax operating margins averaged 35.33% for U.S. chip firms in January 2026, but they swing widely through the cycle.
fund.drivers.2

Research and development (about 15% of sales), wafer prices charged by foundries, fab depreciation, HBM and other memory bought for accelerators, packaging and substrates, energy, and engineers' pay, much of it in stock.
fund.drivers.3

Low on the business, high on the shares. Most chip firms carry little debt, so higher rates barely raise their costs. But customers' capital budgets, consumer credit for devices and the valuation of fast-growing chip stocks are all rate-sensitive, and fab-building plans depend on the cost of capital and subsidies.
fund.drivers.4

Sensitive to GDP and jobs through consumer electronics, cars and industrial equipment, which still drive analog, microcontroller and much memory demand. Inflation raises wafer, energy and labour costs, though strong pricing has usually offset it. Commodity exposure is limited to energy, metals and specialty gases. In 2026 AI spending has swamped all of these.
fund.drivers.5

Cyclical around a secular-growth trend. Revenue has historically fallen sharply every few years on inventory gluts and then recovered, around a long-run line driven by digitisation; U.S. chip firms grew revenue 11.18% a year over five years. AI has added a strong secular leg, but memory and older-node segments remain deeply cyclical.
fund.financials.0

Over the five years to January 2026, U.S. chip firms grew revenue and net income at about 11% a year (11.18% and 11.19%), and analysts expected 22.88% annual EPS growth over the next five years. 2026 results have run far ahead of that, with Nvidia's revenue up 106% and Micron at record revenue.
fund.financials.1

Gross margins averaged 58.97% and pre-tax operating margins 35.33% for 66 U.S. chip firms in January 2026, against 37.76% and 12.82% for the whole market. Leaders run higher: Texas Instruments earned about a 64.2% gross margin and a 47.5% operating margin in Q3 2026.
fund.financials.2

Very high. Damodaran shows an unadjusted ROE of 31.36% and a return on capital of 41.83% for U.S. chip firms, against an ROE of 17.21% for the total market. Treating R&D as an investment lowers the ROE to 22.33%, still well above average.
fund.financials.3

Low. Market debt is only about 2.5% of capital for U.S. chip firms, against about 26% for the market as a whole. Debt on balance sheets mostly comes from acquisitions, as at Broadcom, or from building fabs, as at Intel and Micron; many fabless designers hold net cash.
fund.financials.4

Strong for fabless and analog leaders. Broadcom turned 46% of revenue into free cash flow in its latest quarter, and Texas Instruments generated $8.4 billion over twelve months after $2.6 billion of capex. Memory makers' free cash flow swings from large to thin across the cycle because their capex stays high.
fund.financials.5

Across U.S. chip firms net capex was 4.41% of sales and capex ran at 126.73% of depreciation, so the asset base is growing. That average blends asset-light designers with manufacturers that spend far more heavily, such as Micron.
fund.financials.6

At a premium. Firms with positive EBITDA traded at 34.75 times EV/EBITDA in January 2026, against 19.73 times for the total market. The iShares Semiconductor ETF showed a P/E of 42.73 on 4 November 2026, basis not stated. Multiples look high on peak-cycle earnings and are best judged across a full cycle.
fund.risks.0

Export controls matter most: U.S. rules decide which accelerators can be sold to China and on what conditions, and Nvidia's guidance assumes no China data-centre revenue. Subsidies such as the U.S. CHIPS Act and similar European and Asian programmes, tariffs, and for solar the Section 232 action and tax credits also reshape where and how profitably chips are made.
fund.risks.1

AI is mostly an opportunity, as the main source of demand growth. The risks are architectural: customers' own custom chips could take share from merchant GPUs, new memory or packaging technologies could reshuffle the leaders, and the end of easy transistor scaling raises the cost of each new node. A leader that misses a product generation can lose share fast.
fund.risks.2

They barely matter directly. Ageing populations and a growing middle class in emerging markets shift which electronics get bought, such as medical devices and phones. The bigger demographic issue is on the supply side: a shortage of skilled engineers and fab technicians in the U.S. and Europe could slow new fabs.
fund.risks.3

It matters through device cycles. Consumers keeping phones and PCs longer reduces demand for those chips, while AI features could shorten replacement cycles again. The electrification of cars raises chip content per vehicle, a steady tailwind for analog and power chipmakers.
fund.risks.4

The largest new competitors are the customers: cloud giants designing their own AI chips, usually with partners such as Broadcom. State-backed Chinese chipmakers are building capacity in older nodes, which could pressure prices in commoditised segments. Open instruction sets such as RISC-V lower the barrier for new processor designers.
fund.risks.5

The concentration of leading-edge manufacturing in Taiwan is the industry's largest single tail risk: a blockade or conflict would disrupt supply worldwide. U.S.-China tensions affect sales, access to equipment and materials such as gallium and germanium, where China has restricted exports. Companies are spending to diversify their fabs, at higher cost.
fund.risks.6

There is no substitute for semiconductors themselves; the competition is between chip types. Custom accelerators substitute for GPUs, new memory types for DRAM or NAND, and photonics for some electrical links. In solar, crystalline-silicon modules compete with First Solar's thin film, and perovskite cells may in future.
horizon.opportunities.0
The AI data-centre build-out keeps lifting demand for accelerators, networking and HBM, and Nvidia already calls its next-year outlook supply-constrained.
horizon.opportunities.1
Electrification and automation raise chip content in cars, factories and the power grid, a steadier source of growth for analog and power chips.
horizon.opportunities.2
Re-shoring subsidies and customers' demand for secure supply could fund new fabs outside Asia and lock in long-term contracts.
horizon.threats.0
A pause in hyperscaler spending would hit memory and AI accelerators first, from margins that look like cyclical peaks.
horizon.threats.1
Tighter export controls or a Taiwan crisis could cut off markets or supply almost overnight.
horizon.threats.2
Customers' in-house chips and new Chinese capacity in older nodes could erode pricing power outside the leaders.
horizon.assessment

Our view is that AI has added a genuine secular leg to an industry that remains cyclical. Over 3 to 5 years the winners are likely to be the few firms that control leading-edge designs, software ecosystems or scarce capacity, while memory and commoditised segments go through the usual boom and bust. The 2026 surge, which WSTS figures put at roughly double the prior year's revenue, sets a very high base. The key question is whether AI spending keeps compounding or pauses to digest, and the biggest threats are policy and geopolitics rather than end demand.
sec.macro.0

Semiconductors are in the steepest upswing in the industry's history, and it is driven more by an AI capital-spending cycle than by the usual consumer and inventory rhythm. The Semiconductor Industry Association reported on 3 Nov 2026 that third-quarter global sales reached $517.7 billion, up 24.1% from the second quarter, with September sales of $172.6 billion up 146.8% from a year earlier (three-month moving averages compiled by WSTS). Growth was strongest in the Americas, at 191.7% year on year, but every region was up by more than 70%. WSTS said first-half 2026 sales were $702 billion, up 102%, led by memory (up 305%) and logic (up 45%).
sec.macro.1

Interest rates and the broader economy matter less than customer budgets here. The wider market is not expensive: FactSet put the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 19.0 on 30 Sep 2026, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and down from 20.4 at the end of June. We think that gap between a cheap-looking index and a surging chip group points to a cycle that is concentrated in AI infrastructure rather than broad. Our read is that the risk is not a macro recession tipping demand over, but a pause in hyperscaler spending, which would hit memory and AI accelerators first. We did not find a sourced reading of central-bank policy rates or currency effects for this brief, so we do not quantify them.
sec.demand.0

WSTS's spring forecast, as updated in August, implies a 2026 market of about $1,655 billion, roughly 108% growth, and about $2.1 trillion in 2027, roughly 29% growth. WSTS stresses that these are not new forecasts, only the spring scenario with second-quarter actuals substituted. Memory is the swing factor, with 2026 growth of about 302% in that update. These numbers are extraordinary against any history, and we would treat them as a snapshot of a supply-constrained pricing boom as much as a volume boom.
sec.demand.1

Company commentary supports the structural story. Nvidia reported fiscal Q2 2027 revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106%, with data center at $89.0 billion, and guided Q3 to $108.0 billion plus or minus 2%. Its CFO called a preliminary fiscal 2028 growth outlook of about 70% supply-constrained. Micron said memory and storage supply and demand would be much tighter in fiscal 2027 and 2028 than in fiscal 2026, expected DRAM bit shipments to grow in the low-20% range and NAND in the mid-20% range in calendar 2027 and 2028, and said more than 75% of its 2027 output is already committed.
sec.demand.2

Chips are historically cyclical, and demand is not very price elastic in the short run for AI accelerators but is highly so for consumer devices. AMD's client and gaming revenue fell 8% year on year in Q3 while data center rose 97%, a split that shows how uneven demand is. Long-term demand prospects rest on whether AI customers keep investing; this brief did not find a reliable independent forecast of that spending.
sec.structure.0

Industry structure differs sharply by segment, so we describe Porter's five forces at the level of AI compute and memory. Rivalry is intense but among few players: Nvidia, AMD and custom-silicon partner Broadcom in accelerators, and a handful of memory makers. Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue was $16.7 billion in the quarter ended 2 Aug 2026, up 221%, and is guided to $21.7 billion next quarter. AMD's data center segment reached $8.5 billion, up 97%, on EPYC and the launch of Instinct MI450.
sec.structure.1

Barriers to entry are very high: leading-edge design requires large R&D budgets and ecosystems, and manufacturing needs huge capital. Micron's capex plan of about $25 billion in the first half of fiscal 2027 illustrates the scale needed even for one memory maker. Supplier power sits with foundries and equipment makers, which we did not quantify with sourced figures, and Nvidia is working with Micron on a custom HBM4E product, showing how tightly suppliers and customers are tied. Buyer power is concentrated in a few hyperscalers and AI labs; Broadcom's fortunes rest on a small number of such customers, which we infer from its AI revenue scale rather than from a disclosed customer list.
sec.structure.2

Pricing power is currently strong. Micron has agreed most of its calendar 2027 high-bandwidth memory volume with significant price increases, and Nvidia guided a gross margin of about 74%. The threat of substitutes is custom chips versus merchant GPUs. Market-share tables by segment were not found in the sources opened.
sec.environment.0

Regulation is the largest swing factor for the largest companies. On 15 Jan 2026 the Bureau of Industry and Security moved license review for exports of Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X-class chips to China from presumption of denial to case-by-case, subject to conditions: China shipments capped at 50% of volumes for U.S. end use, third-party lab testing, and Know Your Customer rules to prevent unauthorized remote access. Nvidia's August guidance for Q3 assumes zero China data center compute revenue, so any China sales would be upside. We did not find a verified October 2026 export-control update, so this brief does not describe one.
sec.environment.1

Industrial policy also reshapes the solar-cell and module makers GICS places in this sub-industry. First Solar's CEO called Section 232 action a structural change in how the United States approaches solar manufacturing, and its guidance flags risk from tariffs, export controls, other trade remedies and the Inflation Reduction Act as amended in 2025, including Section 45X credits. The company assumes the current policy environment persists.
sec.environment.2

Technology risk comes from the pace of AI architecture change and custom silicon. Nvidia and AMD ship new accelerator generations on roughly annual cadences, as AMD's MI450 launch shows. First Solar signed a perovskite patent licence, a reminder that solar technology also shifts. We view geopolitical supply disruption, especially around advanced fabrication in Asia, as a standing tail risk but did not find a figure to size it.
sec.economics.0

Semiconductor economics are unusually strong in this upcycle. Damodaran's January 2026 U.S. dataset, covering 66 semiconductor firms, shows an after-tax operating margin of 34.66% and a return on capital of 41.83%; the 31 equipment firms show 24.24% and 44.88%. Those are industry-wide figures from before the 2026 surge, and company data suggests they have since risen.
sec.economics.1

Texas Instruments, the analog bellwether, earned a gross margin of about 64.2% and an operating margin of about 47.5% in Q3 2026 (our calculations from its release), on revenue of $6.06 billion, up 28%. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow was $8.4 billion on capex of $2.6 billion. Broadcom generated $13.7 billion of free cash flow on $29.6 billion of revenue, 46% of revenue, with capex of only $0.5 billion. Micron reported an 87% gross margin in fiscal Q4 2026, on revenue of $54.2 billion. Nvidia reported a 75.0% gross margin.
sec.economics.2

Operating leverage is high: AMD's revenue rose 45% to $13.4 billion with non-GAAP gross margin of 56%. Capital intensity differs widely, from fabless Broadcom to memory makers spending about $25 billion in a half-year. First Solar shows the other side: Q3 sales fell 23% year on year, though it still earned about a 57.9% gross margin by our calculation from its release. Margins like these are cyclical peaks in our judgment, not a base case to extrapolate.
sec.earnings.0

Reported results and guidance have been far above prior expectations. Nvidia guided Q3 FY2027 revenue to $108.0 billion against a consensus near $104 billion, with a fiscal Q4 gross margin expected to trough at 71% to 72% on memory costs. Micron guided fiscal Q1 2027 to $61.5 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $38.15, which is the company's own guidance. Broadcom guided fiscal Q4 revenue to about $34.8 billion, up 93%. AMD guided Q4 to about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, implying roughly 66% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.
sec.earnings.1

Not everything is rising. TI guided Q4 revenue to $5.80 billion to $6.30 billion and EPS to $2.45 to $2.79, a wide range on a business where its CEO cited broad growth in industrial, automotive and data center. First Solar cut 2026 net sales guidance to $4.6 billion to $4.9 billion from $4.9 billion to $5.2 billion and module volume to 16 to 17 GW. FactSet said Information Technology was one of five sectors expected to post double-digit Q3 earnings growth, but its preview did not give the sector figure. We did not find a consensus 2027 EPS growth number for this sub-industry.
sec.earnings.2

Our view differs from the headline in one respect: the guidance numbers imply that much of the earnings power rests on memory pricing and a few AI customers, so revisions have been upward but are exposed to a change in either.
sec.valuation.0

Valuation is hard to state cleanly because sub-industry forward multiples were not available from the sources we opened. The iShares fund page showed the Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) at a P/E of 42.73 and a price-to-book of 9.13 as of 4 Nov 2026. BlackRock does not say on that page whether that P/E is trailing or forward, and trailing earnings in a year of rapid growth would overstate the multiple. For context, FactSet put the S&P 500 forward P/E at 19.0 at 30 Sep 2026, versus a 10-year average of 19.1.
sec.valuation.1

A sourced forward P/E for the group and its own history was not available to us, so we avoid stating one. What the reported company numbers do suggest is that expectations are very high. Nvidia is guiding to roughly 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, versus about 44% that analysts had modeled, according to a summary of its call, and Micron guided gross margin of 86.25% as its fiscal 2027 low point. A price that capitalizes numbers like these assumes memory pricing and AI budgets stay near current levels.
sec.valuation.2

Our read is that the group is priced for continuation of the cycle rather than for a normal mid-cycle; any normalization of memory margins or a slowdown in customer orders would compress earnings faster than the multiple. Free cash flow yields were not available in the sources opened, though the strong cash conversion at Broadcom and TI is noted above.
sec.positioning.0

Momentum has been exceptional. BlackRock's page showed the iShares Semiconductor ETF with a year-to-date NAV total return of 50.04% as of 4 Nov 2026, net assets of about $37.6 billion as of 5 Nov 2026, and an expense ratio of 0.33%. We did not find a sourced figure for the S&P 500 over the same period in the pages we opened, so we do not state relative performance. Other secondary reports gave different year-to-date numbers for the chip index, partly reflecting timing and the fund's share split, and we did not rely on them.
sec.positioning.1

Fundamental results support the trend: Q3 sales rose for a third straight quarter by more than 20% sequentially, in the words of SIA's president. Nvidia's shares reportedly fell about 4% after hours following its August results and then reversed to gain more than 4%, a sign of high expectations in the reaction.
sec.positioning.2

We did not find short-interest, institutional-flow or breadth data for this sub-industry in the sources opened. Leadership appears narrow, since the group's growth is concentrated in AI compute and memory while analog and solar are mixed, as TI and First Solar results show.
summary

Systems software is growing fast on AI-driven infrastructure and security demand, but financing and execution risk are rising. Gartner's October forecast has total software spending up 15.2% in 2026, and Microsoft's Azure grew 48% in the September quarter. Security and database vendors are guiding to rising revenue and strong margins. Oracle's $664 billion backlog came with negative free cash flow. The Fed held at 3-3/4 to 4 percent with two dissenters favouring a hike. IGV is up 5.34% year to date after a 41% rally from April, and we found no current sector forward multiple.
basics.intro

Systems software is the layer that runs, connects and protects computers, rather than software for a particular business task: operating systems, databases, cybersecurity, and the platforms and tools that run data centres and the cloud. Customers are mostly businesses and governments, and most revenue now comes from subscriptions or pay-as-you-go cloud services. GICS puts Microsoft and Oracle here, including their cloud businesses. Software for business tasks, such as accounting, sales or design, sits next door in Application Software.
basics.products.0

Operating systems and core platforms: The software that runs a PC or server and the platforms built around it, along with the productivity suites bundled with them. e.g. Microsoft Windows and Windows Server, Microsoft 365
basics.products.1

Databases and data platforms: Software that stores, organises and retrieves a company's data. Once the core systems are built on it, switching is slow and risky. e.g. Oracle Database, Microsoft SQL Server
basics.products.2

Cloud infrastructure and AI platforms: Computing power, storage and AI models rented over the internet and billed by usage, so customers don't need their own data centres. e.g. Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
basics.products.3

Network security: Firewalls and secure-access services that inspect traffic and block attacks at the edge of a company's network and in the cloud. Sold as hardware appliances and as subscriptions. e.g. Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, Check Point
basics.products.4

Endpoint, identity and cloud security: Software that protects laptops, servers and cloud workloads, controls who can log in to what, and helps security teams detect and respond to attacks. e.g. CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender and Entra
basics.products.5
Infrastructure and developer tools: Software for building, deploying, monitoring and managing applications and servers. e.g. Microsoft GitHub and Visual Studio
basics.drivers.0
Enterprise IT budgets: Companies spend more on software when profits and confidence are good. In slowdowns they delay new projects and trim seats, so new bookings slow before revenue does.
basics.drivers.1

Cloud migration and AI workloads: Moving systems to the cloud and running AI models raises usage of cloud infrastructure and databases. That lifts consumption revenue directly, but needs heavy data-centre spending first.
basics.drivers.2

The threat level in security: Major attacks, ransomware and new disclosure rules push security up boards' priority lists. Security budgets therefore hold up better than other IT spending in downturns.
basics.drivers.3
Pricing power and seat counts: Price rises and new tiers (for example AI add-ons) lift revenue per user. Fewer hires at customers, or AI agents replacing some users, can cut the number of seats.
basics.drivers.4
Interest rates: Much of a software company's value lies in profits expected years ahead, so higher long-term rates lower what investors will pay today, even if the business is unchanged.
basics.drivers.5

Capacity and financing of AI data centres: Cloud vendors can only book revenue once they have chips, power and buildings in place. Building that capacity takes heavy borrowing and spending, so free cash flow can fall even while revenue grows.
basics.terms.0
SaaS (software as a service): Software delivered over the internet for a recurring subscription fee, instead of a one-off licence. Revenue is more predictable, but it arrives over time.
basics.terms.1
Licence and maintenance: The older model: a one-off fee to install the software, then a yearly fee for support and updates. It still matters for databases and some security products.
basics.terms.2
ARR (annual recurring revenue): The yearly value of all subscriptions in force. Many companies use it as their main growth measure.
basics.terms.3

RPO (remaining performance obligations): Revenue already contracted but not yet recognised, effectively the backlog. Fast RPO growth points to future revenue, but very large multi-year deals can take years to convert.
basics.terms.4
Billings: Revenue plus the change in deferred revenue: roughly what customers were invoiced in the period. It shows demand earlier than revenue does.
basics.terms.5
Net revenue retention: This year's revenue from last year's customers divided by what they paid last year. Above 100% means existing customers are buying more.
basics.terms.6
Seat-based vs consumption pricing: Charging per user, or by how much computing, storage or data the customer uses. Consumption revenue grows faster in booms and slows faster when customers cut back.
basics.terms.7
Hyperscaler: One of the few giant cloud providers, such as Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud. They are both big customers of other vendors and competitors to them.
basics.terms.8
Platformisation: Persuading customers to buy several products from one vendor rather than the best tool for each job. It is the main competitive battle in security.
basics.terms.9
Gross margin: Revenue minus the direct cost of delivering it. Very high for pure software, because an extra copy costs almost nothing; lower for cloud, which needs data centres.
basics.terms.10
Rule of 40: Revenue growth rate plus free-cash-flow margin. Investors use 40% or more as a rough sign of a healthy software business.
basics.terms.11
Stock-based compensation: Paying employees in shares. It is a real cost to shareholders through dilution, but is usually left out of adjusted earnings, so compare both versions.
basics.terms.12
Capex intensity: Capital spending as a share of revenue. It was low for traditional software, but is now high for companies building AI data centres, which squeezes free cash flow.
watch.0
Whether Azure growth keeps accelerating after 48% in the September quarter.
watch.1
Fed path: two FOMC members already wanted a quarter-point hike on 28 Oct, and the next decision is the December meeting.
watch.2
Conversion of Oracle's $664 billion backlog while free cash flow is negative.
watch.3
Whether application-adjacent vendors keep growth: ServiceNow guides Q4 current RPO growth to 18.5% against 20.5% reported in Q3.
watch.4
Final publication of the EU AI Act Digital Omnibus delays for high-risk systems.
bellwethers
Microsoft, Oracle, Palo Alto Networks, CrowdStrike, Fortinet, Check Point
fund.business.0

Subscriptions are now the core: cloud services billed by usage, such as Azure and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure; software subscriptions per user or device, such as Microsoft 365 and security platforms; and, for older products, licences plus annual maintenance. Security vendors such as Fortinet also sell hardware appliances with service subscriptions attached. Consulting and support are a small share.
fund.business.1

Mainly businesses and governments of every size, from small firms buying Microsoft 365 to large enterprises running Oracle databases. AI labs and model developers are now large cloud customers. Consumers matter only at Microsoft, through Windows and personal subscriptions. Big deals are negotiated with IT and security leaders; smaller ones are sold online or through resellers.
fund.business.2

People are the main cost. Across U.S. system and application software firms, R&D ran at 15.98% of sales and selling, general and administrative costs at 24.38%, with stock-based compensation at 7.83%. Cloud vendors add data centres, chips and power, which show up in cost of revenue and capex.
fund.business.3

Switching costs are the root: moving a database, operating system or security stack is slow and risky, so renewals are sticky and price rises usually hold. Platform breadth, integration with what the customer already runs and a proven security record also matter. Basic cloud computing has less pricing power, though scarce AI capacity currently supports it.
fund.business.4

Assets are mostly intangible: code, customer relationships, brands and goodwill from acquisitions, plus cash. Cloud providers now also own large data centres and chip fleets. The distinctive liability is deferred revenue, cash collected in advance for subscriptions, which helps fund growth. Debt is modest overall, though Oracle is now spending more than its operating cash flow on cloud capacity.
fund.business.5

Traditionally asset-light, but no longer uniformly. Pure software firms spend little on capex, while Microsoft and Oracle are building AI data centres. Damodaran's data show net capex at 17.82% of sales for U.S. system and application software firms, with capex at 244.55% of depreciation, a sign of heavy infrastructure building at the largest players.
fund.overview.0

Gartner, as reported, puts worldwide software spending at $1,464 billion in 2026, up 15.2%, and $1,679 billion in 2027. That includes application software; we found no figure for systems software alone. U.S. system and application software firms grew revenue 19.56% a year over the five years to January 2026.
fund.overview.1

Operating systems and productivity platforms; databases and data management; cloud infrastructure and platform services; security software (network, endpoint, identity and cloud); and infrastructure management, observability and developer tools. Cloud infrastructure and security are the fastest-growing parts, as Azure's 48% growth and Palo Alto's 63% next-generation security ARR growth show.
fund.overview.2

Systems software sits between hardware and applications. It runs on chips, servers and storage made by other sub-industries, increasingly inside cloud data centres, and application software and companies' own systems run on top of it. Channel partners, consultants and IT services firms help sell, install and manage it.
fund.overview.3

The industry moved from mainframe software and packaged licences, through client-server computing and enterprise databases in the 1990s, to subscription software and public cloud from the 2010s. Security grew from antivirus into a broad platform as attacks multiplied. AI is the next shift, raising demand for cloud capacity and data platforms.
fund.overview.4

Sales are global but led by the U.S., which is also home to most large vendors. Europe is the second big market, and Israel is a major centre for security firms such as Check Point. China largely uses domestic alternatives. Development is spread across the U.S., India, Israel and Eastern Europe.
fund.competition.0

In each segment a handful of large players compete with many smaller specialists. Cloud infrastructure has three hyperscalers plus Oracle; PC operating systems are dominated by Windows, with Apple and open-source Linux; databases have a few large vendors plus open source; security has about a dozen sizeable platforms and hundreds of start-ups.
fund.competition.1

Microsoft is the largest, with Windows, Microsoft 365, Azure, SQL Server and a large security business; Azure alone had $33.2 billion of revenue in a quarter. Oracle leads enterprise databases and is growing cloud infrastructure fast. In security, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, CrowdStrike and Check Point lead. We found no sourced market-share table.
fund.competition.2

Consolidated at the top, fragmented in the long tail. A few platforms take most of the profit while hundreds of venture-backed firms compete in niches. The large firms often buy the successful ones, which keeps consolidating the industry, especially in security.
fund.competition.3

High for core platforms: decades of code, customer trust, certifications, ecosystems of partners and developers, and, in cloud, tens of billions of dollars of data centres. Barriers are lower in niche tools, where a good product can win quickly, though selling to large enterprises takes scale.
fund.competition.4

Very large. Writing software is costly but an extra copy costs almost nothing, so gross margins are high, 71.72% for U.S. system and application software in January 2026, and bigger vendors spread R&D and sales costs over more customers. In cloud, scale lowers the cost of buying chips, power and buildings.
fund.competition.5

Mostly differentiated, especially where switching costs are high. Basic cloud computing and storage are closer to commodities, sold partly on price, and open-source software caps what vendors can charge for some products. Security buyers are moving toward fewer, broader platforms, which rewards differentiation.
fund.competition.6

Vendors usually hold more power once installed, because switching is hard; large enterprises negotiate discounts but rarely leave. Supplier power is rising for cloud vendors, who depend on scarce GPUs and memory from a few chipmakers, and Gartner says hardware inflation will persist through 2027.
fund.drivers.0

Enterprise IT budgets, workloads moving to the cloud and AI, more users and devices, price increases and selling new products to existing customers. Security spending grows with the threat level. In 2026 AI is the biggest swing factor, visible in Azure's 48% growth and Oracle's backlog.
fund.drivers.1

Gross margin depends on the mix between pure software, which is very profitable, and cloud infrastructure, which carries data-centre costs. Operating margin depends on how fast a company spends on sales and R&D to grow. Mature leaders reach close to 40% non-GAAP operating margins, as Fortinet's 38.2% shows.
fund.drivers.2

Engineers' and salespeople's pay, including stock; data-centre depreciation; chips and power for cloud and AI; the cost of winning customers; and acquisitions. For AI-heavy vendors, GPU and memory prices and access to power are now key.
fund.drivers.3

Moderate on operations, high on valuation. Most software firms have little debt, but their value rests on cash flows far in the future, so higher long-term rates lower share prices. Rates also affect customers' budgets and the cost of financing AI data centres.
fund.drivers.4

Moderate. Subscriptions and switching costs keep revenue stable in mild downturns, but new deals and seat growth slow when unemployment rises, because many products are priced per employee. Inflation helps where price increases stick. Commodity exposure is limited to power and hardware costs for cloud vendors.
fund.drivers.5

Secular growth with mild cyclicality. Revenue rarely falls, and U.S. system and application software firms grew it 19.56% a year over five years, but growth rates and valuations swing with IT budgets and interest rates. Security is close to defensive; cloud infrastructure is more tied to capex cycles.
fund.financials.0

Fast. Damodaran's data show five-year compound growth of 19.56% in revenue and 29.81% in net income for U.S. system and application software firms to January 2026. FactSet's Software industry, which also includes application software, posted 19% revenue growth and 17% earnings growth in Q3 2026.
fund.financials.1

Gross margins averaged 71.72% and pre-tax operating margins 32.98% for U.S. system and application software firms, against 37.76% and 12.82% for the whole market. Leaders run higher: Microsoft's fiscal 2026 operating margin was about 46.8%. Stock-based pay of 7.83% of sales is left out of many adjusted margins.
fund.financials.2

High. Damodaran shows an unadjusted ROE of 29.62% for U.S. system and application software firms, against 17.21% for the total market; treating R&D as an investment lowers it to 20.21%. Buybacks that shrink book equity also flatter ROE. We found no sourced sub-industry ROIC.
fund.financials.3

Low to moderate. Market debt is about 5% of capital for the group, against about 26% for the market. Some leaders borrow for acquisitions or data centres, and Oracle's spending now outruns its operating cash flow, but many security firms hold net cash.
fund.financials.4

Usually strong, because customers pay upfront and capex is low: Fortinet's free-cash-flow margin was 41.6% in Q3 2026 and Palo Alto's adjusted free-cash-flow margin 38.4% for fiscal 2026. Cloud builders are the exception: Oracle's free cash flow was negative $5 billion in a quarter as it built capacity.
fund.financials.5

Low for pure software, very high for cloud builders. Across U.S. system and application software, net capex was 17.82% of sales and capex was about 2.4 times depreciation, figures driven by the big cloud platforms. Security and tools vendors spend far less.
fund.financials.6

Above the market. U.S. system and application software traded at 24.48 times EV/EBITDA for firms with positive EBITDA in January 2026, against 19.73 times for the total market. Fast-growing firms are often valued on revenue multiples or the Rule of 40, because their earnings are still small.
fund.risks.0

AI regulation, including the EU AI Act, whose high-risk deadlines have been provisionally delayed; data-protection and data-residency rules; cybersecurity disclosure requirements; and competition cases against bundling by large platforms. Government purchasing rules, such as security certifications, can open or close large markets.
fund.risks.1

AI is both the biggest opportunity and the biggest risk. It drives demand for cloud, databases and security, but AI agents could reduce the number of software seats customers need, and AI coding tools lower the cost of building rival products. The early-2026 software sell-off reflected this fear.
fund.risks.2

Limited. Ageing workforces and shortages of IT and security staff push companies to automate, which helps software vendors. A shrinking working-age population in some countries could eventually cap growth in products priced per user.
fund.risks.3

This is mostly a business market, so consumer behaviour matters mainly at Microsoft. More important is how business buyers are changing: they are consolidating vendors, preferring platforms to single products, and pushing for usage-based pricing that ties cost to value.
fund.risks.4

AI model companies are moving into software and infrastructure; hyperscalers bundle security and data tools into their clouds; and open-source projects compete with paid databases and operating systems. Business models are shifting from per-seat pricing toward consumption and outcome-based pricing.
fund.risks.5

Data-sovereignty rules in Europe and elsewhere favour local or locally hosted providers. U.S.-China tensions limit sales in China and constrain chip supply for AI data centres. State-sponsored cyberattacks raise demand for security, but also raise the stakes of a breach at a vendor.
fund.risks.6

Open-source software, in-house tools built with AI, and features bundled free inside larger platforms, for example security included with an operating system or a cloud. For cloud infrastructure, customers can run their own data centres, though few are moving that way.
horizon.opportunities.0
AI workloads should keep lifting demand for cloud infrastructure, databases and data platforms, as Azure's 48% growth shows.
horizon.opportunities.1
Rising attacks and regulation keep security a top budget priority, and platform consolidation favours the largest vendors.
horizon.opportunities.2
Huge contracted backlogs, such as Oracle's $664 billion, give unusual revenue visibility if they convert.
horizon.threats.0
AI agents and AI-built tools could shrink seat counts and lower barriers to entry.
horizon.threats.1
Financing and capacity strains could slow AI data-centre build-outs and backlog conversion; Oracle's free cash flow is already negative.
horizon.threats.2
Higher-for-longer interest rates would weigh on the valuations of long-duration software stocks.
horizon.assessment

We think systems software is better placed for AI than application software, because AI needs infrastructure, data and security whoever writes the applications. Over 3 to 5 years the leaders should keep growing faster than the economy, but the business is becoming more capital-intensive, which lowers free-cash-flow conversion and raises financial risk for the cloud builders. The main open question is whether AI reduces the number of paying users faster than it creates new spending.
sec.macro.0

The macro backdrop for systems software is strong demand colliding with tighter money. On 28 Oct 2026 the Federal Open Market Committee held the federal funds target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent by a 10-2 vote, with Governor Cook and Cleveland Fed President Hammack dissenting in favour of a quarter-point increase, and the statement opens its inflation passage with 'Inflation remains elevated'. We read that as a late-cycle setting in which the policy rate is not falling and the risk of further tightening is live, which matters because long-duration software equities are sensitive to discount rates.
sec.macro.1

Corporate budgets, however, have not tightened. Gartner's October 2026 forecast, as reported by TechIntelPro, puts worldwide IT spending at $6,391 billion in 2026 (up 14.5%) and $7,352 billion in 2027 (up 15.0%), with software at $1,464 billion in 2026 (up 15.2%) and $1,679 billion in 2027 (up 14.6%). The same table shows data center systems up 73.8% in 2026, so a large share of the increase is AI infrastructure rather than traditional licences. Gartner also warns that memory-driven hardware inflation will persist through 2027.
sec.macro.2

Profit growth in the wider market supports spending: FactSet says S&P 500 blended Q3 2026 earnings growth is 30.2% and analysts expect 32.9% for calendar 2026. The sources we opened did not give a systems-software-specific currency effect; Microsoft's non-GAAP EPS growth was 18% reported and 19% in constant currency, so the effect there was small.
sec.demand.0

Gartner's forecast is the best sizing we found. Total software spending is $1,464 billion in 2026, up 15.2%, and $1,679 billion in 2027, up 14.6%. That is a market growing more than three times as fast as the 4.4% Gartner shows for IT services in 2026. This is Gartner's broad software category, so it includes application software that sits outside the GICS Systems Software sub-industry; we found no Gartner figure that isolates systems software alone.
sec.demand.1

The structural drivers show up in company results. Microsoft's Azure revenue was $33.2 billion in the September 2026 quarter, up 48%, and Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, up 30%. Oracle reported total cloud revenue of $11.6 billion, up 62%, with infrastructure revenue of $7.4 billion, up 121%, and remaining performance obligations of $664 billion in the quarter ended 31 Aug 2026. Snowflake's product revenue grew 37% to $1.49 billion, and its CEO told Reuters that roughly half of the recent acceleration came from AI. Datadog's revenue grew 35% to $1.20 billion in Q3 2026.
sec.demand.2

Security is the other pillar. Palo Alto Networks' next-generation security annual recurring revenue rose 63% to $9.10 billion in the July 2026 quarter, and Fortinet billings rose 29% in Q3 2026. Our read is that demand is cyclical only at the margin, because infrastructure, database and security spending is increasingly treated as a prerequisite for AI deployment, but the large backlogs are contracts, not delivered revenue, and rest on customers financing AI buildouts.
sec.structure.0

Systems software is a concentrated, high-barrier industry. Using Porter's five forces: rivalry is intense among a few scale players, with Microsoft, Oracle and the hyperscale clouds competing in databases and infrastructure while Palo Alto, Fortinet and CrowdStrike compete in security. Barriers to entry are high because of switching costs, data gravity, certification requirements and, increasingly, the capital needed to build AI capacity. Oracle's decision to keep investing despite negative free cash flow illustrates the capital scale now required.
sec.structure.1

Buyer power is moderate: large enterprises negotiate, but migrating a database or a security stack is slow and risky, and platform consolidation gives vendors leverage. Supplier power is rising because AI infrastructure depends on scarce chips and memory, which Gartner says is driving hardware inflation through 2027. The threat of substitutes is the live debate: the software sell-off in early 2026 was attributed in coverage to AI agents undermining seat-based pricing, although that thesis mainly concerns application software.
sec.structure.2

Moats show up in margins. Damodaran's January 2026 dataset shows 309 US-listed system and application software firms with a 71.72% gross margin, against 62.58% for internet software. Fortinet's non-GAAP operating margin of 38.2% and Palo Alto's guided 29.5% for fiscal 2027 point to pricing power, though we found no consolidated market-share table for this sub-industry.
sec.environment.0

Regulation is a moderate rather than acute pressure. In the EU, the AI Act's general-purpose AI obligations have applied since 2 Aug 2025 and are unchanged by the Digital Omnibus. Per Gibson Dunn, a provisional agreement reached in May 2026 would delay standalone high-risk obligations from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 Dec 2027 and product-embedded ones to 2 Aug 2028, but at the time of its alert formal adoption was still pending. We did not find confirmation of final publication, so the dates should be treated as agreed but unverified as law. The deal also gives the EU AI Office exclusive competence over AI systems built on a general-purpose model when the same provider develops both.
sec.environment.1

Compliance burdens on model providers sit mostly with the cloud and AI platform companies that bundle systems software, which raises costs but also creates demand for governance and security tooling. We did not find a verified 2026 change to the SEC's cybersecurity incident disclosure rules, so we do not rely on one.
sec.environment.2

Technological disruption is the main risk and opportunity. The Fed environment adds a financial constraint to AI buildouts. Oracle's free cash flow was negative $5 billion in its August 2026 quarter as it funded cloud infrastructure. Our judgment is that the technology cycle, not regulation, is the dominant external variable, and that a financing squeeze on AI infrastructure would reach systems software through slower backlog conversion.
sec.economics.0

Systems software has software-like margins, but the mix is shifting toward capital-intensive infrastructure. Damodaran's January 2026 data for 309 system and application software firms show a 71.72% gross margin, a 35.93% EBITDA margin and a 25.49% net margin. These are application and system software together and describe the prior fiscal year, so they are a baseline rather than a current reading.
sec.economics.1

Recent company results show the range. Fortinet delivered a Q3 2026 non-GAAP operating margin of 38.2% and free cash flow of $865 million, a 41.6% margin on $2.08 billion of revenue. Palo Alto's fiscal 2026 adjusted free cash flow margin was 38.4% on $11.48 billion of revenue, and it guides fiscal 2027 to a 29.5% non-GAAP operating margin and 38.0% adjusted free cash flow margin. Datadog's Q3 non-GAAP operating margin was 28% and its free cash flow margin 21%. Microsoft's fiscal 2026 operating income was $155.2 billion on $331.8 billion of revenue, a margin of about 46.8% by our calculation.
sec.economics.2

Capital intensity is the counter-trend. Oracle's operating cash flow was $23 billion in its latest quarter but free cash flow was negative $5 billion, while ServiceNow's September 2026 quarter showed a 32.5% non-GAAP operating margin but only a 20% non-GAAP free cash flow margin. We did not find sub-industry ROE or ROIC from the sources opened, so we make no claim on returns on capital; the gap between operating margin and free cash flow margin at ServiceNow and Oracle is the clearer signal of how much cash conversion varies.
sec.earnings.0

Reported earnings momentum is strong and guidance is mostly rising. FactSet's 30 Oct 2026 report shows the Software industry within the S&P 500 Information Technology sector with blended Q3 2026 earnings growth of 17% and revenue growth of 19%, well below semiconductors at 132% and 83% respectively. Note that FactSet's Software industry includes application software, so it is a proxy for this sub-industry rather than a measure of it.
sec.earnings.1

Company guidance supports the picture. Microsoft's Q1 FY27 non-GAAP EPS was $4.89, up 18%. Palo Alto guides fiscal 2027 revenue of $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion, up 23% to 24%, and non-GAAP EPS of $4.16 to $4.19. Fortinet raised its 2026 revenue guide to $8.125 billion to $8.215 billion. ServiceNow guides 2026 subscription revenue of $15.78 billion to $15.79 billion, up 22.5%, with Q4 current RPO growth guided at 18.5%.
sec.earnings.2

Our read is that consensus for this group is anchored on backlog conversion. Palo Alto itself guides fiscal 2027 next-generation security ARR growth to 22% to 23%, a sharp deceleration from the 63% just reported; the release does not explain the gap and we have not determined the cause. We did not find consensus estimate revision data specific to systems software. At index level, 28 S&P 500 companies have issued positive Q4 EPS guidance and 19 negative. Where we are more cautious is on sequencing: Datadog's Q4 revenue guide of $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion is flat against its $1.20 billion Q3, and ServiceNow guides Q4 current RPO growth to 18.5%, below the 20.5% just reported.
sec.valuation.0

We could not find a current forward price-to-earnings ratio for the Information Technology sector or for systems software, so we frame valuation with what we could verify. FactSet puts the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 18.7 as of 30 Oct 2026, below the 5-year average of 19.8 and the 10-year average of 19.1. That implies the market overall is not expensive on that measure, while sector-level multiples for software were not published in the report text we reviewed.
sec.valuation.1

Damodaran's January 2026 dataset is the only structured industry multiple we opened: US system and application software trades at 24.48 times EV/EBITDA for firms with positive EBITDA, against 19.73 times for the total market, and 32.41 times EV/EBIT against 29.12 times. That is a premium of roughly 24% on EV/EBITDA by our calculation, and it is ten months old, since which time the group has fallen sharply and recovered. The dataset covers application as well as system software, so it is a loose proxy.
sec.valuation.2

The price path shows the multiple has swung. iShares' software ETF IGV rose 41.46% from 13 Apr to 12 Oct 2026 but was only up 5.34% year to date, and the source described the rally as multiple expansion rather than earnings growth, without giving valuation figures. Our judgment is that the group is priced for continued double-digit growth in billings and backlog, so a miss in conversion would matter more than a modest change in rates, but we cannot quantify implied growth without a verified forward multiple.
sec.positioning.0

Positioning has whipsawed. IGV closed at $111.31 on 12 Oct 2026, up 41.46% from its 13 Apr low and up 5.34% year to date, down 0.68% over one year. Earlier in the year it was weak: an early-July article had it down 10.5% year to date, and a September article reported a single-session outflow of about $700 million from the fund before Snowflake's report. On 4 Sep it was about $105, down 1% year to date, with net assets of $13.5 billion at 30 Jun across 111 positions.
sec.positioning.1

IGV is application-heavy, so it is an imperfect gauge of systems software, which also includes Microsoft, Oracle and the security vendors. We did not find sub-industry ETF flow data, short interest or breadth statistics from the sources opened, and we do not infer them. Snowflake rose in the session after its September report and was up 54% year to date by 4 Sep.
sec.positioning.2

On sector-level sentiment, FactSet reports that Information Technology has the highest expected price upside to analyst target prices after Communication Services, at 27.9% against the S&P 500's 20.8%. This is analyst target data, not our view, and we treat it as a sentiment gauge. Our read is that the recovery is narrow and earnings-driven for leaders with accelerating cloud and security backlogs, while seat-based application vendors remain the contested part of the group.
summary

Technology Hardware, Storage and Peripherals is splitting in two. Consumer devices are being squeezed by memory costs: IDC data show third-quarter smartphone shipments down 22% and PC shipments down 20%. Infrastructure is booming: Dell holds a $95 billion AI server backlog, while Seagate and Western Digital earn operating margins near 50%. Apple is the large exception, with record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion. Memory pricing is the swing factor for both sides. Sub-industry consensus and current sector multiples were not available to us, so valuation views here rest on single-name data.
basics.intro

These companies make the physical computers and the devices attached to them: smartphones, PCs, servers, data storage, and printers. Most design the product, buy chips and other parts from suppliers, and pay contract manufacturers in Asia to assemble it. They sell through phone carriers, retailers and resellers, or straight to businesses and cloud companies. Apple is by far the largest company here and also earns a large share of its profit from services sold to iPhone users. Networking gear and the parts inside devices sit in neighbouring sub-industries.
basics.products.0
Smartphones, tablets and wearables: Consumer devices bought every few years, plus watches and earbuds sold alongside them. e.g. Apple iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch and AirPods
basics.products.1

PCs and workstations: Laptops and desktops for consumers and businesses. Business buyers replace them on regular cycles, often triggered by a new version of Windows. e.g. Dell, HP Inc and Lenovo laptops and desktops, Apple Mac
basics.products.2

Servers, including AI servers: The computers that fill data centres. AI servers pack in several GPUs, cost far more per unit and earn thinner margins than ordinary servers. e.g. Dell PowerEdge, Super Micro, Hewlett Packard Enterprise
basics.products.3
Hard disk drives: Magnetic drives that store large amounts of data cheaply. High-capacity 'nearline' drives sold to cloud data centres are now the main market. e.g. Seagate, Western Digital
basics.products.4
Flash storage and storage systems: Solid-state drives, and storage arrays that let a company manage its data across many drives. e.g. NetApp, Dell PowerStore, SanDisk
basics.products.5
Printers and supplies: Printers sold at a thin margin, followed by years of profitable ink and toner sales. e.g. HP Inc printers and ink
basics.products.6
Services built on devices: App stores, cloud storage, subscriptions, warranties and payment services sold to people who already own the device. e.g. Apple App Store, iCloud, AppleCare
basics.drivers.0

Consumer spending and upgrade cycles: Phone and PC demand rises with household income and confidence, and with reasons to upgrade, such as a strong new iPhone, new AI features, or the end of support for an old version of Windows.
basics.drivers.1

Memory and component costs: When DRAM and NAND prices jump, the parts bill rises. Device makers must raise prices, which cuts unit demand, or absorb the cost, which cuts margins. Storage makers can gain from the same shortage.
basics.drivers.2
Data-centre and AI build-out: Cloud and AI spending lifts orders for servers and high-capacity drives. AI servers add a lot of revenue but at low margins, so profit grows more slowly than sales.
basics.drivers.3
Corporate IT budgets: Businesses buy most PCs, servers and storage arrays. They delay purchases when profits are under pressure and catch up later.
basics.drivers.4

Tariffs and where things are made: Most devices are assembled in China and other Asian countries. Tariffs and trade rules change costs, and moving production to India, Vietnam or Mexico is slow and expensive.
basics.drivers.5
The dollar: Much revenue comes from outside the U.S., so a stronger dollar lowers reported revenue unless prices abroad are raised.
basics.terms.0
Shipments (units): The number of devices sold into the market in a period, usually counted by research firms such as IDC. They are the headline demand measure for phones and PCs.
basics.terms.1
ASP (average selling price): Revenue divided by units. A shift towards premium models can lift revenue even when unit sales fall.
basics.terms.2
Installed base: The number of devices in use. It drives replacement demand and, for Apple, services revenue.
basics.terms.3
Replacement or refresh cycle: How many years people and companies keep a device before replacing it. A longer cycle cuts annual demand even if the installed base is stable.
basics.terms.4
Bill of materials (BOM): The cost of all the parts in a device. Memory and processors are the largest items, so chip prices feed straight into hardware makers' margins.
basics.terms.5
Contract manufacturer / ODM: A company, often in Taiwan or China, that assembles devices for the brand, such as Foxconn. An ODM (original design manufacturer) also does much of the design.
basics.terms.6
Component pass-through: Whether a hardware maker can raise prices when parts get dearer. If it can't, its gross margin shrinks; if demand is strong, it may even widen.
basics.terms.7
HDD vs SSD: Hard disk drives store data magnetically on spinning platters; solid-state drives use NAND flash chips. SSDs are faster, HDDs far cheaper per terabyte.
basics.terms.8
Nearline storage and exabytes: Nearline drives are high-capacity HDDs for cloud data centres. Drive makers track total capacity shipped in exabytes (a billion gigabytes) more than units.
basics.terms.9
AI server backlog: Orders for AI servers that are booked but not yet shipped. It points to future revenue, but is tied to the customer's GPU supply and financing.
basics.terms.10
Attach rate: How many extra products or services are sold per device, such as storage, warranties or subscriptions.
basics.terms.11
Razor-and-blade model: Selling the device cheaply and earning the profit on supplies or services later, as with printers and ink.
watch.0
Whether memory prices keep rising: DRAM hit a record in October while NAND stalled after 21 months of increases.
watch.1
IDC warns the worst is yet to come for smartphones and that weak demand could build inventory into 2027.
watch.2
IDC says a weaker economy could cut PC demand further into 2027, with channel promotions possible.
watch.3
Dell's ability to convert its $95 billion AI server backlog, with supply availability the stated constraint.
watch.4
Whether tariff refunds that flattered Apple and HP margins recur; they are one-off benefits.
bellwethers
Apple, Dell Technologies, HP Inc, Seagate Technology, Western Digital, Super Micro Computer, Lenovo
fund.business.0

Most revenue is one-off device sales: phones, PCs, servers, storage drives and arrays, and printers. Recurring streams come from services attached to devices (Apple's Services revenue was a record $31.6 billion in one quarter), printer ink and toner, warranties and support contracts, and storage subscriptions.
fund.business.1

Consumers buy most phones, many PCs and printers, through carriers, retailers and online stores. Businesses and governments buy PCs, servers and storage, often through resellers. Cloud and AI companies are now the biggest buyers of servers and high-capacity drives.
fund.business.2

Components dominate: cost of goods sold averaged 61.64% of sales for U.S. computer and peripheral firms in January 2026, and memory and processors are the largest items. Then come contract assembly, logistics, tariffs, R&D at 7.08% of sales, and marketing.
fund.business.3

Brand, ecosystem and technology. Apple's combination of hardware, software and services lets it charge premium prices, with a 47.9% gross margin, and the hard-drive duopoly has pricing power when supply is tight. Makers of standard PCs, Android phones and servers have little, so they must pass on component costs or absorb them.
fund.business.4

Assets are inventory, receivables from carriers and resellers, brands, patents and, for drive makers, factories. Many are asset-light because contract manufacturers own the assembly plants. Liabilities are mainly payables to suppliers, which fund working capital, and debt used for buybacks or acquisitions; Seagate repaid about $1.2 billion of debt in one quarter.
fund.business.5

Mostly asset-light. Net capex was 2.90% of sales across U.S. computer and peripheral firms, and sales were 3.62 times invested capital, high turnover by any standard. Drive makers, which run their own factories, are the more capital-intensive part.
fund.overview.0

We found no sourced total market size for this sub-industry. Shipments give the scale: IDC counted 255.3 million smartphones and 62.7 million PCs in Q3 2026, each down about a fifth. U.S. computer and peripheral firms grew revenue 6.71% a year over five years: a mature industry with a fast-growing server niche.
fund.overview.1

Smartphones and tablets; PCs and workstations; servers, now split between traditional and AI servers; storage (hard drives, flash and storage systems); printers and imaging; and wearables and accessories. Smartphones are the largest by revenue, led by Apple, and AI servers are the fastest growing.
fund.overview.2

Hardware makers sit between component suppliers (chips, memory, displays, drives) and buyers. Most rely on contract manufacturers in Asia for assembly. Downstream they sell through carriers, retailers, distributors and resellers, or directly to large customers. Operating systems and apps from other sub-industries make the devices useful.
fund.overview.3

The industry grew from mainframes and minicomputers to PCs in the 1980s and 1990s, then to smartphones after 2007, which made Apple the dominant profit pool. PC and phone markets have matured, with long replacement cycles. Cloud computing moved server buying to a few big customers, and AI is now making servers the growth engine again.
fund.overview.4

Design and brands are concentrated in the U.S., China, South Korea and Taiwan. Assembly is concentrated in China, with growing shares in India, Vietnam and Mexico. Sales are global, and Chinese brands Xiaomi, OPPO and vivo rank third to fifth in smartphones worldwide.
fund.competition.0

Few in each product. Smartphones and PCs each have about five global brands with most of the market; high-capacity hard drives effectively have two; servers have several big names plus Asian makers selling directly to cloud companies; printers have a handful.
fund.competition.1

Apple is the largest company here. Samsung (22.6%) and Apple (22.4%) lead smartphones; Lenovo (23.8%), HP (16.5%) and Dell (12.1%) lead PCs; Dell, Super Micro and Hewlett Packard Enterprise are big in servers; Seagate and Western Digital dominate hard drives; and HP leads printers.
fund.competition.2

Consolidated. Decades of exits and mergers (IBM sold its PC business to Lenovo, and Hitachi's drive business went to Western Digital) have left a few leaders in each product. The top five brands hold most of the PC and smartphone markets.
fund.competition.3

High at scale: brands, distribution, supplier relationships and the volume needed to win good component prices take years to build, and hard-drive technology needs deep engineering know-how. Barriers are lower in assembling standard servers or PCs, which is why Asian makers compete there on price.
fund.competition.4

Important. Bigger makers buy components more cheaply, get priority in shortages, and spread R&D and marketing over more units. The 2026 memory squeeze shows it: IDC said smaller smartphone brands fell further than Samsung and Apple.
fund.competition.5

Mixed. Standard PCs, Android phones and servers are close to commodities with thin margins; HP's PC business earned 4.6%. Apple's devices and high-capacity drives are differentiated and earn far more.
fund.competition.6

In 2026, suppliers: a few memory makers control a scarce input whose cost IDC says is up about 350% for phones. Large buyers such as cloud companies have strong power over server makers, which in our view is one reason AI servers earn thin margins. Apple holds unusual power over its own suppliers because of its volume.
fund.drivers.0

Replacement cycles, new features such as AI on devices, consumer and corporate budgets, and the data-centre build-out for servers and storage. Price and mix matter as much as units: Apple's revenue rose 12% in a quarter while global smartphone shipments fell 22%.
fund.drivers.1

Component costs relative to selling prices, product mix between premium and entry-level, services and supplies revenue, and scale. The average pre-tax operating margin was 22.48% for U.S. computer and peripheral firms in January 2026, an average lifted by Apple; PC makers earn single digits.
fund.drivers.2
Memory (DRAM and NAND), processors, displays, contract assembly, freight, tariffs and currency. In 2026 memory is the dominant swing cost.
fund.drivers.3

Moderate. Consumer devices are partly financed through carriers and credit, and corporate IT budgets react to the cost of capital, but most of these firms carry little debt relative to their market value. The larger effect is indirect, through consumer spending and valuations.
fund.drivers.4

Sensitive to employment and consumer confidence, because phones and PCs are purchases that can be delayed; IDC says a weaker economy could cut PC demand further. Component inflation is the main commodity exposure. A strong dollar lowers reported sales, because much revenue is earned abroad.
fund.drivers.5
