Cyclical and mature for consumer devices, with secular growth in servers and data-centre storage. U.S. computer and peripheral firms grew revenue 6.71% a year over five years, against 12.77% for the market. Apple's services add a steadier, more defensive element.
fund.financials.0

Modest. Revenue grew 6.71% a year and net income 14.01% a year over the five years to January 2026 for U.S. computer and peripheral firms, and analysts expected 25.42% annual EPS growth over the next five years, driven by AI servers and storage.
fund.financials.1

The average gross margin was 38.36% and pre-tax operating margin 22.48% in January 2026. The spread is wide: Apple's gross margin was 47.9%, the drive makers' operating margins are near 50%, and HP's PC business earned 4.6%.
fund.financials.2

Damodaran's unadjusted ROE for the group is -0.17%, which we read as distorted by firms with tiny or negative book equity after years of buybacks; adjusted for R&D it is 48.43%. Asset-light leaders such as Apple earn very high returns on the little capital they use, but we found no sourced sub-industry ROIC.
fund.financials.3

Low against market value: market debt is under 5% of capital. Book debt is high relative to book capital, at 61.31%, because buybacks have shrunk equity. The drive makers carry more debt and are paying it down.
fund.financials.4

Generally strong, because capex is low and suppliers fund working capital. Seagate generated $1.48 billion of free cash flow in one quarter on $211 million of capex, and Western Digital $1.38 billion. Apple returned $28 billion to shareholders in one quarter.
fund.financials.5

Low: net capex was 2.90% of sales, and capex was 119.84% of depreciation across the group. Assembly is outsourced, so most capital goes into tooling, data centres for services and, at the drive makers, factories.
fund.financials.6

In January 2026 the group traded at a forward P/E of 36.15 and at 25.42 times EV/EBITDA, against 19.73 times for the market. Those averages are lifted by Apple and the storage rally, and single names vary widely: Seagate traded on a forward P/E of 25 in October.
fund.risks.0

Tariffs and trade rules are the main lever, as recent tariff refunds at Apple and HP show. Right-to-repair laws, app-store and competition rules (which touch Apple's services), e-waste and energy-efficiency standards, and privacy rules also matter.
fund.risks.1

AI features on phones and PCs could revive replacement cycles, and AI data centres drive demand for servers and storage. The risks are flash storage replacing hard drives in more uses, AI moving work to the cloud so that devices matter less, and new device types reshuffling the leaders.
fund.risks.2
Limited but real. Saturated markets in rich, ageing countries mean growth must come from replacement and premium upgrades, while younger emerging markets such as India still add many new users.
fund.risks.3

People keep phones and PCs longer, which lowers unit demand, but they are buying more premium devices and paying for services, which lifts revenue per user. Printing continues a long decline as documents go digital.
fund.risks.4

Chinese brands compete on price in phones and PCs, Asian contract makers sell servers directly to cloud companies, and hyperscalers design their own servers. Subscription models, sometimes called hardware as a service, could change how businesses buy PCs.
fund.risks.5

The industry depends heavily on assembly in China and on chips and memory from Taiwan and South Korea. Tariffs, export controls and tensions around Taiwan could disrupt supply or raise costs. Shifting production to India and Vietnam is under way but slow.
fund.risks.6

Smartphones have already absorbed cameras, music players and many PC tasks. Cloud storage substitutes for local drives, and flash substitutes for hard drives in faster tiers. Smart glasses and other wearables could one day take over some phone use.
horizon.opportunities.0
AI servers and data-centre storage keep growing, with Dell's $95 billion AI server backlog and rising exabyte demand for drives.
horizon.opportunities.1
AI features on devices could shorten replacement cycles after a weak 2026 for phones and PCs.
horizon.opportunities.2
Services and other recurring revenue raise profit per device, led by Apple's record Services revenue.
horizon.threats.0
Memory shortages could keep squeezing device demand and margins into 2027 and beyond.
horizon.threats.1
Tariffs and supply-chain disruption, especially around China and Taiwan, could raise costs.
horizon.threats.2
AI servers earn thin margins, and storage pricing could reverse from today's peak.
horizon.assessment

This sub-industry is really two businesses. Consumer devices are mature, and over 3 to 5 years their growth depends on whether AI features revive upgrades and memory costs ease; IDC does not expect a smartphone recovery before 2028. Data-centre hardware is growing fast, but with thin margins in servers and cyclical pricing in storage. Apple's ecosystem and services make it the steadiest earner. Our view is that the biggest risk is assuming today's peak storage margins and AI server growth will last a full cycle.
sec.macro.0

This group is being driven less by the general economic cycle than by an input-cost shock. IDC says memory costs for smartphones have risen about 350% since last year, with sequential increases slowing to the low double digits in the third quarter from roughly 50-100% in earlier quarters. For PCs, IDC says the economy has weakened since last quarter, which could reduce demand further through the rest of 2026 and into 2027. Pricing will stay well above year-ago levels, and channel concern about inventory could bring promotions in the near term. Consumer-facing hardware therefore faces a squeeze: higher bills of materials meet softer household budgets.
sec.macro.1

Enterprise-facing hardware sits in a different part of the cycle. Dell's fiscal second quarter 2027 revenue rose 58% to $47.0 billion, with a $95 billion AI server backlog, as data-centre spending ran well ahead of the broader economy. Trade policy is a second macro variable. Apple said tariff refunds added about one percentage point to its September-quarter gross margin and $0.05 to earnings per share, and HP's guidance includes $0.19 of tariff-refund benefit for fiscal 2026. Those are one-off gains, and we would not treat them as run-rate. I did not locate a current source on interest-rate or currency effects specific to this sub-industry, so I make no claim there.
sec.demand.0

Demand has split in two. Consumer devices are shrinking on price. IDC's preliminary data show third-quarter 2026 smartphone shipments fell 22.0% to 255.3 million units, the largest year-over-year decline IDC has recorded, and it expects growth to stay constrained through 2027 with recovery possibly not until 2028. Worldwide PC shipments fell 20.1% to 62.7 million units, as early-year pull-forward ahead of price rises and supply constraints removed the usual seasonal lift.
sec.demand.1

Infrastructure demand runs the other way. Dell booked $60.9 billion of AI server orders in one quarter and lifted its fiscal 2027 AI-optimized server revenue outlook to $74 billion from $60 billion. In storage, Western Digital's chief financial officer attributed growth to robust exabyte growth and improved pricing, and Seagate guided fiscal second quarter revenue to $4.8 billion, plus or minus $100 million, against $4.2 billion in the quarter just reported. Memory makers are shifting capacity toward AI servers, and TrendForce-sourced reporting says PC DRAM supply could fall in 2027. Our read is that AI data creation is a structural driver for storage and servers, while for phones and PCs the 2026 decline is mostly a cost-and-price effect that could ease if memory supply loosens. Shortage end-date forecasts vary by company, from 2028 to 2030 for some memory makers.
sec.structure.0

Concentration differs sharply by product. In PCs, IDC's third-quarter data show Lenovo with 23.8% share (14.9 million units), HP 16.5%, Dell 12.1%, Apple 9.5% and ASUS 8.7%. In smartphones, Samsung (22.6%) and Apple (22.4%) lead, followed by Xiaomi (12.0%), OPPO (10.0%) and vivo (7.5%). Hard drives are described as a virtual duopoly between Seagate and Western Digital in high-capacity drives, though that source gives no share figures.
sec.structure.1

Applying Porter's five forces: supplier power has risen sharply because a handful of memory makers control a scarce input whose cost IDC says is up about 350% for phones. Buyer power is high for PC and phone makers selling to price-sensitive consumers, but weaker for storage vendors, since Western Digital cites deeper customer relationships and expanding visibility into future demand. Threat of substitutes is modest for devices, though cloud storage substitutes for local capacity in some uses. Threat of new entrants is low in hard drives and premium phones, given scale and technology barriers. Rivalry is intense in PCs and Android phones, where Xiaomi, OPPO and vivo saw deeper declines than Samsung and Apple. Pricing power is therefore strongest at Apple, whose September-quarter gross margin was 47.9%, and at the storage duopoly, whose gross margins were 57.3% (Seagate, GAAP) and 57.8% (Western Digital, GAAP).
sec.environment.0

Policy risk is mainly trade. Apple reported tariff refunds that lifted its fiscal fourth quarter gross margin by about one percentage point, and HP's guidance includes tariff-refund benefits of $0.08 in its fiscal fourth quarter and $0.19 for the full fiscal 2026 year. Both show tariffs have been a live cost and are now generating one-off reversals. I was unable to open a source on the current tariff status for computers and phones, so I do not characterise the forward tariff regime.
sec.environment.1

Technology is the other lever. HP said it is mitigating memory costs through pricing, redesigning some PCs and similar actions. In storage, Seagate's chief executive tied its HAMR-based roadmap to meeting growing exabyte demand through areal density gains while maintaining supply discipline. In servers, Dell's traditional servers and networking grew 122% and storage 26% in its latest quarter, showing AI is pulling through adjacent infrastructure. Supply-chain concentration is an emerging risk: suppliers are moving capacity toward AI servers, and one report, unconfirmed by the companies, claims Samsung and SK hynix may cut PC DRAM output by 20% to 40% in 2027. Treat that as a rumour, not a fact.
sec.economics.0

Economics are diverging by sub-segment. Apple's September-quarter revenue was $114.5 billion, up 12%, with iPhone at $57.6 billion and Services at a record $31.6 billion; fiscal 2026 revenue was a record $478.8 billion. At Dell, the infrastructure group earned a 15% operating margin against 8.8% a year earlier, while the client group earned $1.14 billion on $15.0 billion of revenue, roughly 7.6% by our arithmetic. HP's Personal Systems margin was 4.6%, down from 5.4%, as higher commodity costs outweighed repricing.
sec.economics.1

Storage vendors are the most profitable. Seagate posted $4.23 billion of revenue, a 57.8% non-GAAP gross margin, a 50.7% non-GAAP operating margin and $1.48 billion of free cash flow in a quarter with only $211 million of capital expenditure. Western Digital reported $4.38 billion of revenue, a 49.1% non-GAAP operating margin and $1.38 billion of free cash flow. Capital intensity is therefore low relative to profit at the drive makers, and operating leverage on price has been large. Super Micro's fiscal fourth quarter adjusted EPS was $1.70 against a $0.92 analyst forecast, although I could not retrieve its margin or revenue from an opened page. I did not find sub-industry ROIC or ROE from a source I opened.
sec.earnings.0

Guidance is strong at the infrastructure and storage end. Dell guided fiscal 2027 revenue to $192 billion, up 69%, and non-GAAP EPS to $25.50, up 148%; for the third quarter it guided revenue to about $49 billion and non-GAAP EPS to $6.50. Seagate guided fiscal second quarter non-GAAP EPS to $9.20, plus or minus $0.20; Western Digital guided revenue to $5.1 billion, gross margin to 60%-61% and EPS to $5.80. HP raised fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $3.19-$3.29 including tariff refunds, and expects PC units to fall in the high teens in the second half. Apple gave no forward guidance in its release.
sec.earnings.1

For context on the market, FactSet reports blended third-quarter S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.2% as of 30 October 2026 and names Information Technology among the sectors with double-digit growth, though it did not give the sector figure in the text I opened. I could not obtain consensus estimates for this sub-industry. Our view is that unit declines of around 20% in phones and PCs make consumer-hardware earnings dependent on pricing and mix, so consensus for those names carries more risk than for storage, where guidance already embeds sharply higher pricing. That is judgment, not a sourced estimate.
sec.valuation.0

The most recent sub-industry multiple I could open is dated. Damodaran's January 2026 US dataset for Computers/Peripherals (36 firms) shows a trailing P/E of 81.13, a forward P/E of 36.15 and a PEG ratio of 1.35. These predate the large price moves since, so I treat them as a historical reference, not a current reading. For the broad market, FactSet put the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 18.7 on 30 October 2026, below the five-year average of 19.8 and the 10-year average of 19.1. I did not find a current Information Technology sector forward multiple.
sec.valuation.1

Single-name data show wide dispersion. A Motley Fool article lists Seagate at a forward P/E of 25 and Western Digital at 23, with five-year PEG ratios of 0.53 and 0.90 respectively. Those multiples sit on guidance of very high earnings growth, for example Seagate's guided EPS of $9.20 against $7.68 in the prior quarter. Our read is that storage is priced for the memory and exabyte upcycle to persist, and the risk is a normalisation of pricing, while consumer-device names must be judged on whether memory costs can be passed through. I did not obtain free-cash-flow yields.
sec.positioning.0

Price momentum is concentrated in storage. A Motley Fool article reports Seagate up 235% year to date and 292% over 12 months, and Western Digital up 164% and 278%; its quote data show both shares falling sharply on 5 November 2026, with Seagate down 16.25% to $466.53 and Western Digital down 17.36% to $267.63. Whether that reflects earnings reactions or a broader rotation is not stated in the source, and I have not verified the cause.
sec.positioning.1

The fundamental backdrop for those moves is the pricing cycle: DRAM contract prices hit a record in October 2026 while the 128Gb MLC NAND price held flat after 21 months of increases, a pause that may reflect inventory adjustment rather than a turn. Western Digital raised its dividend 17% to $0.175 per share, and Seagate repaid about $1.2 billion of debt in the quarter, so balance sheets are being repaired while shares trade at high multiples to earnings growth. Apple returned $28 billion in the September quarter. I did not find ETF flow, short-interest or breadth data for this sub-industry from a source I opened, so I do not characterise institutional positioning.
summary

Application software is growing at a double-digit rate, but investors are still arguing about whether AI helps or hurts seat-based vendors. FactSet has the Software industry (which also includes systems software) at 19% revenue growth and 17% earnings growth in Q3 2026. Salesforce guides to 11% to 12% revenue growth, Adobe grew 13% in its August quarter, ServiceNow to 22.5% subscription growth and Palantir to 91%. IGV rose 41.46% from 13 April to 12 October yet was only up 5.34% year to date, after an April selloff tied to seat-based pricing fears. We found no current forward multiple for this sub-industry.
basics.intro

Application software is code that does a specific job for a business or a consumer: managing customer relationships, payroll and HR, accounting and tax, design and creative work, or analysing data. Customers are companies, governments and households, and most revenue now comes from subscriptions delivered over the internet. GICS puts Salesforce, Adobe, Intuit, Workday and Palantir here. The operating systems, databases, cybersecurity and infrastructure that these programs run on sit next door in Systems Software, and video games sit in Entertainment.
basics.products.0

Customer relationship management (CRM): Software that tracks leads, sales, service cases and marketing for a company's customers. Increasingly sold with AI agents that answer or act on customers' behalf. e.g. Salesforce Sales, Service and Agentforce; Adobe marketing tools
basics.products.1

Human resources and finance cloud: Systems of record for payroll, hiring, planning and accounting, typically run for years by the finance and HR departments of large employers. e.g. Workday HCM and Financials; Oracle and SAP equivalents
basics.products.2
Workflow and IT service platforms: Platforms that automate requests and approvals across IT, HR and customer service, then sell add-on modules to the same customers. e.g. ServiceNow
basics.products.3

Creative and document software: Tools for designing, editing and managing content and documents, sold per user per month to professionals, businesses and consumers. e.g. Adobe Creative Cloud, Acrobat and Express; Autodesk
basics.products.4

Tax, accounting and small-business software: Software for households and small firms to file taxes, keep books, pay staff and take payments, often with a fee on transactions. e.g. Intuit TurboTax, QuickBooks and Credit Karma
basics.products.5

Data analytics and AI application platforms: Platforms that turn a customer's data into decisions and increasingly AI agents. They are usually priced on a mix of licences and usage. e.g. Palantir Foundry and AIP
basics.drivers.0

Corporate IT budgets: Businesses spend more on software when profits and confidence are high. In a slowdown they pause new projects and trim seats, so new bookings and cRPO slow before reported revenue does.
basics.drivers.1

Seat counts and pricing model: Where revenue is per user, employment and AI-driven staffing cuts change revenue directly. Price rises and AI add-ons lift revenue per user; usage pricing moves with activity instead.
basics.drivers.2

AI as feature, product or substitute: AI add-ons and agents can add revenue and justify price rises. AI coding tools could also lower the cost of building rival software, which would weaken switching costs and compress margins.
basics.drivers.3

Switching costs and retention: Because systems of record are hard to replace, renewals are sticky. High retention keeps churn low, so growth can come from selling more to existing customers at low cost.
basics.drivers.4

Operating leverage: Once built, extra copies cost little, so gross margins are high and extra revenue falls to profit. The flip side is that costs are mostly people, so growth that stalls hurts margins fast.
basics.drivers.5
Interest rates: Much of value lies in profits years ahead, so higher long-term rates cut what investors will pay for the same business, even when its earnings are unchanged.
basics.drivers.6
Acquisitions: Large vendors buy data, workflow or AI companies to widen platforms. This lifts reported growth but adds goodwill and integration risk, and can mask slower organic growth.
basics.terms.0

SaaS (software as a service): Software rented by subscription and run by the vendor over the internet, rather than installed once and paid for upfront. Revenue is steadier but arrives over the contract.
basics.terms.1
Seat-based pricing: Charging per user. Revenue rises with a customer's headcount, which is why AI that reduces the number of workers is read as a risk.
basics.terms.2
Consumption pricing: Charging by how much the customer uses, such as AI actions or data processed. It can grow faster when usage rises and slow faster when customers cut back.
basics.terms.3
ARR (annual recurring revenue): The yearly value of subscriptions in force. Many vendors quote it as a growth measure because it filters out one-off items.
basics.terms.4
RPO and cRPO: Remaining performance obligations are contracted revenue not yet recognised; cRPO is the part due in the next 12 months. It shows how much revenue is already locked in.
basics.terms.5
Net revenue retention: This year's revenue from last year's customers divided by what they paid then. Above 100% means existing customers expand; below means they shrink or leave.
basics.terms.6
Gross retention: The share of last year's recurring revenue kept after cancellations and downgrades, before upsells. It measures how sticky the product is.
basics.terms.7
System of record: The program where a company's authoritative data lives, such as customer or employee records. Replacing one is slow and risky, which gives incumbents pricing power.
basics.terms.8

Agentic AI: AI that carries out multi-step tasks on its own inside business software, rather than just answering questions. Vendors sell it as a new revenue line; critics see a threat to per-user pricing.
basics.terms.9
Rule of 40: Revenue growth plus free cash flow margin. Investors use 40 or more as a rough marker of a healthy software business.
basics.terms.10
Stock-based compensation: Paying staff in shares. It is a real cost through dilution but is often left out of adjusted profit, so check both versions.
basics.terms.11
Billings: Billings are what was invoiced in the period (revenue plus change in deferred revenue). They can lead revenue when annual contracts are signed up front.
watch.0
Whether AI agents shrink seat counts at seat-priced vendors: the April selloff was tied to that fear, and Adobe was down 24% year to date in early September.
watch.1
Salesforce's cRPO growth against its roughly 14% guide, and whether pending acquisitions close as assumed in its full-year outlook.
watch.2
ServiceNow's Q4 cRPO growth guide of 18.5% against 20.5% reported in Q3.
watch.3
Intuit's first full year without excluding stock compensation from non-GAAP results, with fiscal 2027 revenue growth guided to 9% to 10% against 14% in fiscal 2026.
watch.4
The Fed: two FOMC members dissented in favour of a quarter-point hike on 28 Oct 2026, and long-duration software stocks are rate sensitive.
bellwethers
Salesforce, Adobe, Intuit, ServiceNow, Workday, Palantir
fund.business.0

Mostly recurring subscriptions: Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow and Adobe sell per-user or per-module plans, with Adobe reporting $6.56 billion of subscription revenue out of $6.76 billion total in its August 2026 quarter. Intuit sells consumer products such as TurboTax and Credit Karma alongside its small-business software. Services and one-off licences are a minor share of the group.
fund.business.1

Enterprises and governments buy the large platforms (Salesforce, Workday, ServiceNow, Palantir); professionals, small firms and households buy Adobe and Intuit products. Intuit's fiscal 2026 revenue split into Global Business Solutions at $12.9 billion and Consumer at $8.6 billion. Palantir sells to both governments and commercial customers, with U.S. commercial revenue of $984 million in Q3 2026.
fund.business.2

People, mainly engineers and salespeople. For US system and application software firms Damodaran shows R&D at 15.98% of sales, SG&A at 24.38% and stock-based compensation at 7.83%. Cost of goods is only 28.28% of sales. Cloud hosting and, increasingly, AI computing add to cost of revenue.
fund.business.3

Switching costs and data. A payroll, CRM or tax system holds years of a customer's records, so renewals are sticky; Workday's 12-month subscription backlog grew 14.2% to $9.034 billion. Breadth of the platform and the ability to bundle AI help raise prices. Pricing power is weakest where the product is a point tool that rivals, or a customer's own AI, can copy.
fund.business.4

Mostly intangible: software, brands, customer relationships and goodwill from acquisitions, plus cash. The key liability is deferred revenue, from subscriptions paid up front, which funds operations. Salesforce is executing a $25 billion accelerated share repurchase, and Adobe repurchased $2.23 billion of stock in one quarter.
fund.business.5

Asset-light. Damodaran shows book debt to capital of 34.14% but market debt to capital of only 5.37% for US system and application software firms. Capex is mainly capitalised software and offices, though systems vendors are different and the figure in the dataset mixes both. Free cash flow is usually close to or above earnings.
fund.overview.0

Gartner, as reported, puts worldwide software spending at $1,464 billion in 2026 (up 15.2%) and $1,679 billion in 2027 (up 14.6%). That covers all software, including systems software; we found no free figure for application software alone. US system and application software firms grew revenue at 19.56% a year over five years to January 2026.
fund.overview.1

CRM and customer experience; HR, finance and planning; IT and business workflow; creative, design and document tools; tax and small-business accounting; and data and AI application platforms. In IDC's CRM data Salesforce held 20.0% of 2025 sales, with Oracle 4.1%, Microsoft 4.0%, Adobe 3.4% and SAP 3.1%. Fast growth is concentrated in AI-linked platforms such as Palantir.
fund.overview.2

Application software sits at the top of the technology stack. It runs on cloud infrastructure, databases and security from the hyperscalers and Systems Software firms, and it is sold directly or through partners, consultants and resellers. Its customers are the business departments, such as HR, sales and finance, that decide how to use the data and AI beneath it.
fund.overview.3

From boxed licences and on-premise suites to subscriptions delivered over the internet, with the cloud model now standard. The latest shift is toward AI agents that perform tasks inside the software. Vendors report rapid early uptake: Salesforce's Agentforce ARR exceeded $1.5 billion, up over 240%, and ServiceNow raised its 2026 AI contract value target to $1.7 billion.
fund.overview.4

Heavily United States: Salesforce, Adobe, Intuit, Workday, ServiceNow and Palantir are all US-listed, with Europe's SAP the main non-US peer. Development talent is spread across the US, India, Israel and Europe. We did not find a free geographic split of application software revenue.
fund.competition.0

Hundreds of listed companies: Damodaran counts 309 US system and application software firms, plus thousands of private ones. A handful of large vendors dominate each category, but each category also has many specialist rivals.
fund.competition.1

Salesforce is first in CRM at 20.0% of 2025 sales, ahead of Oracle at 4.1%. Adobe leads creative software, Intuit leads US consumer tax and small-business accounting, Workday and SAP lead in enterprise HR and finance, and ServiceNow in IT workflow. We found no sourced shares outside CRM.
fund.competition.2
Concentrated by product but fragmented overall. Even in CRM, 'other' providers hold 65.4% of the market, up from 63.5% a year earlier, so smaller vendors have been gaining share.
fund.competition.3

Building a product is easier than ever, but winning customers is hard because it needs distribution, data, integrations and trust. The barrier is a customer's reluctance to move a system of record, not the code itself. The newest risk is that AI coding tools lower the cost of copying features.
fund.competition.4

Scale spreads R&D and sales cost over a larger revenue base, and Damodaran shows industry-average R&D of 15.98% and SG&A of 24.38% of sales. Bigger vendors also hold more data to train AI. Gross margins of 71.72% mean added revenue is highly profitable.
fund.competition.5

Differentiated at the platform level and increasingly commoditised at the feature level. A deeply embedded payroll or CRM platform is hard to replace, but a single feature, such as a design tool or note summariser, may be copied or bundled by a rival or by a general-purpose AI model.
fund.competition.6

Customers hold more of it than in most technology niches, mainly because they can switch tool by tool or build with AI. Against that, backlog growth at systems of record such as Workday (12-month backlog up 14.2%) suggests switching costs still limit it. Suppliers, mainly the hyperscalers and AI model labs, hold bargaining power over costs of compute and models.
fund.drivers.0

Growth comes from new customers, more seats or modules sold to existing customers, price rises and, now, AI products. ServiceNow's subscription revenue grew 21% in Q3 2026 and Salesforce's cRPO grew 14% in constant currency. Acquisitions add further growth, as Informatica did for Salesforce.
fund.drivers.1

Gross margin is high, so margins depend on how much is spent on R&D and sales relative to revenue, and on stock compensation. Non-GAAP operating margins ran from 31.1% at Workday to 44% at Adobe and 34.1% at Salesforce in their latest quarters. Palantir's was 62%.
fund.drivers.2

Salaries and stock compensation (7.83% of sales in Damodaran's data), sales and marketing, and cloud hosting. Vendors that run large AI workloads face rising compute costs that depress gross margin. Foreign exchange matters little: Adobe's growth was 13% reported and 12% in constant currency.
fund.drivers.3

Indirectly, through valuation more than through demand. Most application software firms carry little debt (market debt to capital 5.37% in Damodaran's data), so financing costs are small. But long-dated profit expectations make the shares sensitive to long-term yields; the Fed held at 3-3/4 to 4 percent on 28 Oct 2026 with two members favouring a hike.
fund.drivers.4

Hiring and employment matter most because many products are priced per seat. GDP and corporate profits drive the size of IT budgets: FactSet has S&P 500 Q3 2026 earnings up 30.2%. Inflation matters through price rises (contracts often reprice at renewal) and wage costs. Commodity prices have little direct effect.
fund.drivers.5

Secular growth with a cyclical edge. Gartner expects software spending to grow around 15% in both 2026 and 2027, and the industry's earnings are growing even in a tight-money year. But new bookings and seat counts can slow quickly when budgets are cut, and the April 2026 selloff showed that sentiment can change independently of earnings.
fund.financials.0

Fast. Damodaran's data show five-year compound growth of 19.56% in revenue and 29.81% in net income for US system and application software firms to January 2026, against 12.77% and 12.83% for the whole market. Large incumbents now grow more slowly: Salesforce guides 11% to 12% and Workday subscription 13%.
fund.financials.1

Gross margins averaged 71.72% and pre-tax operating margins 32.98% (40.81% before stock compensation), against 37.76% and 12.82% for all US firms. At the top end, Adobe guides to a non-GAAP operating margin of about 45% for fiscal 2026, and ServiceNow to 31.5%.
fund.financials.2

High. Damodaran shows an unadjusted ROE of 29.62% for US system and application software firms against 17.21% for the total market. Treating R&D as an investment lowers it to 20.21%. The page does not report ROIC, and we found no sourced sub-industry ROIC.
fund.financials.3

Low. Book debt to capital is 34.14% but market debt to capital only 5.37%, with interest cover of 18.95 and debt to EBITDA of 1.71, against 6.52 for the whole market. Intuit, Adobe and Salesforce nonetheless use cash for large buybacks.
fund.financials.4

Strong. Adobe produced $2.52 billion of operating cash flow in one quarter. ServiceNow guides to a 36% free cash flow margin for 2026, Palantir to $4.8 billion to $5.0 billion of adjusted free cash flow, and Salesforce to 4% to 5% growth in cash flow. Workday's quarter showed lower cash flow than a year earlier.
fund.financials.5

Low in most of the industry. The Damodaran category combines systems and application software, and shows capex of 244.55% of depreciation and net capex of 17.82% of sales, a figure we think is driven by the large cloud builders in the grouping. For pure application vendors such as Adobe and Workday, we do not see a sourced capex figure.
fund.financials.6

Rich on earnings and cash flow. Damodaran's January 2026 data have a forward P/E of 34.13 against 27.66 for the market, and EV/EBITDA of 24.48 against 19.73 for the positive-EBITDA firms. Both pre-date the April selloff and the rebound that followed, so they are dated for current use.
fund.risks.0

Data privacy, AI and competition rules apply. The EU AI Act's high-risk obligations were provisionally delayed to 2 December 2027 for stand-alone systems such as recruitment and credit scoring, from 2 August 2026, if formally adopted. HR and finance software is directly exposed to that category of rules.
fund.risks.1

The central question. Bulls see AI agents as a new revenue line, with Salesforce's Agentforce ARR above $1.5 billion. Bears fear AI agents will reduce the seats customers need and AI coding will cut the cost of building rival software, as the April 'SaaS apocalypse' narrative held.
fund.risks.2
Mostly through the workforce. If AI shrinks white-collar headcount, seat-priced vendors lose volume, and we think demographics otherwise matter little. We found no sourced figure on this effect.
fund.risks.3

Users expect AI features in the product for free or at lower prices, and want a single platform. In the consumer segment Intuit's TurboTax grew only 7% in fiscal 2026 against 20% for Credit Karma, a sign of how mature products compare with new ones.
fund.risks.4

AI-native start-ups, the AI model labs and hyperscalers are entering application categories. 'Other' CRM vendors gained 1.9 points of share in 2025. Palantir is an example of a new-model entrant that has become large, with revenue up 96% in Q3 2026.
fund.risks.5

Less direct than for hardware. Exposure comes through cloud capacity and chips for AI, and through data-residency rules. Currency effects were small in the latest results, such as Adobe's 13% reported against 12% constant-currency growth. We found no sourced figure on geopolitical revenue exposure.
fund.risks.6

General-purpose AI assistants and in-house tools built with AI coding could substitute for packaged software in simple tasks. The evidence so far is mixed: ServiceNow reports agentic AI in production up more than 13x year on year, while IGV's 2026 performance has diverged between consumption-priced and seat-priced names.
horizon.opportunities.0
AI agents and add-ons can open new revenue lines and support price rises, as Agentforce ARR above $1.5 billion and ServiceNow's $1.7 billion AI contract value target suggest.
horizon.opportunities.1
Gartner expects software spending to grow about 15% in both 2026 and 2027, a favourable backdrop for budgets.
horizon.opportunities.2
High margins and cash flow let vendors fund buybacks and acquisitions: Salesforce's $25 billion repurchase and Intuit's $5.5 billion fiscal 2026 buyback are examples.
horizon.opportunities.3
Consolidation onto fewer platforms favours large vendors with broad suites and embedded data.
horizon.threats.0
Seat compression and cheaper software creation from AI could slow growth at seat-priced vendors; the April 2026 selloff priced that fear.
horizon.threats.1
Growth is decelerating at the largest names: Intuit guides fiscal 2027 revenue growth to 9% to 10% from 14%, and ServiceNow guides Q4 cRPO growth to 18.5%.
horizon.threats.2
Higher-for-longer rates or a hike would weigh on valuations of long-duration growth stocks.
horizon.threats.3
Regulation of AI in hiring, credit and similar uses adds compliance cost, even though deadlines have been pushed back.
horizon.assessment

Over the next three to five years we think the industry is likely to keep growing faster than the economy, because software budgets are expected to grow at roughly 15% a year and the leading vendors keep high margins and cash flow. The main uncertainty is who captures the value from AI. If agents are priced on usage and stay inside existing platforms, incumbents could extend growth; if customers need fewer seats or build their own tools, growth and pricing could fall to the low single digits for the weakest. Results so far point to a split between consumption-linked or platform winners and seat-based laggards. That makes company selection within the sub-industry matter more than the sub-industry average.
sec.macro.0

The macro backdrop pairs strong corporate spending with firm monetary policy. On 28 Oct 2026 the Federal Open Market Committee held the federal funds target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent by a 10-2 vote, with Governor Cook and Cleveland Fed President Hammack dissenting in favour of a quarter-point increase, and the statement says 'Inflation remains elevated'. We read that as a late-cycle setting in which cuts are not imminent, which matters for application software because so much of its value lies in profits years away, making the shares sensitive to long-term yields.
sec.macro.1

Corporate demand has held up. FactSet puts S&P 500 blended Q3 2026 earnings growth at 30.2% and revenue growth at 13.4%, with Software industry earnings up 17% and revenue up 19% (a group that also contains systems software). Gartner's October forecast, as reported, has worldwide software spending up 15.2% in 2026 and 14.6% in 2027, in total IT spending of $6,391 billion in 2026. Company currency effects were small in the results we read: Adobe's Q3 revenue grew 13% reported and 12% in constant currency.
sec.demand.0

Structural demand rests on businesses digitising work and now adding AI. Gartner's reported forecast of $1,464 billion of software spending in 2026 and $1,679 billion in 2027 covers all software, so it overstates the application-only market; we found no free application-only figure. Damodaran's data show US system and application software revenue compounding at 19.56% a year over five years, against 12.77% for the whole market, and analysts expecting EPS growth of 22.76% a year for the next five years, versus 13.95% for the market.
sec.demand.1

Within that, the largest vendors are slowing as they mature while AI-linked platforms accelerate. Salesforce guides to 11% to 12% revenue growth for fiscal 2027, including acquisitions. Workday guides subscription revenue growth of 13%. ServiceNow grew subscription revenue 21% in Q3 and Palantir grew 96%, with U.S. commercial up 148%. Demand is steady rather than cyclical in the large systems of record, but seat-based pricing exposes the group to changes in customer headcount, a point investors made forcefully in April.
sec.structure.0

Using Porter's five forces, rivalry is intense inside each category but moderated by specialisation: Salesforce held 20.0% of the CRM market in 2025, while 'other' vendors collectively held 65.4%, up from 63.5%. The threat of new entrants is rising because AI lowers the cost of building features, a bear argument in the 2026 debate. Buyer power is moderate to high on point tools but limited for systems of record, where Workday's 12-month subscription backlog grew 14.2%.
sec.structure.1

Supplier power sits with the cloud and AI-model providers, which control the compute that agents need. The threat of substitutes comes from general-purpose AI and in-house builds. The moat is mainly switching costs and accumulated customer data, plus brands and integrations. Pricing power is therefore strongest in embedded platforms and weakest in tools that rivals can copy. Scale also helps: Damodaran's industry average has 71.72% gross margin and 15.98% R&D to sales, which large vendors can fund more easily.
sec.environment.0

Technology is the main force. The April 2026 selloff, described as the 'SaaS apocalypse', was tied to the fear that AI agents will do the work of several employees and cut the licences customers need. Vendors are answering with agents of their own: Salesforce reports Agentforce ARR above $1.5 billion, and ServiceNow raised its 2026 AI annual contract value target to $1.7 billion.
sec.environment.1

On regulation, a provisional EU agreement of 6 May 2026 would delay high-risk AI obligations (for example in recruitment and credit scoring) to 2 December 2027, from 2 August 2026, once formally adopted. HR and finance software is the natural target of such rules. Palantir's 96% Q3 revenue growth shows how much demand AI-linked platforms are drawing. Privacy law, tax policy and trade tensions also matter, but the sources we opened did not quantify them for application software.
sec.economics.0

Application software economics are among the best in the market. For US system and application software firms Damodaran shows a 71.72% gross margin and a 32.98% pre-tax operating margin (40.81% before stock compensation), against 37.76% and 12.82% for all US firms. Unadjusted ROE is 29.62% against 17.21%, falling to 20.21% when R&D is capitalised. Leverage is low, with debt to EBITDA of 1.71 against 6.52 for the whole market. These numbers include systems software.
sec.economics.1

Company results show the spread. Non-GAAP operating margins were 44.0% at Adobe, 34.1% at Salesforce, 32.5% at ServiceNow, 31.1% at Workday and 62% at Palantir. Operating leverage is the key: costs are mostly people, so growth that holds lets margins widen, and growth that stalls forces cuts. Cash generation is high: ServiceNow guides to a 36% free cash flow margin for 2026, and Palantir's adjusted free cash flow margin was 53% in Q3. Intuit will stop excluding stock compensation from its non-GAAP measures from fiscal 2027, which lowers its reported margin.
sec.earnings.0

FactSet's blended Q3 2026 numbers show the Software industry growing earnings 17% and revenue 19% year over year, well below the 67.5% earnings growth of the Information Technology sector, which is dominated by semiconductors (132%). We did not find a public consensus earnings forecast for application software alone.
sec.earnings.1

Management guidance points to steady but slowing growth at the biggest vendors. Salesforce raised fiscal 2027 revenue guidance by $200 million to $46.1 billion to $46.4 billion, helped by pending acquisitions. Adobe raised its fiscal 2026 targets to $26.576 billion to $26.626 billion, with ending ARR growth of 10.2%. Workday raised its margin outlook to 31.0%. Palantir raised 2026 revenue guidance to $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion. Intuit guided fiscal 2027 revenue growth of 9% to 10%, against 14% in fiscal 2026, and ServiceNow guided Q4 cRPO growth to 18.5% from 20.5%. We think expectations are being reset by company: faster for platform and AI names, lower for mature seat-based products.
sec.valuation.0

We could not find a current forward P/E for application software alone. The latest industry dataset, Damodaran's January 2026 edition for US system and application software firms, shows a forward P/E of 34.13 against 27.66 for the total market, a PEG ratio of 1.65 against 1.90, and EV/EBITDA of 24.48 against 19.73 for positive-EBITDA firms. Those figures include systems software and pre-date the April selloff and the rebound that followed.
sec.valuation.1

At market level, FactSet has the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 18.7, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and 10-year average of 19.1. The software group's 41.46% rally from April to October with only 5.34% gained year to date suggests prices fell sharply and recovered. One commentator argues the rebound reflected multiple expansion rather than earnings growth, though that is opinion and the article gives no multiple. Our read is that the group's premium to the market rests on durable high margins and high cash conversion, and that the AI debate is about whether that growth lasts. Price therefore embeds an expectation of continued double-digit growth.
sec.positioning.0

Positioning is mixed. IGV, the main software ETF, rose 41.46% from 13 April to 12 October 2026 to $111.31, but was up only 5.34% year to date and down 0.68% over one year, against gains of 20.84% for QQQ and 13.41% for SPY over the same six months. Be careful with what IGV measures: its largest holdings at 30 June 2026 were Palo Alto Networks at 10.37%, Microsoft 8.07%, Palantir 7.70%, CrowdStrike 7.28% and Oracle 6.26%, with Salesforce at 4.81% and Adobe at 3.13%, so it blends systems and application software.
sec.positioning.1

Flows were choppy. An article reported roughly $700 million pulled from IGV in one session in early September, just before Snowflake's report; the fund held $13.5 billion in net assets at 30 June 2026. The same piece observed a split between consumption-priced names, which benefit from AI workloads, and seat-based laggards such as Adobe, down 24% year to date at the time. We found no sourced short-interest figures for the group.
summary

Chip equipment is in a steep, AI-and-memory-led upcycle. SEMI's July forecast has 2026 equipment sales at about $165 billion, up 23%, and the latest earnings were records: Lam revenue $8.22 billion, KLA $4.14 billion, ASML net sales EUR 11.7 billion. Lam talks of wafer fab equipment above $200 billion in 2027, while ASML says planned 2027-28 supply will not meet demand. Supply limits and China controls are the main constraints. We found no sourced forward P/E for this sub-industry; the S&P 500 trades at 17.7 times.
basics.intro

These companies make the machines, and some of the materials, that other companies use to build chips. Customers are chipmakers such as foundries, memory makers and logic producers, who buy tools to add capacity or move to newer processes. Revenue comes from selling tools, then from servicing, spare parts and upgrades on the installed base. GICS also puts test equipment makers here, such as Teradyne. The chip designers and chipmakers themselves sit next door, in Semiconductors.
basics.products.0

Lithography: Machines that print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers using light. EUV uses very short wavelengths for the finest patterns; DUV is the older, cheaper generation. e.g. ASML EUV and DUV immersion systems
basics.products.1

Deposition and etch: Tools that lay down thin films of material on a wafer and then carve away parts of them to form transistors and wiring. These are the largest tool categories by spending. e.g. Applied Materials deposition, Lam Research etch and deposition
basics.products.2

Process control and inspection: Systems that measure and inspect wafers during manufacturing to find defects early, which protects yield (the share of good chips per wafer). e.g. KLA inspection and metrology
basics.products.3
Test equipment: Machines that check finished wafers and packaged chips work before they ship. Complex AI and memory chips need longer, more expensive testing. e.g. Teradyne semiconductor test systems
basics.products.4

Services and spares: Maintenance, parts and upgrades sold to fabs that already own the tools. This revenue is steadier than new-tool sales because it follows the installed base. e.g. Applied Global Services, Lam customer support, ASML Installed Base Management
basics.products.5

Packaging equipment: Tools that assemble chips into packages, including stacking memory dies for AI accelerators. It is a smaller but growing part of equipment spending. e.g. Applied Materials advanced packaging tools
basics.drivers.0
Chipmaker capex: Tool revenue follows what foundries and memory makers decide to spend. Their budgets follow their own profits and demand forecasts, so equipment sales swing more than chip sales.
basics.drivers.1
Technology transitions: Each new node, 3D memory layer or advanced package adds process steps, so the same wafer volume needs more tools. This lifts equipment demand even when wafer output is flat.
basics.drivers.2
Memory pricing cycle: Memory makers cut capex when prices fall and raise it when prices rise, so DRAM and NAND swings reach equipment orders with a lag.
basics.drivers.3
Export controls: U.S. and allied rules decide which tools can go to which Chinese customers, which changes the share of revenue from China and can strand shipments.
basics.drivers.4
Supply constraints: Tools are built from scarce components and need clean-room space. When demand outruns supply, deliveries slip and revenue shifts between quarters.
basics.drivers.5
Installed-base services: As the number of tools in use grows, service and spares revenue grows with it and cushions downturns in new-tool sales.
basics.terms.0
WFE: Wafer fab equipment: tools used inside the factory to process wafers. It is the main measure of chipmaker equipment spending and excludes test and packaging tools.
basics.terms.1
Capex: Capital expenditure by chipmakers on new fabs and tools. It is the customer budget that becomes equipment revenue.
basics.terms.2
EUV: Extreme ultraviolet lithography, needed for the smallest chip features. ASML is the only supplier.
basics.terms.3
DUV: Deep ultraviolet lithography, the older generation still used for most layers of a chip.
basics.terms.4
Node: A generation of chip manufacturing process, loosely named by feature size. Moving to a new node usually needs more tool steps.
basics.terms.5
Installed base: All the tools a vendor has already sold and that still run. It generates service and upgrade revenue.
basics.terms.6
Backlog / bookings: Orders received but not yet delivered. Because tools take months to build, orders signal future revenue, though some vendors do not disclose them.
basics.terms.7
Process control: Inspection and measurement of wafers during manufacturing. It matters more as chips get more complex.
basics.terms.8
HBM: High-bandwidth memory: DRAM chips stacked in layers beside an AI accelerator. It needs extra tool steps for stacking and packaging.
basics.terms.9
Entity List: A U.S. list of foreign companies that need a licence to receive U.S. technology. It can stop tool shipments to named customers.
basics.terms.10
Leading-edge vs mature node: Leading-edge means the newest, smallest processes; mature nodes are older processes used in many everyday chips. They respond to different customers and policies.
basics.terms.11
Book-to-bill: Orders divided by shipments over a period. Above one suggests demand is building ahead of revenue.
watch.0
Lam says clean-room space and component supply may limit how much 2027 demand the industry can serve, and some December-quarter shipments slipped into March.
watch.1
The MATCH Act would push allies to match U.S. tool controls on China or face unilateral U.S. action, and it covers DUV immersion lithography.
watch.2
China is a shrinking but large share of sales: 35% of Lam revenue in the September quarter, with a significant fall expected in December, and about 20% of ASML's 2026 sales.
watch.3
Applied Materials guided its October quarter to $10.25 billion of revenue, and results land after this brief's data cut-off.
watch.4
Pricing increases at ASML start to contribute in 2027, while customers asking to order for 2029 and 2030 show how far ahead demand is booking.
bellwethers
Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA, ASML, Teradyne, Tokyo Electron
fund.business.0

Revenue comes from selling new tools, usually priced in the millions of dollars each, and from services, spares and upgrades on tools already installed. Applied Materials reported $7.04 billion from Semiconductor Systems and $1.78 billion from Applied Global Services in its July 2026 quarter.
fund.business.1

Customers are a small group of chipmakers: foundries, DRAM and NAND makers and logic producers. That concentration matters: Lam's systems revenue was split 46% memory, 46% foundry and 8% logic and other in the September 2026 quarter. Test and packaging customers add outsourced assembly firms.
fund.business.2

The main costs are research and development, components bought from suppliers, and factory labour. Applied Materials spent $1.1 billion on research, development and engineering in its July 2026 quarter, about 12% of revenue (our calculation from the release).
fund.business.3

Pricing power comes from technology leadership and switching costs. ASML says price increases begin to contribute in 2027 and take full effect from 2028 because supply is short. Where a vendor has no unique tool, customers can negotiate harder, and Chinese customers have been buying mature-node tools in volume.
fund.business.4

The main assets are intellectual property, inventory, and the installed base of tools that generate service revenue. Liabilities include customer prepayments: ASML's cash rose to EUR 12.7 billion at the end of Q3 2026 from EUR 7.6 billion in Q2, and its free cash flow reflected order momentum and down payments. Applied Materials had $7.04 billion of cash and $6.54 billion of debt on 26 July 2026.
fund.business.5

The business is capital-light compared with its chipmaker customers but heavy on research. Damodaran's January 2026 data show net capital expenditure of 4.14% of sales for 31 U.S. semiconductor equipment firms. Our read is that the real intensity is intellectual: R&D and the engineering time needed to qualify tools at a customer's fab.
fund.overview.0

SEMI's July 2026 forecast puts total equipment sales by manufacturers at about $165 billion in 2026, up 23%, with wafer fab equipment at $143.9 billion, and a 2028 figure of $229 billion. Lam's own view of 2026 wafer fab equipment is in the mid-$150 billion range; the two differ in how they define the market, and we do not reconcile them here.
fund.overview.1

The segments are wafer fab equipment, test, and assembly and packaging. SEMI's July forecast has test equipment up 31% to about $15 billion and assembly and packaging up 9% to about $6 billion. Inside wafer fab equipment the main groups are lithography, deposition, etch and process control.
fund.overview.2

In the value chain, suppliers of components and subsystems feed the tool makers, who sell to chipmakers, who sell chips to designers and device makers. SEMI's 300mm fab outlook counts $133 billion of fab equipment spending in 2026 and $151 billion in 2027.
fund.overview.3

The industry has moved from a pandemic-era boom through a pause to a new cycle driven by AI chips and high-bandwidth memory. Quarterly billings reached $40.53 billion in Q2 2026, up 23% from a year earlier. Lam says leading growth is coming from DRAM, then leading-edge logic and NAND.
fund.overview.4

Spending is concentrated in Asia. SEMI expects China, Taiwan and South Korea to remain the largest equipment markets through 2028, and the 300mm outlook adds the Americas as a substantial spender, citing projects such as TSMC in Arizona and Intel in Ohio and Arizona. Production of the tools is concentrated in the U.S., the Netherlands and Japan.
fund.competition.0

The group is small. A handful of large vendors dominate: Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA, ASML, Tokyo Electron and Teradyne for test. Four of them reported quarterly revenue between $4.14 billion (KLA) and EUR 11.7 billion (ASML) in their latest quarters.
fund.competition.1

ASML is the leader in lithography, and its EUV systems have no commercial alternative; it expects about 65 low-NA EUV systems in 2026, against 44 in 2025. We did not find a sourced market-share table for the other categories, so we do not quote shares.
fund.competition.2

The industry is consolidated at the top, with each major vendor strong in specific process steps rather than competing across the board. Applied Materials is broad, Lam is concentrated in etch and deposition, KLA in process control and ASML in lithography.
fund.competition.3

Barriers to entry are very high: decades of accumulated process know-how, customers who qualify a tool for a specific manufacturing step, and large research budgets. Applied Materials alone spent $3.06 billion on research, development and engineering in nine months.
fund.competition.4

Economies of scale appear in research cost spread over a larger installed base and in service revenue. KLA's roughly 62% gross margin on revenue of $4.14 billion (our calculation) shows what scale in a niche can yield.
fund.competition.5

Products are differentiated, not commoditized, at the leading edge: EUV, advanced etch and high-end inspection. Mature-node tools face more competition, including from Chinese domestic suppliers, though we did not find a sourced figure for their share.
fund.competition.6

Bargaining power is mixed. Customers are few and large, but at the leading edge suppliers hold the stronger hand: ASML says its planned 2027 and 2028 supply will not fully meet demand and customers want to order for 2029 and 2030. Lam cites component shortages and clean-room availability as limits.
fund.drivers.0

Revenue growth follows chipmaker capex, which follows demand for AI chips and memory. Global chip sales were $517.7 billion in Q3 2026, up 24.1% on the quarter, and equipment billings rose 23% year on year in Q2.
fund.drivers.1

Operating margins depend on volume (operating leverage), product mix and service share. Lam's operating margin passed 40% for the first time in the September 2026 quarter, at 40.2%; Applied Materials was 34.0% non-GAAP in its July quarter.
fund.drivers.2
Key cost variables are research spending, component and subsystem costs, and logistics. Lam says component shortages pushed some December-quarter shipments into March.
fund.drivers.3

Interest-rate sensitivity is indirect: higher borrowing costs weigh on chipmakers' willingness to build fabs, but current orders look driven more by AI budgets than by credit conditions. We did not find a sourced reading on rates for this sub-industry, so this is our judgment.
fund.drivers.4
Inflation, GDP and commodity prices matter less than chip demand and policy. Trade policy matters more, through the share of sales that can go to China.
fund.drivers.5

The industry is cyclical, with a secular growth layer from rising process complexity. Damodaran's data show net capex of 4.14% of sales, and SEMI's forecast of $229 billion in 2028 against $165 billion in 2026 implies growth continuing.
fund.financials.0

Growth is currently very fast. Lam's September 2026 revenue was up 54% from a year earlier, KLA's up about 29%, Applied Materials' up 25% in the July quarter, and Teradyne's up 70% in its September quarter.
fund.financials.1

Damodaran's January 2026 data for 31 U.S. semiconductor equipment firms show a gross margin of 46.32% and a net margin of 21.32%. Current margins at the leaders are higher: Lam 52.4% gross, ASML 57.5%, Teradyne 59.1%.
fund.financials.2
Operating margins: Damodaran shows 26.17% pre-tax and 23.56% after-tax unadjusted. Lam reported 40.2% and Applied Materials 34.0% non-GAAP in their latest quarters.
fund.financials.3

Damodaran's January 2026 after-tax ROIC for the group is 45.31%, well above typical industries, a sign of high returns on a small invested capital base. Dataset footers disagree about its update date (header says January 2026), so treat as indicative.
fund.financials.4
Leverage is modest. Applied Materials had $6.54 billion of debt against $7.04 billion of cash; Teradyne reported no short-term debt and $460.7 million of cash.
fund.financials.5

Free cash flow is strong: Lam $3.24 billion in the September 2026 quarter, KLA $1.34 billion, and Teradyne about $227 million by our calculation. Capex is light: Applied Materials spent $707 million in its July quarter, and Damodaran shows net capex at 4.14% of sales.
fund.financials.6

Damodaran's EV/EBITDA for the group was 24.74 times (positive-EBITDA firms) and EV/EBIT 28.81 times on January 2026 data. Prices have moved since; SOXX, a broader semiconductor fund, showed a P/E of 41.57 on 5 Nov 2026.
fund.risks.0

Regulation is the largest policy risk. The MATCH Act would require allies to align on tool controls within 150 days or face unilateral U.S. action, and covers DUV immersion lithography. It was introduced in April 2026; we did not confirm its current status.
fund.risks.1

Technology disruption is mostly an opportunity: AI chips and HBM add process steps. The risk is the reverse, an efficiency shift that lowers chip volume needs. We found no sourced evidence of this happening.
fund.risks.2
Demographics hardly matter for the industry directly, and only through end demand for electronics. Our read is that the AI buildout matters far more than population trends.
fund.risks.3

Changing consumer behavior is a second-order factor. Tool demand follows data-centre and device chip orders, not consumer choices directly. We did not find a sourced figure for consumer-driven demand.
fund.risks.4

New competitors are a risk mainly in mature-node tools from China, where policy is pushing domestic supply. Customers in China bought heavily: they were 35% of Lam's September 2026 revenue, though ASML expects China at about 20% of 2026 sales.
fund.risks.5

Geopolitical and supply-chain risks are material: Lam cites component shortages and clean-room availability, and China made up about 30% of ASML's sales last year. Taiwan and Korea concentrate customer spending.
fund.risks.6

Substitutes are limited for the main tools; there is no commercial alternative to EUV for the smallest features. Alternative architectures such as chiplets and advanced packaging change the tool mix but raise packaging spend.
horizon.opportunities.0
SEMI's mid-year forecast points to equipment sales of about $229 billion in 2028, from about $165 billion in 2026.
horizon.opportunities.1
Lam's preliminary view of 2027 wafer fab equipment is above $200 billion, led by DRAM, then leading-edge logic and NAND.
horizon.opportunities.2
SEMI counts $228 billion of logic and $175 billion of memory fab equipment spending cumulatively over 2027-2029.
horizon.opportunities.3
ASML sees customers wanting to order for 2029 and 2030 and expects pricing to contribute from 2027.
horizon.threats.0
Tool supply is constrained by components and clean-room space, which could push revenue out.
horizon.threats.1
The MATCH Act and similar rules could cut China sales, which were 35% of Lam's latest quarter.
horizon.threats.2
A pause in AI-related chipmaker budgets would hit memory and leading-edge orders first; we found no sourced sign of one yet.
horizon.assessment

Over the next three to five years we think the sub-industry's direction is set by whether chipmakers keep building for AI. Current signals are strong: record results across Lam, KLA, ASML and Applied Materials, forecasts of rising spending through 2028, and suppliers who say they cannot meet planned demand. The offsets are supply limits, policy on China and the cyclical habit of overbuilding. Our read is that growth is likely to stay positive but uneven, with lumpy quarters from shipment timing, and that a year of lower spending is the normal pattern after a surge like this one.
sec.macro.0

Chip equipment sits at the front of the semiconductor cycle, and the cycle is in an extraordinary upswing. The Semiconductor Industry Association reported on 3 Nov 2026 that global chip sales reached $517.7 billion in the third quarter, up 24.1% on the second, with September sales up 146.8% from a year earlier. Equipment follows that spending with a lag: SEMI said Q2 2026 equipment billings were $40.53 billion, up 23% year on year and 11% on the quarter.
sec.macro.1

Broader markets are not stretched. FactSet put the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 17.7 on 6 Nov 2026, below its 5-year average of 19.8 and 10-year average of 19.1, and estimated calendar 2026 earnings growth at 33.3%. Interest rates and currency matter less here than customer budgets, and we did not find a sourced reading of policy rates for this brief. Our read is that the risk to the cycle is not recession but a pause in AI-related chip spending, which would reach tool orders after a delay. Supply is also a macro limit: Lam says component shortages moved some December-quarter shipments into March.
sec.demand.0

Structural demand rests on chips getting more complex and on AI infrastructure. SEMI's mid-year forecast has total equipment sales at about $165 billion in 2026, up 23%, with wafer fab equipment at $143.9 billion and a 2028 figure of $229 billion. SEMI's 300mm outlook projects fab equipment spending of $133 billion in 2026 and $151 billion in 2027. Lam's preliminary 2027 view is above $200 billion of wafer fab equipment, led by DRAM; the definitions of these totals differ, so we compare direction, not levels.
sec.demand.1

Mix matters. Over 2027-2029 SEMI counts $228 billion of logic and micro spending, driven mainly by sub-2nm foundry capacity, and $175 billion for memory, of which $111 billion is DRAM and $62 billion 3D NAND. ASML says its 2026 memory system sales will rise about 75% and logic about 10%.
sec.demand.2

Demand is cyclical and elastic to chipmaker profits, but the pull of AI is long-dated: ASML reports that customers want to order for 2029 and 2030. Demographics matter only through end-device demand, which we think is far less important than the AI buildout.
sec.structure.0

Porter's five forces point to a favourable structure at the top. Rivalry is limited among a few large vendors with different specialties: ASML in lithography, Lam in etch and deposition, KLA in process control, Applied Materials across many steps, and Teradyne in test. Threat of new entrants is low because of qualification time and research budgets; Applied Materials spent $3.06 billion on research, development and engineering over nine months.
sec.structure.1

Buyer power is concentrated but tempered by scarcity: a few chipmakers buy, yet ASML says planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not meet demand and it is looking to lift 2028 capacity beyond a 30% increase. Supplier power rises when scarce components are the bottleneck, as Lam's comments on shortages show. Substitutes are few: ASML's EUV has no commercial alternative.
sec.structure.2

We did not find a sourced market-share table across categories. Pricing power looks strongest where products are unique: ASML expects price increases to begin contributing in 2027 and take full effect from 2028. Moats are technology, installed base and service. Applied Global Services brought in $1.78 billion in its July 2026 quarter. Chinese buyers use mature-node tools heavily, where competition is likelier.
sec.environment.0

Policy is the main outside force. U.S. export controls restrict which tools can go to which Chinese chipmakers, and Congress is pushing further. The MATCH Act, introduced in early April 2026, would direct Commerce to identify choke-point equipment, bar sale or servicing at targeted Chinese facilities, and give allies 150 days to strengthen their controls before the U.S. extends its Foreign Direct Product Rule. It covers DUV immersion lithography and names Hua Hong, ChangXin and Yangtze Memory facilities. We did not confirm whether it has passed.
sec.environment.1

Exposure to China has been falling but remains large. China was 28% of Applied Materials' July 2026 quarter revenue, against 35% a year earlier. For Lam it was 35% in the September 2026 quarter, up from 26% in June, with a significant decline expected in the December quarter. ASML expects China at roughly 20% of 2026 sales, versus about 30% last year.
sec.environment.2

Technology is largely a tailwind. ASML's High-NA EUV, with Intel having exposed more than one million wafers, and the next low-NA system shipping in small quantities in early 2027, extend its lead. Other PESTEL factors: government subsidy programmes support fab building in the U.S. and elsewhere, as SEMI's 300mm outlook notes for TSMC and Intel projects; supply chains for components are a physical constraint.
sec.economics.0

Economics are among the best in the market and have improved. Lam's September 2026 quarter showed revenue of $8.22 billion, gross margin of 52.4%, operating margin of 40.2% and free cash flow of $3.24 billion. ASML's Q3 gross margin was 57.5% on EUR 11.7 billion of sales. Teradyne's was 59.1% on $1.31 billion. KLA's revenue was $4.14 billion and free cash flow $1.34 billion; from the release we calculate a gross margin near 62% and an operating margin near 45%.
sec.economics.1

Operating leverage explains the pace. Applied Materials grew revenue 25% year on year in its July quarter and non-GAAP EPS 41%. The structural base is strong: Damodaran's January 2026 data for 31 U.S. semiconductor equipment firms show 46.32% gross margin, 21.32% net margin and after-tax ROIC of 45.31%, all before the 2026 surge.
sec.economics.2

Capital intensity is low for the sellers. Damodaran shows net capex of 4.14% of sales, and Applied Materials spent $707 million on capex in a quarter with $9.12 billion of revenue. Cash is returned: KLA repurchased $935.8 million of stock and paid $305.1 million in dividends in the quarter; ASML repurchased about EUR 4.1 billion in Q3. Teradyne's gross margin eased slightly from 59.8% in Q2 and revenue slipped from $1,329 million, so margins are not rising everywhere.
sec.earnings.0

Guidance points to a further step up. Applied Materials guided its October quarter to revenue of $10.25 billion plus or minus $0.5 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $4.02. Lam guided December to $8.6 billion plus or minus $0.4 billion and EPS of $2.33, with operating margin of 40.5%. KLA guided to $4.7 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $1.44. ASML guided Q4 net sales to EUR 14.2-15.2 billion and 2026 to EUR 44-45 billion. Teradyne guided to $1.25-1.35 billion, flat to slightly down from Q3.
sec.earnings.1

Management commentary supports 2027: Lam's preliminary view is wafer fab equipment above $200 billion, and ASML says planned supply will not meet 2027-2028 demand. Both flag supply limits that could cap how much is delivered.
sec.earnings.2

We could not source consensus estimates for this sub-industry or its estimate-revision trend. At the market level, FactSet shows Q3 2026 blended S&P 500 EPS growth of 31.4%, with information technology among the leading sectors and the leaders of positive surprises, and calendar 2026 growth of 33.3%. Our view is that guidance is more informative than consensus here, because shipment timing can move revenue between quarters, and that the differences to watch are supply, not demand.
sec.valuation.0

We could not find a sourced forward P/E or free-cash-flow yield for this sub-industry, so we use proxies. Damodaran's January 2026 data for 31 U.S. semiconductor equipment firms show EV/EBITDA of 24.74 times and EV/EBIT of 28.81 times on positive-EBITDA firms. Those are trailing multiples from before the 2026 surge in earnings, so they overstate today's multiple on current earnings; we cannot say by how much.
sec.valuation.1

The broader market is not expensive on FactSet's measure: the S&P 500 forward P/E was 17.7 on 6 Nov 2026 against 19.8 for the 5-year and 19.1 for the 10-year average. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, SOXX, which is about 84% semiconductors and 16% equipment, showed a P/E of 41.57 on 5 Nov 2026. That is a trailing-style fund figure for a broader group, not a measure of equipment makers.
sec.valuation.2

Our read is that the group is priced for the growth the guidance describes, including a 2027 market above $200 billion, and that the margin for disappointment is on supply and timing rather than demand. Applied Materials generated $3.04 billion of cash from operations in one quarter; Lam generated $3.24 billion of free cash flow. Without a sourced sub-industry multiple we do not claim a premium or discount to history.
sec.positioning.0

Equipment makers are held mostly through semiconductor funds. SMH, a 26-stock fund with $67.25 billion of assets on 5 Nov 2026, held KLA at 4.21%, ASML at 4.45%, Applied Materials at 4.05% and Lam at 3.60%, about 16.3% together (our sum), against 20.47% for Nvidia. SOXX had $37.56 billion of net assets, 15.89% in semiconductor equipment and a year-to-date NAV return of 30.71% on 5 Nov 2026.
sec.positioning.1

That leaves the group tied to the AI trade through its funds as well as its customers. We did not find sourced fund-flow, short-interest or breadth data for equipment stocks specifically, so we do not draw conclusions on positioning.
sec.positioning.2

In our view momentum is supported by results and guidance, but sentiment is sensitive to policy headlines on China and to any sign that chipmakers are slowing orders. Teradyne is the reminder that strong demand does not mean every quarter rises, with Q3 revenue slightly below Q2.
summary

Communications Equipment has become an AI-networking story with a flat telecom backdrop. Cisco booked $9.3 billion of hyperscale AI orders in fiscal 2026, about 4.5 times the prior year, and Arista's third-quarter revenue grew 58.5% to $3.66 billion. Ciena and Nokia report optical and IP growth tied to cloud builders, while Ericsson calls the mobile RAN market flat. Dell'Oro expects supply, not demand, to constrain AI switching for one to two years. Component costs are weighing on margins at Arista and Ericsson. Sub-industry consensus and forward multiples were not available to us; Damodaran's January 2026 data is the multiple reference.
basics.intro

These companies build the equipment that moves data: routers and switches in offices and data centres, optical gear that carries traffic over long distances, Wi-Fi access points, and the radio and core equipment telecom operators use for mobile networks. GICS also puts two-way radios and public-safety communications here, as with Motorola Solutions. Customers are telecom carriers, cloud giants and enterprises. Revenue comes from hardware, software and recurring support. Handsets and servers sit in Technology Hardware, Storage and Peripherals, and chips sit in Semiconductors.
basics.products.0

Data-centre switching and routing: High-speed Ethernet switches and routers that connect servers and AI accelerators inside and between data centres. Speeds are quoted in gigabits per second. e.g. Arista Etherlink and EOS, Cisco Silicon One systems, Nokia IP Networks
basics.products.1

Campus networking and Wi-Fi: Switches and wireless access points that connect offices, schools and homes, usually managed through cloud software. e.g. Cisco Catalyst and Meraki, HPE Aruba and Juniper Mist, Ubiquiti UniFi
basics.products.2

Optical transport and optics: Gear that sends light signals across fibre between cities and data centres, plus pluggable optical modules that fit into switches. e.g. Ciena WaveLogic, Nokia Optical Networks, Cisco coherent optics
basics.products.3
Mobile network equipment: Radios, antennas and core software that let carriers run 4G and 5G networks. Sales follow carrier spending cycles. e.g. Ericsson Networks, Nokia Mobile Infrastructure
basics.products.4

Mission-critical communications: Two-way radios, emergency-dispatch networks, video security and related software sold to police, fire services and governments. e.g. Motorola Solutions radios, body cameras and command-centre software
basics.products.5

Software, security and support: Subscriptions, security products and support contracts sold on top of the hardware, which smooth out lumpy hardware sales. e.g. Cisco Security and Splunk, Arista CloudVision, Motorola Software and Services
basics.drivers.0

Cloud and AI capex: Hyperscalers' spending on data centres turns into orders for switches, routers and optics within quarters. Raised spending guidance lifts order books; paused projects delay shipments.
basics.drivers.1
Carrier spending cycles: Telecom operators buy radio and optical gear in waves tied to 5G build-outs and network upgrades. Mobile equipment revenue is flat when carriers hold back budgets.
basics.drivers.2
Enterprise refresh: Companies replace Wi-Fi and campus switches on multi-year cycles, with new standards such as Wi-Fi 7 acting as triggers. It supports steady orders and software attach.
basics.drivers.3
Component costs and supply: Memory, switch chips and optical parts are bought in. When they rise or run short, vendors either raise prices or accept lower gross margin, and shipments can lag orders.
basics.drivers.4
Product mix: Systems sold to hyperscalers often carry lower gross margins than campus or software products, so faster AI growth can dilute margins even as profit dollars rise.
basics.drivers.5
Public-sector budgets: Government and public-safety customers buy on multi-year budgets and long contracts. This gives Motorola Solutions a backlog that moves slowly.
basics.terms.0
Hyperscaler: A very large cloud operator such as Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet or Meta. Its orders are large and uneven, so a few customers can move a vendor's results.
basics.terms.1
Back-end network: The network that links AI accelerators to each other inside a training cluster. Front-end networks connect servers to users and storage.
basics.terms.2
Scale-out, scale-up, scale-across: Ways of linking AI chips: scale-up inside a rack, scale-out across racks in a building, scale-across between buildings. Each needs different switches or optics.
basics.terms.3
Ethernet vs InfiniBand: Two networking standards for AI clusters. Ethernet is open and sold by many vendors; InfiniBand is mainly Nvidia's.
basics.terms.4
Merchant silicon: Switch chips sold by outside chip makers rather than designed in-house. Vendors using it compete on software and system design.
basics.terms.5
Coherent optics: Technology that packs more data into each fibre by encoding it on the light wave. It lets operators carry more traffic over existing fibre.
basics.terms.6
RAN: Radio access network: the towers, radios and baseband equipment that connect phones to a carrier. It is the core of Ericsson's and Nokia's mobile business.
basics.terms.7
Backlog / RPO: Contracted but not yet recognised revenue. Remaining performance obligations (RPO) is the accounting version. It shows visibility but not margin.
basics.terms.8
Deferred revenue: Cash received for products or services not yet delivered or recognised, often from multi-year deals. Arista's deferred revenue is watched as a sign of AI demand.
basics.terms.9
Non-GAAP margin: Operating margin excluding items such as stock compensation and acquisition costs. Companies here report it prominently, so compare with GAAP.
basics.terms.10
Channel inventory: Stock held by distributors and resellers. Cisco and others sell through two tiers of channel, so shifts in that stock can distort end-demand.
basics.terms.11
Design win: A customer choosing a vendor's product for a future build. Revenue arrives months or years later as the customer deploys.
watch.0
Whether hyperscaler capex keeps rising into 2027: Alphabet and Amazon both signalled higher spending, while Meta's budget is unset.
watch.1
Supply limits: Dell'Oro expects AI switching to stay supply-constrained for at least one to two years, so shipments, not orders, may set the pace.
watch.2
Gross-margin pressure from mix and component costs, visible at Arista (64.0% vs 65.2%), and Ericsson, which flags 2027.
watch.3
Cisco's fiscal 2027 guide of $72.2-73.4 billion revenue and whether hyperscale AI orders, $4 billion in the July quarter, keep climbing.
watch.4
Customer concentration at the optical and switching names: two customers were 41.7% of Ciena's revenue, and Arista depends on large cloud operators.
bellwethers
Cisco Systems, Arista Networks, Motorola Solutions, Ciena, Nokia, Ericsson, Ubiquiti, Juniper (now HPE)
fund.business.0

Revenue comes from hardware (switches, routers, optical systems, radios), software and subscriptions, and support and services. Cisco's non-GAAP gross margin was 66.3% in its July 2026 quarter, with services at 71.6% against 64.8% for products.
