Test and measurement gear sits in Electronic Equipment and Instruments, contract assemblers in Electronic Manufacturing Services, and chips in Semiconductors.
basics.products.0
Connectors and interconnect: Plugs, sockets, cables and assemblies that link boards, boxes and vehicles, from high-speed data links to rugged power connectors. e.g. Amphenol, TE Connectivity, Molex
basics.products.1

Passive components: Capacitors, resistors and inductors that store charge, limit current and filter signals on every circuit board. They are cheap per part but needed in huge numbers. e.g. Murata and Vishay capacitors and resistors
basics.products.2
Sensors: Devices that measure pressure, temperature, position or current and turn it into an electrical signal, widely used in vehicles and factories. e.g. TE Connectivity and Amphenol sensors
basics.products.3
Circuit protection and power control: Fuses, switches and other parts that protect equipment from surges and overloads and control power in vehicles and industrial systems. e.g. Littelfuse
basics.products.4
Optical connectivity: Fibre, cable and connectors that carry data as light inside data centres and across telecom networks. e.g. Corning Optical Communications
basics.products.5
Display and specialty glass: Glass for screens, vehicles and other uses, a materials business that GICS places here alongside electronic parts. e.g. Corning Glass Innovations
basics.drivers.0

Data-centre and AI build-out: AI servers use more high-speed connectors, optical links and capacitors per rack than ordinary servers. Orders and backlog rise first, then revenue, so the segment is a main growth engine.
basics.drivers.1
Automotive and electrification: More sensors, connectors and power-protection parts go into each vehicle, but sales follow vehicle production, which is cyclical and tariff-sensitive.
basics.drivers.2

Industrial and defence spending: Factory automation, energy and aerospace buy rugged, long-life parts. Orders follow capital spending and government budgets, with longer product cycles than consumer goods.
basics.drivers.3
Consumer device volumes: Phones and PCs use many commodity parts. Weak unit demand cuts volume and prices for the simplest parts quickly.
basics.drivers.4

Capacity and supply tightness: Ceramic capacitors and similar parts need years to expand capacity. When demand jumps, shortages let suppliers raise prices and widen margins; when supply catches up, pricing reverses.
basics.drivers.5
Metals and input costs: Copper, gold, silver, palladium and plastics are major inputs. Makers pass costs through with a lag, so quick metal moves can squeeze or flatter margins.
basics.drivers.6
Acquisitions: The leaders buy product lines to widen coverage. Deals lift reported growth and add debt and integration costs.
basics.terms.0
Passive component: A part that does not amplify or switch a signal, such as a capacitor, resistor or inductor. Each is cheap, but boards use hundreds or thousands of them.
basics.terms.1
MLCC: Multilayer ceramic capacitor, the most common capacitor type. Servers, phones and cars use huge numbers, and high-capacitance versions can run short in an AI build-out.
basics.terms.2
Interconnect: The wiring layer that links chips, boards and systems: connectors, cables and backplanes. Speed and reliability requirements make it a design-led, not a pure commodity, business.
basics.terms.3
Content per device: The dollar value of a company's parts in one phone, car or server. Rising content (for example in AI servers or electric vehicles) lets sales grow faster than unit volumes.
basics.terms.4
Design-in: When a customer's engineers choose a specific part for a product that will ship for years. It creates sticky revenue and makes switching suppliers costly.
basics.terms.5
Book-to-bill: Orders divided by shipments in a period. Above 1.0 means the order book is growing and future revenue should rise.
basics.terms.6
Backlog: Orders booked but not yet shipped. It gives visibility, and in shortages it also shows how long customers are queuing.
basics.terms.7
Organic growth: Growth excluding acquisitions, disposals and currency. It shows whether the existing business is expanding or whether deals are doing the work.
basics.terms.8
Core sales: Corning's adjusted sales measure, which excludes certain items such as the effects of hedging. Read the reconciliation to GAAP sales.
basics.terms.9
Distribution channel: Sales through distributors rather than directly to manufacturers. Distributor stocking can amplify swings when they build or run down inventory.
basics.terms.10
Harsh environment: Connectors and sensors built to survive heat, vibration, moisture or radiation, as in aircraft, military and industrial equipment. They carry higher margins than standard parts.
basics.terms.11
Operating leverage: Fixed plant and engineering costs spread over more sales. When volumes jump, margin rises faster than revenue; when they fall, it drops faster too.
watch.0
Fourth-quarter guidance sets the bar: Amphenol guides sales of $10.3-10.5B excluding deals not yet closed, Corning $5.2-5.3B of core sales, Vishay about $990M and Littelfuse $750-770M.
watch.1
High-end MLCC (multilayer ceramic capacitor) shortages are expected to last through 1H27, price talks for 1Q27 begin in November, and Murata says new capacity is unlikely before 2028.
watch.2
Amphenol's CommScope integration: the 10-K expects net interest expense to rise from $367.8M in 2025 to about $800M in 2026 after the debt-funded deal.
watch.3
Policy and costs: the Fed held at 3.75-4.00% with two dissents favouring a hike, the ISM prices index is 75.2, and TE carries an $87M reconciling item for IEEPA tariff refunds.
watch.4
Consumer weakness is the offset: major notebook makers expect 4Q26 orders down 10-15% year on year.
bellwethers
Amphenol, TE Connectivity, Corning, Littelfuse, Vishay Intertechnology, Murata Manufacturing
fund.business.0

Revenue comes from selling physical parts and assemblies in large volumes: connectors, cables, sensors, capacitors, fuses, optical fibre and glass. Amphenol reports three segments, Communications Solutions (52% of 2025 sales), Harsh Environment Solutions (26%) and Interconnect and Sensor Systems (22%). TE splits into Transportation (54%) and Industrial (46%). Software and services are a minor share.
fund.business.1

Customers are manufacturers: Amphenol sells to thousands of OEMs, EMS companies, ODMs and service providers, with distributors about 19% of 2025 sales and no customer at 10% or more. Its end markets were IT datacom about 36%, industrial 19%, automotive 15%, communications networks 10% and defence 9%. TE had about 41% of fiscal 2025 sales in automotive.
fund.business.2

Principal costs are raw materials, manufacturing labour, and engineering. Raw materials include gold, silver and palladium for plating, copper, aluminium, steel and plastic resins. TE has about 93,000 employees, roughly 55,000 of them in manufacturing; Amphenol has about 170,000. Damodaran's broad Electronics (General) group spends 4.23% of sales on R&D.
fund.business.3

Pricing power rests on design-in, qualification and specialisation. Standard parts compete on price and delivery, while high-speed, harsh-environment and optical products earn more: Amphenol's Communications Solutions margin was 33.1% against 20.0% in Interconnect and Sensor Systems. In shortages pricing power shifts to suppliers, as with high-end MLCCs.
fund.business.4

Main assets are plants, inventory, receivables, and acquired goodwill. Liabilities are mainly debt taken for acquisitions: on our arithmetic from the balance sheet, Amphenol's debt less cash was about $12.6B at 30 September 2026, Corning's debt was $8.2B and Littelfuse's net debt was $437.3M.
fund.business.5

The business is moderately capital-intensive, between asset-light and heavy industry. Damodaran's Electronics (General) group has net capex of 5.68% of sales against 4.23% for the whole US market. Vishay spent $253.4M on capex in nine months, $47.5M in its latest quarter. Roughly 79% of Amphenol's long-lived assets sit outside the US, about 37% in China.
fund.overview.0

No single authoritative figure covers the whole sub-industry. Bishop & Associates says the global connector market grew by more than $12.7B in 2025, or 14.7%; that growth rate implies a base of about $86B in 2024 and roughly $99B in 2025 on our arithmetic. TE puts the combined market its two segments serve at about $200B. We found no sourced passive-components market size.
fund.overview.1

Main segments are connectors and interconnect, passive components, sensors, circuit protection, optical connectivity and display glass. Bishop ranks telecom and datacom first among connector end uses, driven by data centres and AI, and automotive second. Corning's largest segment is Optical Communications at $2,379M of Q3 core sales.
fund.overview.2

In the value chain these firms sit between materials suppliers (metals, resins, ceramic and glass inputs) and equipment makers, EMS contractors and distributors, which assemble the parts into servers, vehicles and devices. Chips are bought and sold separately; the parts here connect and protect them.
fund.overview.3

The industry has shifted toward AI-linked and electrified end markets and consolidated. Amphenol spent about $3.8B on five acquisitions in 2025 and closed the $10.5B CommScope business in January 2026, the largest in its history. Connector growth was uneven by region: Asia Pacific rose 32.6% in 2025 and Japan 2.9%.
fund.overview.4

Sales are global but production is Asia-heavy. About 65% of Amphenol's 2025 sales were outside the US, with China about 16%. TE's fiscal 2025 split was Asia-Pacific 38%, EMEA 33% and Americas 29%, with about 25% of sales to Chinese customers. Bishop reports Asia Pacific as the fastest-growing connector region.
fund.competition.0

There are thousands of competitors, but a handful of scaled players. TE says it competes with thousands of firms, from multinationals to local manufacturers. Amphenol names Aptiv, Belden, Corning, Foxconn Interconnect, Glenair, Huber+Suhner, Luxshare, Jonhon, Molex, Rosenberger, Sensata, TE and Yazaki.
fund.competition.1

Leaders are Amphenol, with $10.2B of Q3 2026 sales, and TE, with $19.9B of fiscal 2026 sales. In optical and glass, Corning had $5.1B of Q3 core sales. In passives, TrendForce names Murata and Samsung Electro-Mechanics among the key MLCC suppliers, and Vishay's quarterly sales were $978.9M. We found no sourced market-share percentages, so we quote none.
fund.competition.2

The group is fragmented overall but concentrated in niches such as high-speed data connectors and high-capacitance MLCCs, where a few firms supply most of the volume. The leaders keep consolidating, as Amphenol's CommScope deal shows.
fund.competition.3

Barriers to entry include qualification and design-in cycles, global manufacturing and service networks, tooling and process know-how, and capital for capacity. In MLCCs, capacity takes years to add: Murata says new capacity is unlikely before 2028. Amphenol cites technology, quality, price, service and delivery time as the competitive basis.
fund.competition.4

Economies of scale matter in purchasing, tooling, global plants and engineering. Amphenol's 29.5% operating margin and TE's 22.1% adjusted margin sit well above Damodaran's 10.42% pre-tax margin for the broad Electronics (General) group, which includes lower-margin assemblers.
fund.competition.5

Products range from commodity to highly differentiated. Consumer-grade MLCCs are close to commodities and spot prices fell about 5% in early October, while high-end AI-grade parts are in shortage. Gross margins show the split: Vishay 25.5% against Damodaran's group at 26.76%.
fund.competition.6

Bargaining power depends on the part. Large server, auto and phone makers negotiate hard on standard parts, while suppliers hold power in shortages: TrendForce says the shortage gives suppliers leverage in pricing talks. Customers are diversified, as Amphenol has no customer at 10% or more of sales, which limits any one buyer's leverage. Raw material suppliers are fragmented, but metals prices pass through with a lag.
fund.drivers.0

Revenue growth follows end-market demand and content per device. AI infrastructure is currently the strongest: Amphenol's orders of $12.2B and organic growth of 37%, TE's Industrial sales growth of 19.8% in the fiscal fourth quarter, and Corning's Optical Communications segment at $2,379M. Acquisitions added 28 points to Amphenol's growth.
fund.drivers.1

Operating margins depend on volume leverage, mix, pricing and input costs. Amphenol's adjusted operating margin was 29.7% on sales up 65%, and its Communications Solutions segment earned 33.1%. Vishay's operating margin was 9.4% on a 25.5% gross margin.
fund.drivers.2

Key costs are metals (copper, gold, silver, palladium), plastics, labour and freight. TrendForce says nickel, copper and silver raised electrode material costs, with Japan's import price index up 24.5% year on year in September. The ISM raw-materials price index has risen 25 months straight.
fund.drivers.3

Interest-rate sensitivity is moderate. Customers' capital spending is financed, and the leaders carry acquisition debt: Amphenol expects net interest expense to rise to about $800M in 2026. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October with two members preferring a hike. Damodaran's broad group has debt of 2.69 times EBITDA versus 6.52 for the market.
fund.drivers.4

Inflation, GDP and employment matter through manufacturing activity and consumer spending. The ISM Manufacturing PMI was 55.5 in October, the tenth straight month of expansion, with prices at 75.2. Commodity prices pass through to costs with a lag. Weak consumer spending shows in notebook orders expected down 10-15%.
fund.drivers.5

The group is cyclical, with secular growth layers. Datacom, electrification and automation are structural drivers, while consumer electronics and inventory swings are cyclical. Vishay's book-to-bill of 1.29 and Bishop's 14.7% connector growth in 2025 show an upswing phase.
fund.financials.0

Growth is strong but uneven. In the latest quarters Amphenol grew 65% (organic 37%), TE 11.9% (13.4% organic), Corning's core sales 19%, Vishay 24% and Littelfuse 22.7%. FactSet puts the broader Electronic Equipment, Instruments and Components industry at 27% blended Q3 revenue growth and 46% earnings growth.
fund.financials.1

Margins vary with mix. Damodaran's Electronics (General) group of 114 US firms has a 26.76% gross margin, 10.42% pre-tax operating margin and 6.47% net margin as of January 2026. Leaders are higher: Amphenol 29.5%, Corning 22.7% core, Littelfuse 20.0%, TE 22.1% adjusted; Vishay is lower at 9.4%.
fund.financials.2

Returns on capital are high on Damodaran's data: after-tax ROIC of 24.48% against 10.08% for the total market and a ten-year normalized ROIC of 17.47% against 7.72%. The page's header says January 2026 but its footer says January 2025, so the vintage is uncertain. The table has no ROE column, so we quote none.
fund.financials.3

Leverage is moderate for the broad group, with book debt to capital of 33.97% against 61.72% for the market and debt of 2.69 times EBITDA against 6.52. Company balance sheets vary: Littelfuse net debt is $437.3M, Vishay holds $1,139.9M of cash against $735.5M of long-term debt, and Amphenol and Corning carry far more after deals.
fund.financials.4

Free cash flow is solid. Amphenol generated $1,622.7M in Q3, about 16% of sales on our arithmetic; TE $3,412M for fiscal 2026, about 17% of sales; Corning $661M adjusted; Vishay $98.5M; Littelfuse $215.7M. Quarterly figures are not annual run-rates.
fund.financials.5

Capital spending needs are moderate and rise with capacity expansions. Damodaran's group shows capex at 141.09% of depreciation, versus 148.57% for the market, and net capex of 5.68% of sales. Vishay's quarterly capex was about 4.9% of sales on our arithmetic.
fund.financials.6

Valuation: Damodaran's January 2026 data show Electronics (General) at a forward P/E of 29.61x against 27.66x for the whole US market and EV/EBITDA of 19.99x for positive-EBITDA firms against 19.73x. These are broad-proxy figures ten months old; current multiples for the GICS sub-industry were not available to us.
fund.risks.0

Regulatory risk is mostly trade policy. Amphenol's 10-K flags new US tariffs, retaliation and export restrictions, and a Chinese tax challenge with potential cost of $100M to $300M, of which $100M is recorded. TE cites tariffs and trade barriers and has an $87M reconciling item tied to IEEPA tariff refunds.
fund.risks.1

Technology and AI are mainly a tailwind, since AI servers lift demand for connectors, optics and capacitors. The disruption risk is faster architecture change: for example, TrendForce notes the shift from AI training to inference is changing which parts are short. We think the larger risk is an AI-spending pause after a heavy order surge.
fund.risks.2

Demographic effects are small and indirect; we found no sourced evidence that they move this industry. Ageing populations raise medical and automation demand at the margin, and medical was the slowest-growing connector end use at 5.9% in 2025.
fund.risks.3

Consumer behaviour matters for phones and PCs. TrendForce says consumer MLCC demand is weak, with notebook ODMs expecting 4Q26 orders down 10-15% and smartphone brands cutting entry and midrange shipments. Mobile devices were only about 6% of Amphenol's 2025 sales.
fund.risks.4

New competitors include Chinese and Taiwanese suppliers that gain spillover consumer orders, and Chinese connector firms such as Luxshare and Jonhon, which Amphenol names as competitors. New business models are limited because the product is physical.
fund.risks.5

Geopolitics and supply chain are material. About 25% of TE's fiscal 2025 sales went to Chinese customers and it has 19 principal plants there; China is about 16% of Amphenol's sales and 37% of its long-lived assets. Currency also matters: about 60% of TE's sales are in non-dollar currencies, unhedged.
fund.risks.6

Substitutes are limited for the core parts: signals still need physical or optical links and boards need capacitors. Wireless links, higher integration of passives into chips and package-level optics could reduce parts per device over time, but we found no sourced estimate, so this stays our judgment. Copper-to-optical shifts help Corning.
horizon.opportunities.0
AI and data-centre build-outs are lifting orders sharply, with Amphenol booking $12.2B of orders in one quarter and high-end MLCCs short into 2027.
horizon.opportunities.1
Electrification and automation keep raising content per vehicle and per factory, with Industrial the faster-growing TE segment at 19.8% in the quarter.
horizon.opportunities.2
Optical demand supports Corning, whose Optical Communications segment had $2,379M of Q3 core sales.
horizon.opportunities.3
Scale through acquisitions, such as Amphenol's $10.5B CommScope deal, widens product coverage in data networks.
horizon.threats.0
An AI-spending pause or inventory correction would hit orders from today's high base, and consumer demand is already weak.
horizon.threats.1
Tariffs and export restrictions could raise costs or block sales in China, where TE earns about 25% of sales.
horizon.threats.2
Metals and input-cost inflation can squeeze margins, with the ISM prices index at 75.2.
horizon.threats.3
Acquisition debt and higher-for-longer rates raise financing costs, such as Amphenol's rising interest expense.
horizon.assessment

We think the next three to five years favour suppliers tied to AI data centres, optical links and electrified vehicles, which are reporting record orders and rising margins. The structural story rests on content per device and on scarce, qualified capacity, particularly MLCCs, where relief is not expected before 2028. The caution is that the current surge sits on a narrow set of AI programmes and a shortage cycle, and shortages historically reverse when capacity arrives; consumer parts are already weak. Margin expansion at Amphenol and Littelfuse shows operating leverage, but the same leverage works in reverse. Acquisition integration and trade policy are the main execution risks. Valuation data for the sub-industry were not available to us, so we cannot say how much of this is priced in.
sec.macro.0

The cycle is supportive. The ISM Manufacturing PMI was 55.5 in October 2026, up from 54.5, the tenth straight month of expansion, with new orders at 55.5. That helps the industrial, automotive and equipment customers that buy connectors, sensors and protection parts. The ISM prices index was 75.2, down from 77.9 but still showing broad input-cost inflation, with raw material prices rising for 25 straight months.
sec.macro.1

The Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October, said inflation remains elevated, and recorded two dissents in favour of a quarter-point rise. Our read is that rates are a modest headwind for financed capital spending and acquisition-led strategies, not a threat to current demand. Amphenol's own 10-K expects net interest expense to rise from $367.8M to about $800M in 2026 after its CommScope purchase.
sec.macro.2

Trade policy and currency are swing factors. TE reports an $87M reconciling item related to IEEPA tariff refunds, and says about 60% of its fiscal 2025 sales were in non-dollar currencies and not hedged. Across the S&P 500, FactSet reports blended Q3 earnings growth of 30.2%, a strong backdrop for corporate spending.
sec.demand.0

The addressable market is large but is measured differently by each source. Bishop & Associates says the global connector market grew by more than $12.7B in 2025, or 14.7%, with telecom and datacom the leading end use and automotive second. TE says its two segments serve a market of about $200B. We found no sourced figure for passive components or the group as a whole.
sec.demand.1

Structural drivers are AI data centres, electrification, factory automation and aerospace and defence. Amphenol's IT datacom was about 36% of 2025 sales, and in Q3 2026 it booked $12.2B of orders against $10.2B of sales. Corning's Optical Communications segment reached $2,379M. TrendForce says AI servers and the shift to inference are lifting demand for high-capacitance MLCCs.
sec.demand.2

Demand is cyclical, with the consumer segment weakest: notebook makers expect 4Q26 orders down 10-15% and smartphone brands are cutting entry-level shipments. Demographics matter little directly. Our view is that long-term prospects are good, but today's growth rate is boosted by a shortage and an AI investment surge, and should not be extrapolated.
sec.structure.0

Applying Porter's five forces: rivalry is moderate to high in standard parts, where Amphenol lists more than a dozen named competitors including TE, Molex, Luxshare and Aptiv, and lower in specialised niches. The threat of new entrants is low at the high end, because of qualification, tooling and capacity needs, but higher in commodity parts where Chinese and Taiwanese suppliers are gaining orders.
sec.structure.1

Buyer power is mixed: large OEMs negotiate on standard parts, but Amphenol has no customer at 10% or more of sales, and in shortages suppliers hold the leverage, as TrendForce notes for high-end MLCCs. Supplier power is moderate: metals such as gold, silver, copper and palladium are bought on world markets, and electrode materials rose in cost. The threat of substitutes is limited, in our view, since signals still need physical or optical links.
sec.structure.2

Concentration is high in niches and low overall. We found no sourced market shares. The leaders are scaling up by acquisition: Amphenol spent about $3.8B on five deals in 2025 and then closed CommScope's connectivity business for about $10.5B. Moats are design-in relationships, qualified capacity and global plants; Murata says new MLCC capacity is unlikely before 2028.
sec.environment.0

Politics and trade dominate. Amphenol's 10-K lists new US tariffs, retaliation and export restrictions as risks, plus a Chinese tax dispute with potential costs of $100M to $300M, of which $100M is recorded. TE cites tariffs and trade barriers and its release shows a reconciling item of $87M for IEEPA tariff refunds.
sec.environment.1

Economically, input-cost inflation is the live issue. The ISM prices index was 75.2, and TrendForce says Japan's import price index rose 24.5% year on year in September, with nickel, copper and silver raising electrode costs. Technologically, AI is the main source of new demand, and the shift from training to inference is changing which components are short.
sec.environment.2

Social and environmental factors are secondary but real: electrification and energy-grid investment support demand for sensors, connectors and protection parts, and TE's Industrial Solutions includes energy (17% of the segment) and medical (9%). We did not find sector-specific regulation that is changing the economics of the group, apart from trade and export controls. Geopolitical concentration is a risk: Amphenol has about 37% of its long-lived assets in China.
sec.economics.0

Economics are attractive at the leaders. Damodaran's broad Electronics (General) group (114 US firms, January 2026) has a 26.76% gross margin, 10.42% pre-tax operating margin and 6.47% net margin, and after-tax ROIC of 24.48% against 10.08% for the whole market. The ROIC page's header and footer disagree on vintage, and it has no ROE column.
sec.economics.1

Bellwethers are above the broad average: Amphenol's GAAP operating margin was 29.5%, Corning's core operating margin 22.7%, TE's adjusted 22.1%, Littelfuse 20.0% and Vishay 9.4%. Operating leverage is visible: Vishay's gross margin rose from 19.5% to 25.5% on 24% sales growth, and Littelfuse's operating margin rose from 15.6% to 20.0%.
sec.economics.2

Capital intensity is moderate: Damodaran's group shows net capex of 5.68% of sales, and Vishay spent $47.5M on capex against $145.8M of operating cash flow in the quarter. Cash conversion is good: Amphenol's free cash flow was $1,622.7M in Q3 and TE's $3,412M for fiscal 2026. Margins are exposed to metals prices, tariffs and the end of shortage pricing.
sec.earnings.0

Reported earnings are strong. Amphenol's adjusted EPS was $0.80, up 74%, and it guides Q4 to $0.81-0.83 on sales of $10.3-10.5B, excluding acquisitions not yet closed. TE's adjusted EPS was $3.14, up 21%, and it guides fiscal Q1 2027 to about $3.30 on sales near $5.35B. Corning guides Q4 core EPS to $0.96-1.00, Vishay guides $990M of revenue and a 26.0% gross margin, and Littelfuse guides adjusted EPS of $5.05-5.25.
sec.earnings.1

Across the broader industry, FactSet reports Electronic Equipment, Instruments and Components blended Q3 earnings growth of 46% and revenue growth of 27%, as of 30 October. For the S&P 500 it reports 30.2% blended Q3 growth, with 82% of companies beating EPS estimates and Q4 growth of 28.4% expected. Sub-industry consensus and revision data were not available to us.
sec.earnings.2

Our view: the guidance implies growth continues but mostly at a slower sequential pace, for example Littelfuse's guide of $750-770M against $766.7M in Q3, which included a $28.5M one-time reduction. The risk is not the next quarter but whether record orders convert, given supply limits and a consumer slowdown.
sec.valuation.0

A current forward multiple for the GICS sub-industry was not available to us. The best proxy is Damodaran's Electronics (General) group of 114 US firms, which in January 2026 traded at a forward P/E of 29.61x against 27.66x for the total US market, and at 19.99x EV/EBITDA for positive-EBITDA firms against 19.73x. That group is a broad mix, and the data are ten months old.
sec.valuation.1

Market context is more current but on a different basis. FactSet puts the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 18.7 on 30 October 2026, below its five-year average of 19.8 and ten-year average of 19.1. Damodaran's market forward P/E of 27.66x is much higher because his method and date differ, so the two should not be compared directly.
sec.valuation.2

Our read: in January, the group traded at a modest premium to the market on both measures, which is not extreme for businesses with ROIC above the market. We cannot say where the sub-industry sits today relative to its own history without current data, and we do not draw a conclusion. Free-cash-flow yields were not available; the cash flows reported by the bellwethers are strong against their capital needs.
sec.positioning.0

Positioning data for this sub-industry, including ETF holdings and flows, short interest, relative performance and price momentum, were not available to us from the sources we opened, so we do not quote any.
sec.positioning.1

What we can say rests on earnings and orders, which are inputs to momentum. FactSet reports that the broader Electronic Equipment, Instruments and Components industry has the second-ranked earnings growth among the Information Technology industries at 46%, behind only Semiconductors at 132%. Breadth within the group is good: Amphenol, TE, Corning, Vishay and Littelfuse all reported growth of 11.9% or more.
sec.positioning.2

Share-price reactions to these reports were not available from the sources we opened. We think momentum will depend on whether record orders such as Amphenol's $12.2B convert into sales, on how long the MLCC shortage lasts, with TrendForce expecting it through 1H27, and on consumer-device demand, which is weakening.
summary

Electronic Manufacturing Services is in an AI-driven growth phase with thin margins. Jabil grew fiscal 2026 revenue about 21% to $36.0B and guides fiscal 2027 to $44.5B. Celestica's September-quarter revenue rose 83% and it guides 2027 to $40.0B. Flex, Fabrinet and Plexus also grew double digits, while Benchmark's growth was 19%. Margins stay in the mid-single to high-single digits, but returns on capital are strong at Celestica and Plexus. Consensus and valuation data for this exact sub-industry were not available to us; US manufacturing is expanding, with the ISM index at 55.5.
basics.intro

Electronic manufacturing services (EMS) companies build, test and ship electronic products designed and sold by other companies. Customers are brand owners in cloud and AI infrastructure, networking, medical, automotive, industrial, defence and consumer markets. Revenue comes from manufacturing programs, plus design, supply-chain and repair services, and most of the revenue is the pass-through cost of components. Margins are thin. GICS places these assemblers here; the brands they build for sit in hardware or other sub-industries, and component makers sit in Electronic Components.
basics.products.0
Printed circuit board assembly: Mounting chips and parts onto boards and testing them. This is the original EMS service and still the base of most programs. e.g. Benchmark, Sanmina, Plexus
basics.products.1

Data-centre systems and rack integration: Building servers, networking switches and full racks for cloud and AI customers, often with power and cooling, and shipping them ready to install. e.g. Celestica, Sanmina (ZT Systems), Jabil, Flex
basics.products.2
Regulated-industry manufacturing: Making medical, aerospace, defence and automotive electronics under strict quality rules, with long program lives and higher margins. e.g. Plexus, Benchmark, Jabil
basics.products.3
Optical and precision manufacturing: Assembling optical modules and complex hardware for communications and data-centre links, often in lower-cost Asian sites. e.g. Fabrinet
basics.products.4
Design, supply chain and aftermarket services: Engineering design, procurement, logistics, repair and recycling that keep a customer's product supplied through its life. e.g. Jabil, Flex, Plexus
basics.products.5
Power and thermal equipment: Power supplies, cooling and electrical infrastructure for data centres, increasingly made by the same companies. e.g. Flex Cloud and Power Infrastructure segment
basics.drivers.0

Customer end-market demand: EMS revenue is the sum of customers' unit builds. AI infrastructure, networking and medical programs have lifted growth, while weaker consumer or industrial demand shows up as cancelled or delayed orders within a quarter or two.
basics.drivers.1
Program wins and ramps: New wins add revenue over several quarters. Early production costs depress margins, then yields and volume improve them.
basics.drivers.2
Mix: Regulated-industry and complex systems work earn higher margins than commodity assembly, so a shift toward them lifts operating margin.
basics.drivers.3
Component cost and availability: Memory and chip shortages delay shipments and tie up working capital. Higher prices raise revenue under turnkey pricing but not profit dollars.
basics.drivers.4
Working capital and cash: Rapid growth means more inventory and receivables. Free cash flow can fall in a growth year, and financing rises.
basics.drivers.5
Trade policy and footprint: Tariffs and export controls change where products are built and who pays duties. Firms with multi-region factories can shift production.
basics.drivers.6
Capital allocation: Firms use cash for buybacks, capacity and acquisitions. Large deals such as Sanmina's ZT Systems purchase change scale and balance sheets.
basics.terms.0
OEM: Original equipment manufacturer: the brand that designs and sells the product and hires the EMS firm to build it.
basics.terms.1

Turnkey vs consignment: In turnkey work the EMS firm buys the components and bills for them, so revenue and working capital rise. In consignment the customer supplies parts and the EMS firm bills only for labour.
basics.terms.2
Core or adjusted operating margin: Operating profit excluding items such as stock compensation, amortization and restructuring. It is the figure most firms guide to; check the reconciliation to GAAP.
basics.terms.3
Program: A specific product a customer asks the EMS firm to build, with a ramp, a peak and an end of life. New program wins drive future revenue.
basics.terms.4
Ramp: The period when a new program rises from first units to volume. Ramps strain cash and margins before they help them.
basics.terms.5
Cash cycle: Days of inventory plus receivables minus payables. A longer cycle ties up cash, especially when firms buy components in advance for AI programs.
basics.terms.6
ROIC: Return on invested capital. EMS firms earn thin margins, so they depend on turning capital quickly to earn acceptable returns.
basics.terms.7
Free cash flow: Operating cash flow less capital spending. It swings with working capital, so fast growth can depress it even when profits rise.
basics.terms.8
Pass-through pricing: Charging customers for component cost changes. Where it works, component inflation lifts revenue but not profit.
basics.terms.9
Customer concentration: Share of revenue from the largest customers. A few large cloud customers can add growth but give them bargaining power.
basics.terms.10
Vertical integration: Making more of the product, such as enclosures, cables or power units, in-house. It lifts content per program and margin.
basics.terms.11
Footprint: The set of factories by country. Moving production close to customers, for example into the US or Mexico, is a response to tariffs and customer demands.
watch.0
Flex holds an Investor Day on 10 November and plans to spin off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure segment, which its fiscal 2027 guidance does not reflect.
watch.1
Whether the AI ramp converts as guided: Celestica sees 2027 revenue of $40.0B, up from $21.0B in 2026, but cut its 2026 free cash flow outlook to $460M from $600M.
watch.2
Memory and component costs and availability: ISM says supplier deliveries are slowing in computer and electronic products, and TrendForce says DRAM contract prices are still rising, more slowly.
watch.3
Customer concentration and working capital: Jabil's five largest customers were about 36% of fiscal 2025 revenue, and Sanmina's inventory rose to $3.15B from $1.99B.
watch.4
Rates and policy: the Fed held at 3.75-4.00% with two dissents favouring a hike, and Sanmina flags tariffs and Middle East conflict as risks.
bellwethers
Jabil, Flex, Celestica, Sanmina, Benchmark Electronics, Plexus, Fabrinet
fund.business.0

Revenue comes from manufacturing programs, design and engineering, supply-chain management and aftermarket repair. Jabil describes revenue from electronics design, production and product management services across three segments: Regulated Industries, Intelligent Infrastructure, and Connected Living and Digital Commerce. Most of the revenue billed in turnkey work is component cost passed through, so revenue is large relative to profit.
fund.business.1

Customers are brand owners that outsource manufacturing. Jabil's five largest customers were about 36% of fiscal 2025 revenue and 87 customers made up about 90%; one customer was 16%. Fabrinet's Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue split was data center 53%, communications 30% and automotive, industrial and other 17% on our arithmetic from its figures. Benchmark's Q3 mix included semi-cap 30% and industrial 21%.
fund.business.2

The principal cost is purchased components and materials, followed by labour, plant costs and depreciation. Benchmark's non-GAAP gross margin was 10.5% in Q3 2026 and Celestica's gross margin was 11.0%. That means about 89 to 90 cents of each revenue dollar is cost of sales, so small changes in yield, mix or component pricing move profit sharply.
fund.business.3

Pricing power is limited and rests on scale, quality certification, speed to ramp and the difficulty of moving a qualified program. Jabil lists cost, time-to-market, global locations, scaling, technology, quality and component pricing as competitive factors. Regulated and complex work earns more: Plexus's goal is a 6.5% to 7.0% non-GAAP operating margin in fiscal 2027.
fund.business.4

Major assets are inventory, receivables and plants; liabilities are payables, customer advances and debt. Sanmina's June 2026 balance sheet showed inventories of $3,152M, receivables of $1,987M and payables of $2,453M, with debt of $2,172M and customer advances of $1,150M. Jabil had debt of $3,379M and cash of $1,739M at 31 August 2026.
fund.business.5

The business is asset-light relative to semiconductors but working-capital heavy. Jabil's net capex was $470M on $35,954M of revenue, about 1.3% on our arithmetic. Capex is now rising at AI-focused firms: Celestica guides 2027 capex of $1.5B to $2.0B and Fabrinet is adding roughly $4B of capacity this fiscal year.
fund.overview.0

No authoritative market-size figure was available to us from the sources we opened; published estimates vary with scope. We size the group by its leaders: Jabil's fiscal 2026 revenue was $35,954M, Flex guides fiscal 2027 net sales of $33.7B to $35.2B, Celestica expects 2026 revenue of $21.0B, Sanmina guides fiscal 2026 to $14.0B to $14.3B.
fund.overview.1

Main segments are cloud and AI infrastructure, networking and communications, regulated industries (medical, aerospace and defence, automotive) and industrial. Jabil reports Regulated Industries, Intelligent Infrastructure and Connected Living and Digital Commerce; Celestica reports CCS and ATS segments, with CCS revenue of $4.87B; Flex is spinning off Cloud and Power Infrastructure.
fund.overview.2

EMS firms sit between component suppliers (chips, memory, boards) and brand owners. They buy parts in volume, assemble, test and ship. That puts them downstream of the memory market: TrendForce says DRAM contract prices are still rising in Q4 2026, though more slowly, and ISM reports slower supplier deliveries in computer and electronic products.
fund.overview.3

The industry moved from consumer and handset assembly toward higher-value work. Jabil now reports regulated and infrastructure segments rather than the older EMS and DMS split. Sanmina has added ZT Systems capacity and says it expects growth to ramp through fiscal 2027 and into 2028.
fund.overview.4

Production is global and concentrated in Asia, Mexico and the US. Jabil operates about 100 locations in 30 countries and has about 135 thousand employees, with 71 thousand in Asia. Fabrinet builds in Thailand, with $10B of revenue capacity planned by January. Flex operates in 30 countries.
fund.competition.0

There are several dozen EMS providers, but only a handful are large and listed in the US. Jabil faces domestic and foreign EMS providers, diversified manufacturing service providers and design providers, as well as customers' own factories. We did not find a sourced count of competitors.
fund.competition.1

Among the listed firms we opened, Jabil, Flex, Celestica and Sanmina are the largest by revenue. We did not open data on non-listed Asian rivals. A sourced global share table was not available to us, so we do not quote shares. Jabil's fiscal 2026 revenue was about 1.7 times Celestica's expected 2026 revenue on our arithmetic.
fund.competition.2

The industry is fragmented overall but concentrated at the top, and it consolidates through acquisitions. Sanmina bought ZT Systems' manufacturing, Flex bought Electrical Power Products, and Celestica and Jabil have expanded in AI systems. Specialists such as Fabrinet and Plexus hold niche positions in optical and regulated work.
fund.competition.3

Barriers to entry are moderate in basic assembly and high in regulated or complex work. Entrants need capital, qualified plants, quality certifications and customer trust, and Plexus's 36 new manufacturing wins in one quarter show that program wins are won one at a time. Basic board assembly can be copied by many smaller shops.
fund.competition.4

Scale matters in purchasing, global footprint and ability to fund inventory. Jabil funds $35,954M of revenue with $1,739M of cash and $3,379M of debt. Larger firms can pre-buy memory and chips for customers, which is difficult for small rivals when components are scarce.
fund.competition.5

Basic assembly is commoditized; system integration, optical, regulated and AI rack work is more differentiated. The spread shows in margins: Fabrinet's non-GAAP operating margin was 10.8% and Celestica's adjusted margin 8.5%, against Benchmark's 5.5% and Flex's 6.7%.
fund.competition.6

Customers hold most bargaining power because they can dual-source and some can build in-house. Cloud customers are especially large: Jabil's biggest customer was 16% of revenue. Component suppliers are strong when parts are short. Differentiated capabilities, such as Fabrinet's capacity and Celestica's AI systems, shift some power back to the EMS firm.
fund.drivers.0

Revenue growth follows customer unit demand and new program wins. In the latest quarters AI infrastructure is the dominant driver: Celestica grew 83%, Fabrinet's data-centre revenue grew 78%, and Jabil guides fiscal 2027 revenue to $44.5B, up 24%. Plexus guides mid- to upper-teens growth.
fund.drivers.1

Operating margins depend on mix, utilisation, yield and component pricing. Jabil's core operating margin was 5.8% for fiscal 2026 and is guided to 6.1% for fiscal 2027. Celestica guides a 9.0% adjusted margin for 2027 against 8.4% in 2026.
fund.drivers.2

Key cost variables are components (memory, chips, boards), labour in each country, freight, energy and tariffs. TrendForce says DRAM contract prices are still rising, and the ISM prices index was 75.2 in October, with prices up for 25 straight months. Where pricing is pass-through, margin dollars are protected but percentage margins are diluted.
fund.drivers.3

Interest-rate sensitivity runs through working capital and debt. The Fed held the target range at 3.75-4.00% and said inflation remains elevated. Sanmina carries $2,172M of debt against $1,845M of cash, while Benchmark's debt is about $158M. Higher rates also affect customers' capital spending plans.
fund.drivers.4

Inflation, GDP and industrial activity matter through customers' orders. ISM's manufacturing index was 55.5 and new orders 55.5 in October. Commodity prices matter through copper, metals and especially memory. We think consumer-linked programs are more exposed to unemployment than regulated or infrastructure programs.
fund.drivers.5

The group is cyclical, with defensive pockets. Programs can be cut quickly: Jabil notes that customers generally do not commit to firm production schedules beyond one quarter. Medical and aerospace and defence work is steadier, and AI infrastructure is currently a secular growth layer, though it depends on a few large buyers.
fund.financials.0

Growth is currently very high at AI-exposed firms and moderate elsewhere: Celestica 83%, Fabrinet 51%, Plexus fiscal 2026 23%, Jabil 21%, Flex 21%, Benchmark 19%. Over a full cycle growth is much lower, and Jabil's fiscal 2025 revenue grew only 3.2%.
fund.financials.1

Margins are thin. Damodaran's Electronics (General) group of 114 US firms shows a 26.76% gross margin and an 11.80% pre-tax, pre-stock-comp operating margin in January 2026, but it is a broad proxy that is far richer than EMS. Actual EMS margins: Jabil core operating margin 5.8%, Plexus 6.2%, Sanmina 8.0% in Q3.
fund.financials.2

Returns on capital are good at the leaders despite thin margins because capital turns quickly. Celestica's adjusted ROIC was 64.7% and Plexus earned 15.8% against a 9.0% cost of capital. Damodaran's Electronics (General) after-tax ROIC is 24.48%, normalized 17.47%, but its vintage is ambiguous. We did not find ROE figures.
fund.financials.3

Leverage is moderate. Jabil has $3,379M of debt and $1,739M of cash, roughly $1.6B net debt on our arithmetic. Celestica holds $3,961M of cash against $819M of borrowings, Benchmark $291M against $158M, and Sanmina $1,845M against $2,172M.
fund.financials.4

Free cash flow is positive but lumpy because working capital absorbs cash in growth. Jabil generated $1,532M of adjusted free cash flow in fiscal 2026; Celestica's was $412.5M over nine months; Benchmark's $64.9M; Plexus's Q4 was $6.4M; Flex's Q1 was $41M; Sanmina's Q3 was $24M.
fund.financials.5

Capital expenditure is low as a share of revenue but rising with AI. Jabil spent $628M gross on $35,954M of revenue, while Celestica spent $274M in the September quarter alone and guides 2027 capex of $1.5B to $2.0B. Benchmark's capex was $15.5M in Q3.
fund.financials.6

Multiples are modest compared with high-growth technology. Damodaran's January 2026 data show Electronics (General) at 19.99x EV/EBITDA and a 29.61x forward P/E against 27.66x for the total US market, but that group is a broad mix and ten months old. Current multiples for EMS were not available to us.
fund.risks.0

Trade and tax policy is the main regulatory risk. Sanmina lists tariffs and trade policy among its risk factors, and Flex lists tariff and trade tensions between the US and China and others. Rule changes can move production sites and customers' costs. Quality regulation in medical and defence adds compliance cost but also barriers.
fund.risks.1

AI is a demand source rather than a threat to EMS today, since it drives server, networking and optical builds. The risk is a pause in cloud capital spending: Sanmina names adverse changes in cloud and AI infrastructure as a risk, and Fabrinet's data-centre revenue is 53% of its total.
fund.risks.2

Demographic effects are indirect. An ageing workforce and labour costs in Asia and Mexico affect factory staffing and automation spending, and ageing populations raise medical-device demand, but none of the sources we opened quantify this.
fund.risks.3

Consumer and customer behaviour show up as order volatility. Jabil notes that customers do not commit to firm schedules beyond a quarter and can cancel or change orders. ISM respondents in computer and electronic products report customers optimising existing tools rather than buying new ones.
fund.risks.4

New competitors include Asian giants moving into the US and customers integrating production themselves. Jabil competes with customers' internal manufacturing. Sanmina's ZT Systems and Flex's power equipment are examples of EMS firms moving into higher-value areas, which changes who competes with whom.
fund.risks.5

Geopolitical and supply-chain risk is high. Sanmina cites Middle East conflict and tariffs, Flex cites Russia-Ukraine, the Middle East and US-China tension, and Fabrinet concentrates capacity in Thailand. Memory supply is tight: TrendForce says suppliers plan negative PC DRAM supply growth next year.
fund.risks.6

Substitutes are in-house manufacturing by customers and moving to vertically integrated suppliers, such as chip or server makers building their own capacity. Jabil names customers' internal manufacturing as a competitor. We found no sourced figure on how much volume is moving in-house, so this remains our judgment.
horizon.opportunities.0
AI infrastructure demand supports large forward guidance, with Jabil at $44.5B for fiscal 2027 and Celestica at $40.0B for 2027.
horizon.opportunities.1
Vertical integration into power, cooling and optical content can raise margins, as Flex's planned Cloud and Power spin-off and Fabrinet's $10B capacity plan indicate.
horizon.opportunities.2
Higher-margin regulated and aerospace work gives balance; Plexus targets a 6.5% to 7.0% non-GAAP operating margin in fiscal 2027.
horizon.opportunities.3
Onshoring and multi-region footprints could favour firms with plants near customers as trade policy stays unsettled.
horizon.threats.0
A pause in cloud and AI capital spending would hit the firms with the most exposure, such as Celestica and Fabrinet.
horizon.threats.1
Memory and component shortages delay shipments and absorb cash, and Celestica has already cut its 2026 free cash flow outlook.
horizon.threats.2
Tariff, export-control and geopolitical shocks can disrupt factories in Asia and cost-sharing with customers.
horizon.threats.3
Customer concentration lets a few large buyers push prices down or take work in-house.
horizon.assessment

We think the next three to five years favour EMS firms that can build complex AI systems, integrate power and optical content and fund the working capital. Guidance points to strong growth: Jabil expects fiscal 2027 revenue of $44.5B and Celestica $40.0B for 2027. The margin story is more modest, with Jabil guiding a 6.1% core margin, so returns come from asset turns rather than margin, as Celestica's 64.7% ROIC shows. The main risks are a cloud capital-spending pause, memory constraints, tariffs and customer concentration. Valuation data for EMS were not available, and the broader electronics proxy was above the market in January 2026.
sec.macro.0

The cycle is supportive for EMS customers. The ISM Manufacturing PMI was 55.5 in October 2026, up from 54.5, the tenth straight month of expansion, with new orders at 55.5 and inventories back in expansion at 51.4. Employment grew more slowly at 52.4. That is a favourable backdrop for firms that build products for industrial, medical and infrastructure customers.
sec.macro.1

Cost pressure is the counterweight. The ISM prices index was 75.2, with prices rising for 25 straight months, and computer and electronic products respondents reported slower supplier deliveries and customer inventories that were too low. TrendForce says DRAM contract prices are still rising in Q4 2026, though more slowly.
sec.macro.2

On policy, the Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October by a 10-2 vote, with two members preferring a quarter-point increase, and said inflation remains elevated. Our read is that rates mainly matter to EMS through working-capital financing. Sanmina cites tariffs and trade policy among its risks, and Flex lists US-China trade tension. We found no sourced currency data.
sec.demand.0

A reliable total market-size estimate for EMS was not available to us from the sources we opened, so we describe demand through company results and guidance. Jabil reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $35,954M and guides fiscal 2027 to $44.5B, up 24%. Celestica guides 2027 revenue of $40.0B and a 9.0% adjusted operating margin. Flex raised its fiscal 2027 net sales guidance to $33.7B to $35.2B.
sec.demand.1

The structural driver is AI and cloud infrastructure. Fabrinet's data-centre revenue was $777M, up 78%, and 53% of its total; Sanmina says it has strong demand for fiscal 2027 with growth ramping into fiscal 2028. Benchmark's semi-capital equipment sector was $241M, or 30% of its revenue.
sec.demand.2

Demand is cyclical and short-notice: customers generally do not commit to firm schedules beyond a quarter. Medical and aerospace programs are steadier. Demographics matter little except through medical devices. Our view is that long-term prospects are good but concentrated in a few AI-related programs, and the pace of cloud capital spending is the main unknown.
sec.structure.0

Porter's five forces point to a tough but workable industry. Rivalry is intense in basic assembly and moderate in complex work: Jabil says its business is highly competitive and competes with other EMS firms, diversified manufacturers, design providers and its customers' own plants. The threat of new entrants is moderate; qualification, quality systems and capital protect incumbents in regulated work.
sec.structure.1

Buyer power is high because customers can dual-source, and the largest buyers are big: Jabil's five largest customers were about 36% of revenue and one was 16%. Supplier power is high when components are short, with DRAM contract prices still rising. Substitutes, mainly customers manufacturing in-house, are a real limit on pricing.
sec.structure.2

Concentration is high at the top, but we could not source market shares. Consolidation continues, with Sanmina's ZT Systems deal and Flex's spin-off plan. Moats are scale, certification, long customer relationships and, increasingly, specialised capacity. Fabrinet's planned expansion to about $10B of revenue capacity by January is an example. Margins show that moats are modest: Jabil's core operating margin is 5.8%.
sec.environment.0

Politically, trade policy is the dominant factor. Sanmina lists tariffs and trade policy changes and Middle East conflict among its risks. Flex lists tariffs, sanctions and the US-China relationship, plus Russia-Ukraine and the Middle East. These matter because many programs are built in Asia and sold in the US and Europe, and costs depend on who bears duties.
sec.environment.1

Economically, input-cost inflation is live: the ISM prices index was 75.2 and DRAM contract prices are still rising. Technologically, AI drives demand for servers, networking and optical modules, and shifts value toward power, cooling and rack-scale integration, which is why Flex is separating its Cloud and Power Infrastructure segment.
sec.environment.2

Legal and regulatory factors include medical and defence quality rules, which raise barriers for regulated work, and tax-law changes, which Flex lists as a risk. Social and environmental factors, such as labour conditions, sustainability reporting and climate-related physical risks, are named in Flex's risk list. We did not find evidence that any single regulation is changing the economics of the group.
sec.economics.0

EMS economics are high revenue, thin margins and heavy turns. Jabil's fiscal 2026 core operating margin was 5.8% (GAAP 4.7%). Plexus earned 6.2% non-GAAP, Flex 6.7% adjusted, Benchmark 5.5% non-GAAP, Sanmina 8.0% non-GAAP, Celestica 8.5% adjusted and Fabrinet 10.8%. Damodaran's broad Electronics (General) group has a 26.76% gross margin, so it is not a good proxy for EMS.
sec.economics.1

Returns on capital are the redeeming feature. Celestica's adjusted ROIC was 64.7%, and Plexus earned 15.8% against a 9.0% cost of capital. Operating leverage is visible: Celestica's adjusted operating earnings rose to $496.1M from $242.2M on 83% revenue growth. We did not find ROE figures.
sec.economics.2

Free cash flow is real but variable. Jabil generated $1,532M of adjusted free cash flow in fiscal 2026, while Plexus's Q4 was only $6.4M and Flex's Q1 $41M, reflecting inventory build. Celestica cut its 2026 free cash flow outlook to $460M from $600M. Capital intensity is rising for AI capacity: Celestica guides $1.5B to $2.0B of capex in 2027.
sec.earnings.0

Reported earnings are strong. Jabil's fiscal 2026 core EPS was $13.09 and it guides fiscal 2027 to $17.55, up 34%. Celestica guides 2026 adjusted EPS of $11.55 and 2027 of $21.50. Flex raised fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS guidance to $4.42 to $4.74. Sanmina raised fiscal 2026 non-GAAP EPS guidance to $11.90 to $12.20 as of 27 July.
sec.earnings.1

Smaller and specialised names are also growing. Fabrinet's non-GAAP EPS was a record $4.34 and it guides the next quarter to $4.77 to $4.92. Plexus guides fiscal Q1 2027 non-GAAP EPS of $2.46 to $2.62 and mid- to upper-teens revenue growth. Benchmark expects Q4 non-GAAP EPS of $0.85 to $0.91.
sec.earnings.2

Consensus estimates for EMS were not available to us. FactSet reports blended S&P 500 Q3 2026 earnings growth of 30.2% and analysts expecting 28.4% for Q4. Our view is that guidance is already steep, so the question is delivery: Celestica's 2027 outlook implies revenue up about 90% on its 2026 outlook, and its cash flow outlook was cut. Note that Sanmina's fiscal Q4 actuals and Flex's fiscal Q2 are not yet in our sources.
sec.valuation.0

A forward multiple for the GICS sub-industry was not available to us. The best proxy is Damodaran's Electronics (General) group of 114 US firms, which in January 2026 traded at 19.99x EV/EBITDA for positive-EBITDA firms and a 29.61x forward P/E against 27.66x for the total US market. That group is a broad mix that includes component and device makers, and the data are ten months old.
sec.valuation.1

Market context is more current. FactSet reports the S&P 500 forward P/E at 18.7, below its five-year average of 19.8 and ten-year average of 19.1 as of the 30 October report. That is a market figure, not an EMS figure.
sec.valuation.2

We can derive one data point from the sources: Plexus repurchased shares at an average of $254.32 in Q4 against non-GAAP EPS of $2.84 for the quarter and guidance of $2.46 to $2.62 for the next. We do not extrapolate a multiple from that. Free-cash-flow yields were not available. Our read is that expectations are demanding because the guided growth, such as Celestica's 2027 EPS of $21.50, is steep, and we cannot say where the sub-industry sits against its own history.
sec.positioning.0
Positioning data for this sub-industry, including ETF flows, short interest, relative performance and price momentum, were not available to us from the sources we opened, so we do not quote any.
sec.positioning.1

What we can say rests on company actions and market context. Plexus repurchased $85.0M of shares in fiscal 2026 and has a further $100M authorisation for fiscal 2027, and Jabil repurchased $1,060M. Benchmark and Sanmina shared no comparable figures in the releases we opened.
sec.positioning.2

At market level, FactSet reports that companies with positive Q3 EPS surprises saw an average price change of 1.6% around the report, and those with negative surprises fell 2.1%. We think the group's momentum depends on delivery against steep AI-linked guidance, in particular Flex's investor day on 10 November and its planned spin-off, and Celestica's cash conversion. Breadth and revisions are not broken out for EMS in the sources we opened.
summary

Technology Distributors are in a boom that is absorbing cash. Latest-quarter sales rose 38% at TD Synnex, 39% at Arrow, 82% at Avnet (about 71% excluding an extra week), 21% at Ingram Micro and 30% at ScanSource, on AI infrastructure demand and, we think, higher component prices. Margins are thin and mixed: gross margin fell to 6.61% at TD Synnex and 6.55% at Ingram. Operating cash flow was negative at TD Synnex, Arrow and Avnet as receivables and inventory grew. Consensus and valuation for the sub-industry were not available to us; the S&P 500 trades at 18.7x forward earnings.
basics.intro

Technology distributors buy hardware, software, cloud services and electronic components in bulk from manufacturers and sell them on to resellers, system builders and manufacturers. They add logistics, credit, financing, configuration and technical support, and live on small percentage margins earned on very large sales. TD Synnex, Ingram Micro and ScanSource serve IT resellers; Arrow and Avnet serve electronics makers and also sell components. GICS also places IT resellers such as Insight here; we have not verified every constituent. Chip and device makers sit in other sub-industries.
basics.products.0

IT product distribution: Servers, PCs, networking, storage and software bought from vendors and sold to resellers and managed service providers, with credit and delivery. e.g. TD Synnex, Ingram Micro, ScanSource
basics.products.1

Electronic components distribution: Chips, passives, connectors and sensors supplied to equipment makers in small lots, often with design support and stocking programs. e.g. Arrow Global Components, Avnet Electronic Components, Farnell
basics.products.2

Enterprise computing and cloud solutions: Data-center, security and cloud offerings packaged with services and financing for corporate buyers and their resellers. e.g. Arrow ECS, Ingram Micro Cloud-based Solutions
basics.products.3
Hyperscale and custom systems: Building and integrating servers and racks to order for large cloud operators. e.g. TD Synnex Hyve Solutions
basics.products.4
IT reseller and services: Selling hardware, software and services directly to businesses, with cloud and consulting layers. e.g. Insight Enterprises
basics.products.5

Specialty and communications products: Barcode, payments, networking and communications equipment, plus telecom and cloud service brokerage. e.g. ScanSource Specialty Technology Solutions and Intelisys
basics.drivers.0
End-demand for IT and electronics: Distributor sales follow what customers spend on servers, PCs, networking and electronic equipment. Strong cycles lift sales within a quarter or two.
basics.drivers.1
Component prices and shortages: Rising chip and memory prices lift sales values, and shortages lengthen lead times and prompt double ordering, which can inflate sales until customers destock.
basics.drivers.2
Product mix: Large low-margin deals (GPUs, hyperscale racks) add sales but dilute gross margin, while services, cloud and components lift it.
basics.drivers.3
Working capital and financing costs: Faster growth ties up cash in inventory and receivables, forcing more borrowing. Higher interest rates then cut into thin operating profits.
basics.drivers.4
Vendor and customer concentration: A few vendors and customers account for large shares of sales, so program changes at one of them move revenue.
basics.drivers.5
Currency, tariffs and trade rules: Distributors invoice in many currencies and import across borders, so exchange rates and duties alter sales and costs.
basics.drivers.6
Acquisitions: Smaller specialists are bought to add capabilities or geography, lifting reported growth and, after integration, margins.
basics.terms.0

Gross billings: The total value of goods and services a distributor sells, before netting items such as software or cloud licences that are booked on a net basis. TD Synnex reports it as a non-GAAP measure.
basics.terms.1
Net vs. gross revenue: Some sales, such as software and cloud, are recorded as only the distributor's fee. A shift in mix therefore changes reported revenue growth and gross margin.
basics.terms.2
Gross margin: Sales minus the cost of products, as a share of sales. For distributors it is usually single digits for IT products and higher for components.
basics.terms.3
Operating margin: Operating profit as a share of sales. Because gross margin is thin, small cost changes move it a lot.
basics.terms.4
Working capital: Receivables plus inventory minus payables. Growth in sales ties up cash here, so profitable growth can still produce negative operating cash flow.
basics.terms.5
Return on working capital: Operating profit relative to the net money tied up in receivables and inventory. Avnet reports it as a headline efficiency measure.
basics.terms.6
Book-to-bill: Orders received divided by sales shipped. Above 1 means backlog is growing.
basics.terms.7
Backlog: Orders accepted but not yet shipped. A long backlog can reflect strong demand or supply that cannot keep up.
basics.terms.8
Lead time: The wait between ordering and receiving a part. Lengthening lead times often cause customers to over-order.
basics.terms.9
Line card: The list of suppliers a distributor represents. A broad line card helps customers buy in one place.
basics.terms.10
Floor-plan financing: Credit that lets resellers buy inventory from the distributor and pay later. It makes distributors lenders as well as sellers.
basics.terms.11
Supplier finance program: An arrangement where a manufacturer's receivables from the distributor are sold to a bank, usually giving the distributor longer payment terms.
basics.terms.12
Value-added distribution: Services beyond shipping, such as configuration, design help, financing and technical support, which earn higher margins than moving boxes.
watch.0
Fourth-quarter guidance: Arrow guides sales to $11.55-12.15B, TD Synnex to revenue of $21.8-22.6B and Avnet's December quarter to $11.1-11.4B, so any miss would show quickly.
watch.1
Working capital: operating cash flow was negative at TD Synnex (-$916.7M), Arrow (-$441.4M) and Avnet (-$842.4M) in the latest quarter, and Avnet's debt rose to $4.17B.
watch.2
Memory and PC demand: DRAM contract prices are still rising but gains are narrowing, while TrendForce reports weak PC demand and falling notebook shipments.
watch.3
Margin mix: large GPU and AI-infrastructure deals lower gross margin at Ingram Micro, and lower-margin hardware deals hurt ScanSource's specialty segment.
watch.4
Rates and trade policy: the Fed held at 3.75-4.00% with two dissents favoring a hike, and TD Synnex lists tariffs among its risks.
bellwethers
TD Synnex, Arrow Electronics, Avnet, Ingram Micro, Insight Enterprises, ScanSource
fund.business.0

Revenue comes from reselling products bought from manufacturers, plus smaller fees for services, financing and cloud or software brokerage. TD Synnex had $62.5B of revenue in fiscal 2025. Arrow splits into Global Components and Global ECS, Avnet into Electronic Components and Farnell, and Insight sells hardware (62% of Q3 net sales), software and services.
fund.business.1

Customers are resellers, integrators, managed service providers and equipment makers, not end consumers. TD Synnex counts more than 150,000 active reseller customers and about 2,500 vendors. Concentration is meaningful: one customer was 11% of its FY2025 revenue, and Apple and HP were 12% and 10% of revenue as vendors.
fund.business.2

The main cost is the product itself, so cost of sales swallows most revenue. TD Synnex's FY2025 gross margin was 6.99% and operating margin 2.26%. Selling, general and administrative costs (people, warehouses, credit losses) and interest on working-capital debt make up most of the rest. Insight spends more on services and sales staff, with a 21.4% gross margin.
fund.business.3

Pricing power is limited for commodity products because competition rests on availability, credit terms, price and delivery speed. It improves with value-added services and specialized components: Avnet's Farnell earned a 10.1% operating margin against 4.8% in its core components business. In shortages, distributors with allocation from suppliers gain leverage.
fund.business.4

The main assets are receivables and inventory, financed by payables to vendors and by debt. TD Synnex held $15.3B of inventory and $15.0B of receivables against $22.4B of payables at 31 Aug 2026. It also uses supplier finance programs and credit insurance. Debt: about $5.5B of borrowings against $0.75B of cash.
fund.business.5

The model is asset-light in plant and equipment but capital-intensive in working capital. Arrow's capex was $26.9M in the quarter against $10.7B of sales, yet growth consumed cash: its operating cash flow was -$441.4M. Money is tied up in stock and credit extended to customers, not factories.
fund.overview.0

No authoritative market-size figure for technology distribution was available to us. We size it by its leaders: TD Synnex $62.5B of FY2025 revenue, and a quarterly run-rate of $21.6B at TD Synnex, $10.7B at Arrow, $10.7B at Avnet and $15.2B at Ingram Micro. Gartner projects total 2026 IT spending of $6.37T, which is the broader pool distributors serve.
fund.overview.1

Main segments are IT products and services distribution (TD Synnex, Ingram Micro, ScanSource), electronic components (Arrow Global Components $7.94B and Avnet Electronic Components $10.13B in the latest quarter), enterprise computing and cloud (Arrow ECS $2.78B), hyperscale systems (TD Synnex's Hyve) and IT resellers such as Insight.
fund.overview.2

Distributors sit between manufacturers and the people who install or build with products. Upstream are chip, device and software makers; downstream are resellers, system builders and equipment makers. TD Synnex says most vendor agreements are nonexclusive and short-term, so the middle position depends on service rather than contracts.
fund.overview.3

The industry has moved from moving boxes to bundling services, cloud, financing and custom systems, and it has consolidated. ScanSource's fiscal 2027 outlook includes the MicroAge acquisition, closed 1 September 2026. TD Synnex names Hyve as a hyperscale business.
fund.overview.4

Activity is global and concentrated in the Americas, Europe and Asia. About 48% of TD Synnex's FY2025 revenue came from international operations. Avnet's latest quarter was $2.86B Americas, $2.74B EMEA and $5.12B Asia; Ingram Micro's was $5.8B North America, $3.9B EMEA, $4.3B Asia-Pacific and $1.1B Latin America.
fund.competition.0

There are a handful of global distributors and many regional ones. TD Synnex names Ingram Micro, Arrow and Westcon-Comstor as international rivals and ScanSource, ALSO Holding, Esprinet and VSTECS as regional ones, plus hyperscale rivals such as Jabil, Celestica, Flex, Quanta and Wiwynn.
fund.competition.1

By latest-quarter sales the leaders are TD Synnex ($21.6B), Ingram Micro ($15.2B), then Arrow ($10.7B) and Avnet ($10.7B, 14 weeks). Sourced market-share figures were not available to us, so we do not quote any. The IT-reseller specialist Insight reported $2.44B, and ScanSource says its sales grew 30%.
fund.competition.2

The group is concentrated at the top in each niche but fragmented overall, with regional specialists. We read the evidence as consolidating: ScanSource just bought MicroAge, and TD Synnex competes against a mix of other distributors and manufacturers.
fund.competition.3

Barriers to entry are credit capacity, scale in purchasing, vendor authorizations, logistics networks and risk management. Financing needs are visible in the numbers: TD Synnex has about $5.5B of borrowings and Ingram about $3.9B. A newcomer would need that balance sheet before it could win large vendor programs.
fund.competition.4

Scale matters for purchasing terms, warehouse use and the cost of credit. Ingram's operating margin is 1.93% and TD Synnex's is 2.98%, so fixed costs spread over huge volumes are what produce a profit. Smaller players such as ScanSource lean on specialty niches.
fund.competition.5

Commodity hardware is largely undifferentiated, and competition is on availability, credit terms, price and delivery. Differentiation comes from services, solutions and specialty products, as in Farnell's 10.1% operating margin, Insight's 21.4% gross margin and ScanSource's Intelisys services.
fund.competition.6

Bargaining power sits mainly with suppliers and large customers. A few vendors are large (Apple 12% and HP 10% of TD Synnex revenue) and can change programs; customers can switch for small price differences. In shortages, power moves to component makers, as TrendForce's description of an undersupplied memory market suggests.
fund.drivers.0

Revenue growth follows technology spending and prices. Gartner expects 2026 data-center systems spending up 62.5% and devices up 9.8%. The results reflect it: Ingram's Advanced Solutions rose 40% and Insight's hardware sales rose 32%. Component prices add to sales values when they rise.
fund.drivers.1

Operating margin is set by mix, scale and cost control. Ingram's gross margin was 6.55% against 7.06% without large GPU and AI deals. At Arrow, Components earned 5.2% and ECS about 3.5% operating margin on our arithmetic from its segment figures. Value-added services and specialty lines raise margins.
fund.drivers.2

Key cost variables are product cost, labor and freight, credit losses and interest. ScanSource booked a reserve for a Brazilian customer, Oi S.A.. Arrow expects about $50M of interest expense in the fourth quarter, showing that financing is a real cost line for a distributor.
fund.drivers.3

Interest-rate sensitivity is high because inventory and receivables are financed with debt. Avnet's debt rose to $4.17B and TD Synnex's borrowings are $5.5B. The Fed held its target at 3.75-4.00% and two members preferred a hike, which suggests financing costs will not fall soon.
fund.drivers.4

Inflation and GDP matter through IT budgets and component prices. The ISM prices index was 75.2 and the PMI 55.5, while DRAM contract prices keep rising. Gartner says rising hardware and memory costs are straining budgets. Unemployment matters little directly; business investment matters more.
fund.drivers.5

The industry is cyclical, with secular layers from cloud, AI and security. Arrow's interim chief executive cited modernization spending in AI, cloud and cybersecurity; TD Synnex cited enterprise AI adoption. Component distributors also swing with inventory cycles, so we think booms and busts are both amplified.
fund.financials.0

Growth is exceptional at present but cyclical. Latest-quarter sales rose 37.7% at TD Synnex, 39% at Arrow, 81.7% at Avnet (70.6% excluding the extra week), 20.8% at Ingram and about 30% at ScanSource. TD Synnex's fiscal 2025 growth was only 6.9%, so these quarters are far above the norm.
fund.financials.1

Gross margins are low: TD Synnex 6.61%, Ingram 6.55%, Avnet about 10.0%, Arrow about 10.8% and Insight 21.4%. Operating margins run from 1.93% at Ingram and 2.98% at TD Synnex to 4.0% at Arrow, 4.4% at Avnet and 6.8% adjusted at Insight.
fund.financials.2

Returns look decent for the capital used. Damodaran's Retail (Distributors) group (62 US firms) shows after-tax ROIC of 17.41% and a ten-year normalized 16.12% against 10.08% for the whole market. The group is broad: its gross margin of 30.57% is far above tech distributors, so it is only a loose guide. Its ROE was not on the page. Avnet reports a 25.2% return on working capital.
fund.financials.3

Leverage is moderate to high. TD Synnex has about $4.8B of net debt on our arithmetic from its balance sheet; Ingram has $3.9B of debt against $1.0B of cash; Avnet's debt is $4.17B against $5.28B of equity; Arrow has $2.64B of long-term debt and $7.19B of equity; ScanSource is near 2x trailing adjusted EBITDA.
fund.financials.4

Free cash flow is lumpy and turns negative in growth. TD Synnex's free cash flow was -$975.6M in the quarter and -$2,237.0M over nine months; Avnet's operating cash flow was -$842.4M; ScanSource's free cash flow was -$44M. Ingram generated $249.5M of adjusted free cash flow. Cash returns when sales slow and inventory unwinds.
fund.financials.5

Capital spending is light: Arrow spent $26.9M in the quarter, Avnet $24.3M and Insight guides to $20-30M for the year. The big uses of cash are working capital, acquisitions and shareholder returns, such as TD Synnex's $292.4M of nine-month buybacks and $0.48 quarterly dividend.
fund.financials.6

Multiples are low relative to the market for the broad group. Damodaran's January 2026 Retail (Distributors) EV/EBITDA was 13.71x against 19.73x for the whole market. Its forward P/E of 43.84x against 27.66x for the market looks distorted by low earnings in the group, and we do not rely on it. No sub-industry current multiple was available.
fund.risks.0

Trade policy and credit rules are the main regulatory risks. TD Synnex cites uncertainty over global trade policies and tariffs and Ingram lists tariff changes as a risk. Tariffs raise costs and can distort ordering. Export controls on advanced chips and GPUs, which drive Ingram's Advanced Solutions growth, are a further risk we think matters.
fund.risks.1

AI is a demand source today: Ingram's Advanced Solutions grew 40% and TD Synnex describes progress toward broader enterprise AI deployments. The risk is that GPU and server buying is lumpy, low-margin and concentrated with a few hyperscale customers, and that hyperscale builders such as Jabil, Celestica and Quanta compete with Hyve.
fund.risks.2
Demographics matter little directly. The nearest effect is labor: warehouses and service desks depend on workers, and automation is a long-term cost lever. We did not find a source quantifying this.
fund.risks.3

Customer behaviour is shifting toward cloud and subscription buying and away from owned hardware. Insight's software sales fell 3% while cloud gross profit grew more than 20%, and Ingram's cloud-based solutions grew 31%. TrendForce also reports weak PC demand and falling notebook shipments.
fund.risks.4

New competitors and models include vendors selling direct, cloud marketplaces and contract manufacturers moving into hyperscale systems. TD Synnex says its vendor agreements are nonexclusive and short-term, so a vendor can reroute volume. Consolidation also continues, as with ScanSource's MicroAge deal.
fund.risks.5

Geopolitical and supply-chain risks are material: Asia is $5.12B of Avnet's quarterly sales, memory supply is tight with suppliers planning negative PC DRAM supply growth. Supply shortages are listed among TD Synnex's risks. Customer credit risk also matters, as ScanSource's Brazil reserve shows.
fund.risks.6

Substitutes include direct vendor-to-customer sales, hyperscaler marketplaces and manufacturers' own channel programs. TD Synnex notes that supplier finance programs and credit are part of the offer, which direct sellers must replicate. We found no sourced measure of how much volume is moving away from distributors, so this remains our judgment.
horizon.opportunities.0
AI infrastructure and data-center spending: Gartner expects data-center systems spending up 62.5% in 2026, and TD Synnex's Hyve and Ingram's Advanced Solutions are ways to capture it.
horizon.opportunities.1
A growing mix of cloud, security and services can lift margins; Arrow's ECS sales rose 29% and Insight's cloud and core services gross profit each grew more than 20%.
horizon.opportunities.2
Semiconductor growth: WSTS forecasts the chip market to grow 26.6% in 2027 after 89.9% in 2026, supporting component distributors.
horizon.opportunities.3
Acquisitions that add specialist capabilities, such as ScanSource's MicroAge deal.
horizon.threats.0
An inventory correction: customers who over-ordered into shortages may stop buying, as component distributors have seen before; backlogs are growing and memory is undersupplied now.
horizon.threats.1
Working-capital strain and higher interest costs if growth continues and rates stay at 3.75-4.00% or rise.
horizon.threats.2
Margin dilution from large low-margin GPU deals and competition from direct and hyperscale channels.
horizon.threats.3
Tariff and export-control changes that raise costs or limit sales.
